PREFACE 
 
 I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Health and Family Welfare, have been authorized by the Committee to present the Report on 
its behalf, hereby present this 164th Report of the Committee on the Demands for Grants for 
the year 2025-26 (Demand No. 47) of the Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health 
and Family Welfare. 
 
2.  The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees are entrusted with the 
constitutional role of ensuring accountability of executive to the Parliament.  In this regard, 
Rule 270 (a) of Rules & Procedure and Conduct & Business in the Council of States (Rajya 
Sabha) empowered the Department-related Standing Committees to consider the Demands for 
Grants of the related Departments/Ministries with the objective of ensuring financial 
accountability of the executive and report thereon. In exercise of its constitutional mandate, 
the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health & Family Welfare 
scrutinised the Demands for Grants for the year 2025-26 (Demand No. 47) of the Department 
of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. The Committee, in its meeting, 
held on 14th February, 2025 heard the Secretary, Department of Health Research and other 
Officers on Demands for Grants (2025-26) of the Department. 
 
3.  The Committee while making its observations/recommendations has mainly relied 
upon the following documents:– 
(i) Detailed Demands for Grants (2025-26) of the Department of Health Research; 
(ii) Annual Report of the Department for the year 2023-24; 
(iii) Detailed Explanatory Note on Demands for Grants (2025-26) of the Department 
of Health Research; 
(iv) Output-Outcome framework 2025-26 for scheme of the Department of Health 
Research; 
(v) Projection of outlays for the schemes to be undertaken by the Department during 
the Financial Year 2025-26; 
(vi) Written replies furnished by the Department to the Questionnaires sent to them 
by the Secretariat; and 
(vii) Presentation made by the Secretary (Health Research) and other concerned 
officers, etc. 
4. The Committee, in its meeting held on 11th March, 2025, considered the draft report 
and adopted the same. 
 
5. For facility of reference and convenience, observations and recommendations of the 
Committee have been printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.

CHAPTER – I 
 
INTRODUCTION 
 
Health Research in India 
 
1.1 Health Research is primarily a guide to suggest improvements in the health care of the 
population of a country. Along with headway in healthcare delivery, well-directed research is 
essential to improve public health. In India, health research topography is highlighted as a 
potential market, fuelled by a large population, proactive government initiatives, rising public 
-private partnership, increased adoption of digital health technologies, recognition of 
importance of clinical trials, etc. At the same time, the challenges and gaps in the area 
include dearth of proper research culture, infrastructure deficiencies, inadequate funding for 
research initiatives, weak intersectoral linkages, misalignment between funded research 
areas and the country’s actual health needs, etc. 
 
Department of Health Research 
 
1.2 Department of Health Research (DHR) was created as a separate Department within the 
Ministry of Health & Family Welfare by an amendment to the Government of India 
(Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961 on 17thSeptember, 2007. The Department became 
functional with the aim is to bring modern health technologies to the people through research 
and innovations related to diagnosis, treatment methods and vaccines for prevention and to 
translate such innovations into products and processes in synergy with concerned 
organisations and stakeholders and finally introduce these innovations into public health 
system. 
 
Mandate of DHR 
 
 
1.2.1  As per the Secretary, DHR has ten Rules of Allocation of Business, essentially 
comprising of research - basic, applied or clinical, their promotion, conduct, governance and 
other aspects. The autonomous body, ICMR, is also under the administrative control of DHR.  
He informed the Committee that this year DHR has been allocated another business related to 
Health Technology Assessment as their eleventh allocation of business. Health Technology 
Assessment is conceived for Cost effectiveness of the technology developed related to

1.2.3 The Committee takes note of the allocation of a new Business to DHR in the form 
of Health Technology Assessment which will promote evidence-based decision making 
across the healthcare spectrum. An allocation of business suggests enhanced 
responsibility for managing the specific allocation, impacting its policy formulation, its 
implementation as well as coordination with other ministries. This also translates into 
additional financial implications like need for increased budgetary allocation to cover 
the new responsibilities, including staff recruitment, infrastructure development, 
etc. Accordingly, it is expected that DHR takes appropriate measures to continue to 
execute this crucial role and is also able to secure and utilise adequate allocation of 
funds for the work.

1.3.1 In this regard, the Committee sought to know whether the vacancy of almost 60% is 
not affecting the functioning/delivery of services by DHR and whether a work study of DHR 
has ever been conducted. In reply, the DHR stated that presently it has 62 sanctioned posts 
out of which 22 are recently created. These recently created posts include 15 posts of HTAIn 
and 7 posts of Ethics Committee. A proposal for encadrement of the 05 Central Secretariat 
Service posts among them has been sent to DoPT in February 2024. Further, the process for 
filling up the remaining posts of Scientists is underway and has been recently advertised in 
Employment News. With a view to create new posts and fill up vacant positions in DHR, the 
Department is making all efforts at regular intervals. In this regard, a proposal for creation of 
22 Central Secretariat Stenographer Service (CSSS) posts was also sent to DoPT for their no 
objection/ comments in April 2024. Further, a proposal for bifurcation of cadre between 
DoHFW& DHR was sent to DoPT in July 2024. Regular reminders are being sent to DoPT 
for filling up/ creation/encadrement of posts. The last reminder has been sent in the month of 
January 2025. The Committee is apprised that no work study has been conducted of 
Department of Health Research. 
1.3.2 The Committee in its earlier Reports, i.e, 127th, 132nd, 144th& 152nd Reports had taken 
up the issue of vacancies in the posts of Scientist C, D and E in DHR. The Department had 
earlier submitted that efforts are on for their filling up through the UPSC. Recently, in a 
written submission, the Department stated that 06 regular posts of Scientist C, D and E (02 
posts each) to be filled by Deputation (including short term contract). Subsequent, pursuant to 
DoPT notification dated 13.07.2023, wherein post up to level 13A to be filled by Deputation 
or Deputation (ISTC), were exempted from UPSC consultation. Subsequently, these posts 
were advertised and on the basis of the interview conducted by the Selection Committee, 02 
candidates for the post of Scientist C and 01 candidate for the post of Scientist D were 
recommended for selection. These selected candidates joined DHR in March 2024, however, 
incumbent for the post of Scientist D resigned due to personal reasons. Accordingly, the 
vacancies at the level of Scientist D and E have been readvertised and next iteration of the 
recruitment process is in advanced stage and interviews are to be conducted shortly. 
1.3.3  The Department also submitted that schemes under DHR include establishing Multi-
disciplinary Research Units (MRUs), Model Rural Health Research Units (MRHRUs), Viral 
Research and Diagnostic Labs (VRDLs) amongst others having position of Scientist C and D 
on contractual basis, which are currently approved for the 15th Finance Commission period up 

4 
 
to 2025-26. But the contractual scientists working in these schemes are not against any 
regular posts. Nevertheless, the Department is of the opinion that engagement of contractual 
personnel does affect the continuity of the implementation of the programs on their sudden 
departure from the Department.  
1.3.4 The Committee expressesdispleasure that the posts of Scientists of various grades 
in DHR have been lying vacant now for an unacceptably long time. Though, DHR is 
making continuous efforts to fill up these posts, but all have been in vain. It is 
understood that these posts were created in 2017 for specific roles within DHR but seem 
to have never been populated. The Committee has also been appraised in this context 
that contractual appointments of Scientists are being made in DHR which does affect 
the continuity of the implementation of the programmes on their sudden departure 
from the Department. In the considered opinion of the Committee, DHR has to walk the 
extra mile to fill up these posts on regular basis. One of the obvious ways to achieve is to 
make the conditions of service and/or remuneration more attractive to ensure that 
appointed scientists are to stay in DHR instead of deserting. Quicker/shortened 
recruitment process may be another avenue to be explored. Notwithstanding this, the 
Committee takes strong exception to the posts remaining vacant for so long and, 
therefore, the Committee recommends that urgent measures other than ordinary 
procedure to be taken to fill up the vacant posts. Further, Committee would like to put 
on record that adoption of stop gap management like contractual appointments to so 
significant posts of Scientists is totally unacceptable and ad-hoc approach and practise 
of contractual appointment should be discontinued. Contractual appointments to such 
posts that inherently warrant continuity, as a critical prerequisite for their effectiveness, 
would jeopardise the very success of the tasks for which the scientists are engaged.     
1.3.5 Taking into account the requirement of professionals having good scientific astuteness 
in the emerging field of Health Research, the Committee asked about the plans of the 
Government regarding any programme to incentivize Indian researchers working abroad to 
return and contribute to health research in India and also about the programme to encourage 
young scientists and researchers to pursue careers in health research. In response the 
Department has informed about the program “to encourage research personnel [Non-resident 
Indian (NRI), Persons of Indian Origin (PIO), Overseas Citizen of India (OCI)] serving 
abroad, to come back to India for undertaking research in identified areas”. This Scheme has 
been designed to provide contractual research positions to the Indian scientists and 
researchers settled abroad who are willing to come back to India on a full-time basis or for a 
short duration to pursue medical/health research in India and take up health research projects 
in collaboration with Indian scientists, particularly in areas of national health priority. Each 
selected researcher shall be eligible to receive a consolidated stipend of Rs.1.2 lakhs per 
month for 3 years. Research Grants would be available for research studies/projects not 
exceeding Rs. 20 lakhs/year. The project will be extendable for another 2 years at the 
discretion of the Secretary DHR on the recommendation of the Expert Committee. In case the 
researcher finds a permanent position during the tenure of the position, the remuneration shall 
be discontinued from the day he/she joins in permanent position, but he/she may continue 
with the Research Grant for the project, for the remaining duration of the project.  

5 
 
1.3.6 The Committee takes note of the program envisaged by the Department to 
attract Non-resident Indians (NRIs), Persons of Indian Origin (PIO), Overseas Citizens 
of India (OCI) serving abroad back to India. At the same time, the Committee expresses 
its concerns about continuing Brain Drain, the exodus of trained, proficient and talented 
Indian professionals to developed countries. India's brain drain is caused by a lack of 
higher education options, research funding and facilities, pay & perks that is lower than 
global standards in both the public and private sectors and fewer opportunities in terms 
of career progression, especially in specialized fields. Other facilitative factors like 
environment of equity, transparency, protection of ownership of genuine research 
outcomes, delayed systemic response, etc also add to contributing factors.   
1.3.7 The Committee, even though aware of the funding limitations, is not fully 
convinced of the adequateness of a consolidated stipend of Rs.1.2 lakhs per month for 3 
years for a selected researcher under the Scheme to attract professionals from abroad. 
The Committee feels that the Department should consider keeping the window open to 
enhance the quantum of stipend, at least based on the project proposals presented and 
the remuneration the person is receiving in the foreign country. The same flexible 
approach should be adopted in case of the quantum of grant, the Committee desires.  
Accordingly, to address the intricate issue of brain drain, India must adopt a 
comprehensive strategy that includes enhancing higher education, strengthening 
research infrastructure, and implementing policies to improve the standard of living. 
These measures would encourage skilled Indian professionals to return from abroad 
and undertake domestic health research projects. A unified and long-term approach is 
essential for India to retain and recover its most valuable asset—human capital. 
1.3.8 Further, the Department should look into the possibility of involving private 
sector which can contribute through competitive pay packages, which would be well 
within their realm as promotion of PPP.  
Landmarks in Health Research in India 
 
1.4 Certain landmark outcomes or breakthroughs achieved during the last decade in the 
area of health research in India, funded by the Government of India are as follows: 
A. Communicable Disease 
i. Enabling rapid containment and response strategies to outbreak and pandemic 
investigations for Monkeypox, Zika, and Nipah.  
ii. Development of Covaxin, India’s first fully indigenous COVID-19 vaccine, in an 
exemplary public-private partnership (PPP) with Bharat Biotech.  
iii. National Sero Surveys for COVID-19, tracking the virus's spread and informing 
public health policies.  
iv. Indian SARS-CoV-2 Genomics Consortium (INSACOG) contributed to genome 
sequencing for identifying Variants of Concern, shaping India’s pandemic 
response. 

6 
 
v. Transformative initiatives in tuberculosis (TB) control, through the India TB 
Research Consortium (ITRC), which won the prestigious Kochon Prize. Key 
innovations include National TB Survey, newer drug regimens for DR-TB, rapid 
molecular testing with TruNAT, the C-TB test, and the TIE-TB project, which 
won the BMJ Award for its innovative active case finding model. 
vi. Research on the Triple Drug Regimen (IDA) and DEC-fortified salt, significantly 
reducing Filariasis transmission.  
vii. The Vaishali Model for Kala Azar elimination demonstrated a successful 
intervention strategy in eliminating the disease.  
viii. For Malaria, ICMR’s research has demonstrated elimination models in Madhya 
Pradesh, Odisha, and Punjab, guiding India’s national malaria elimination 
roadmap. 
B. Non- Communicable disease (NCD) 
i. The India Disease Burden Study, conducted in collaboration with the Indian 
Council of Medical Research (ICMR), Public Health Foundation of India (PHFI), 
and Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME), provided crucial insights 
into the shifting burden of diseases in India, highlighting the growing prevalence 
of NCDs.  
ii. The National Cancer Registry Program (NCRP) instrumental in tracking cancer 
incidence, mortality, and trends across India. 
iii. The Indian Diabetes Study (InDIAB) has gathered epidemiological data from 22 
states critical for formulating preventive and management strategies.  
iv. The India Hypertension Control Initiative (IHCI), implemented across 104 
districts, integrated hypertension screening into primary healthcare, earning global 
recognition with a UN Award for its impact on reducing cardiovascular risk.  
v. The Stroke Network, aimed at improving stroke surveillance, prevention, and 
treatment outcomes, ensuring timely interventions for stroke patients.  
C. Reproductive Health, Child Health & Nutrition 
i. Invention of RISUG, a male contraceptive.  
ii. The subdermal, single-rod contraceptive implant IMPLANON for long-term birth 
control options.  
iii. Formulation of Balamrutham and Balamrutham Plus for Telangana and Andhra 
Pradesh to combat malnutrition.  
iv. Additionally, the Vitamin A Prophylaxis Program critically analysed the need for 
Mega-dose Vitamin A Supplementation (MDVAS), leading to a recommendation 
for targeted supplementation instead of universal coverage. 

7 
 
v. The Dietary guideline for Indians, revised Recommended Dietary Allowances 
(RDA) and the report on "What India Eats" provide scientific evidence on dietary 
patterns.  
vi. The Indian Food Composition Tables offer comprehensive nutritional data, while 
the District Level Nutrition Project and urban nutrition data collection help 
policymakers address regional disparities in malnutrition. 
vii. The Women and Infant Integrated Interventions for Growth (WINGS) study 
demonstrated that integrated interventions in health, nutrition, psychosocial care, 
and Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WaSH) during preconception, pregnancy, and 
early childhood substantially reduced low birth weight and stunting at 24 months. 
viii. Development of The Nutrition Atlas 2.0 serves as a one-stop digital platform that 
provides interactive access to national nutrition data.   
ix. The Nutrify India Now 2.0 mobile app, an advanced version with updated 
Estimated Average Requirement (EAR) and Recommended Dietary Allowance 
(RDA), integrates wearable devices for personalized diet tracking, to dynamically 
create recipes, monitor nutritional intake, and maintain a personal diet diary. 
D. Innovative initiatives 
The i-Drone project - using drones to transport vaccines & medical supplies in the 
challenging terrains of the North Eastern States and Himachal Pradesh, blood 
bags in metros, Intra-operational tissue samples for advanced diagnosis in 
Karnataka & TB sputum samples in tribal regions of Telangana. 
1.4.1 While going through the major landmarks in Health Research in India in the 
last decade, the Committee notices that the India has done considerably well in the 
field of Communicable Diseases, commensurate to its own needs as well as to 
contributing the global knowledge pool. The Committee is appreciative of this 
achievement. The India Disease Burden Study, mentioned by the Department as a 
breakthrough initiative, provided crucial insights into the shifting burden of diseases 
in India, highlighting the growing prevalence of Non-Communicable diseases (NCDs). 
Going by the indicators provided by the Study, India’s efforts in NCDs needs further 
impetus. 
1.4.2 Accordingly, the Committee observes that the policies, priorities and funding for 
health research in the country should be optimally aligned with its actual health needs 
rather than with the global research agenda. Hence, India should prioritise research on 
under-studied diseases in the country, such as cardiovascular, respiratory diseases, etc. 
along with research on public health, healthcare infrastructure/systems and 
implementation of clinical medicine. The Committee feels that alignment of health 
research with the National Health Policy & Priorities would be cardinal in this direction 
and hence recommends, accordingly. 
 

8 
 
 
Role of public-private partnerships (PPPs) in Health Research Funding 
1.5 Taking into cognizance the successful Public-Private Partnership (PPP) of ICMR 
with Bharat Biotech which led to the development of Covaxin, India’s first fully indigenous 
COVID-19 vaccine, the Committee sought to know about the current scenario regarding the 
private funded health research in India and the measures adopted by the Government to 
encourage PPP for health research in India. In reply, DHR submitted that Public private 
partnerships are pivotal for development of innovations. Despite absence of an institutional 
mechanism for PPP, ICMR has successfully completed several projects under public private 
partnerships.  The Department submitted that ICMR proposes a multi-faceted strategy to 
encourage private funding for health research in India, recognizing the critical role of PPPs, 
Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) contributions, and Venture Capital investments in 
advancing medical innovations. To attract CSR funds, ICMR is engaging with Corporates 
and PSUs to allocate a greater share of their CSR budgets toward priority research areas, 
including vaccines, antimicrobial resistance (AMR), rare diseases, and AI-driven healthcare 
solutions. To facilitate greater industry participation, ICMR also supports technology 
transfer and licensing agreements, allowing private firms to commercialize ICMR-
developed innovations under fair pricing mechanisms.  
1.5.1 The Committee reckons that since the Government is always under compulsion 
to apportion the limited financial resources amongst the varied needs of the country, it 
would be prudent to leverage the financial resources, technological expertise and 
innovation capabilities of the Private sector in furthering the needs of the health 
sector, especially in research. The Committee holds the view that when cutting edge 
research and innovation outcomes, produced in collaboration with the Private sector, 
are dovetailed with policy initiatives and wide access infrastructure of the 
Government, it can change the health care landscape of India. Taking into account the 
fact that promotion of public-private partnership is one of the businesses allocated to 
DHR as per the Allocation of Business Rules of the Government of India. The 
Committee recommends that the Department should consider adopting more 
measures to secure the participation of the Private sector in the health sector in the 
Country with tailor made collaborative and mutually beneficial outreach measures. 
1.5.2 The Committee notes that while on the one hand DHR acknowledges the 
importance of Public Private Partnerships (PPPs) for the development of innovations 
and informs that ICMR has successfully completed several projects under PPP mode, 
there is an absence of an institutional mechanism for PPP. In view of the submission of 
DHR and the fact that promotion of PPP is one of the businesses allocated to DHR as 
per the Allocation of Business Rules of the Government of India, the Committee 
recommends that DHR should come out with an institutionalised mechanism for 
promoting PPP.  
Emerging Technologies and Ethical Concerns related to Health Research 

9 
 
1.6 In the emerging world of AI-driven healthcare solutions, database is crucial, hence 
the Committee was curious to understand the current ethical challenges in research, such as 
informed patient consent, data privacy and its impact on health research landscape in India. 
The Committee also wanted to know the steps taken by Government to ensure ethical 
compliance without compromising innovation, especially when vulnerable populations are 
involved. In their written submission in this regard, the Department shared the various steps 
taken to ensure ethical compliance and to encourage innovation while protecting the rights 
and safety of all, including the vulnerable.  The ICMR National Ethical Guidelines 2017 
established the ethical framework for health research in India. All biomedical and health 
research conducted in the country must follow these guidelines to address ethical concerns 
that may arise including participant consent and data privacy.  
1.6.1 Further, New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019 govern the conduct of Clinical 
Trials, Biomedical and Health Research, Academic Clinical Trials, Bio Availability/Bio 
Equivalence studies, etc., primarily to ensure robust conduct of clinical trials for the 
purpose of approvals to introduce new products in the Indian market with right ethics 
safeguards. The regulatory architecture involved may be summarised as under: 
(i) Registration of Ethics Committees: To ensure ethical compliance and functioning 
of ethics committees, it is mandatory that all ethics committees involved in biomedical 
and health research be registered with the Department of Health Research (Naitik portal) 
and also with Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (SUGAM portal) if 
applicable. This helps to improve transparency and accountability of the ethics review 
process. 
(ii) Ethics Approval: As per the established rules and guidelines, prior approval from 
the relevant ethics committees is mandatory before commencing any biomedical and 
health research. This is to protect the rights, safety, dignity and welfare of research 
participants in any biomedical health research or clinical trials. 
(iii) Protection of Vulnerable: The ICMR National Ethical Guidelines, 2017 provides 
an ethical framework and specifically Chapter 5 of this guidelines outlines the informed 
consent process, while Chapter 6 addresses ethical considerations for research involving 
vulnerable populations, emphasizing measures to safeguard their rights, safety and well-
being. Clinical; and 
(iv) Trials Registry of India: ICMR-CTRI Today, is another initiative to improve 
transparency, accountability, and accessibility of clinical trials in order to re-establish 
public trust in clinical trial data. All clinical trials are required to be prospectively 
registered in a centralized clinical trials registry. 
1.6.2 The Committee recognises the importance of adoption of new technologies, 
innovation and constant endeavour for development of new drugs and treatment 
methods. Clinical trials are an inalienable data generating component of this 
continuing quest. The regulatory architecture now in place in the Country are taken 
note of, however, the Committee would like to emphasise the need to ensure 
‘informed’ consent of the participants of clinical trials which should invariably include 
sharing of information beforehand about how the data generated out of the trial would 

10 
 
be used or shared. It is important to ensure that the participants fully understand the 
risks and benefits of a study, management of sensitive personal information and 
balancing the need for research advancement with individual privacy rights. 
Digitalization and sharing of patient information bears privacy implications that needs 
to be addressed and fixed with appropriate provisions.  
1.6.3 The Committee also wanted to know about the steps taken to leverage new 
technologies like AI in health research in India along with the funds earmarked. The 
Department replied by stating that research is a crucial component for developing India-
specific AI-based solutions for strengthening the healthcare system in the country, with an 
overarching goal of achieving Universal Health Coverage. ICMR has mandated one of its 
institutes (ICMR-NIMS) in Delhi to cater to this objective, and it has been repurposed as 
ICMR-National Institute for Research in Digital Health and Data Science (ICMR-
NIRDHDS) in April 2024. A key vision of the institute is to innovate and develop low-cost 
AI-based technologies which can be translated and integrated into the health system at all 
the levels of healthcare. 
1.6.4 The Committee notes that the Government has taken a key step in setting up 
ICMR-National Institute for Research in Digital Health and Data Science and 
entrusting it with the task of developing India-specific AI-based solutions for 
strengthening the healthcare system with an overarching goal of achieving Universal 
Health Coverage. The Committee finds research in Digital Health and Data Science as 
one of the areas that can be prioritised for collaboration with domain leading private 
sector organisations. The Committee observes that the Department should explore the 
possibility to further augment the efforts in this direction. The Committee in this 
connection recommends that adequate money is allocated to ICMR-NIRDHDS for its 
new responsibility. In this regard, the Committee emphasises the all-important need to 
protect data, personal as well as research based, while developing AI based solutions.

2.1.4 The Committee perceives research in health to be of pivotal importance. 
Solution based core research aligned with the goals associated with the national health 
priorities would be way forward of DHR. The Committee notes that DHR has taken 
cognisance of the Viksit Bharat aim and has accordingly established goals related to 
the field of Health Research. As part of which the Department has envisaged a 
structured approach towards the attainment 6 goals of specific activities in 5-year 
period of 2024-2029. However, the Committee notes with concern that the gap between 
the funds sought by DHR is getting widened since 2024-25. This gap between the 
projected demand and allocation of funds has increased from Rs. 575.09 crore during 
2025-25 to Rs. 1069.34 crore during 2025-26. From the submissions of the Department, 
it is but natural to infer that their activities, including the ones towards the attainment 
of the Viksit Bharat goals, are going to be adversely affected by the dearth of funds. 
The Committee notes in this regard that the fund utilisation by DHR reflects a decent 
percentage of 87 and above over the years, hence, it is imperative that DHR has 
enough justification to lay claim for higher budgetary allocation.  At the same time, 
the Committee appreciates the counter balancing efforts on the part of the 
Department to manage their project with the allocated funds. 
2.1.5 It is the firm view of the Committee that health research has to be accorded 
higher priority by the Government than being given during recent years. Accordingly, 
the assurance of the Ministry of Finance to consider granting Rs.600.00 crore in RE 
for 2025-26 is not enough.  The Committee, accordingly, strongly recommends that the 
total funds as projected by DHR may be allocated an additional fund in the BE 2025-
26 itself and if not so, surely at least at RE stage. This is being recommended under the 
premise that DHR would continue to walk the talk and execute their schemes and 
programmes as per the book. The Committee desires that DHR should pursue with the 
Ministry of Finance with due diligence so that budgetary allocation to DHR must 
match with the projected demand.

2.2.4 The Table above shows that the budgetary allocation to the DHR remained constant 
at 0.02% of the GDP during the last five years. In this regard, the Committee enquired the 
Department about the management of health-related research projects with such lower 
allocation. In reply, DHR informed that National Health Priority related research projects 
were given preference. For product development, the industry and international partnerships 
were sought. Emphasis was placed on high-impact projects. Ongoing projects were 
critically monitored & reviewed, and funds were reallocated to ensure that essential 
programs, including disease surveillance, vaccine research, and translational research, 
remain unaffected. 
 
2.2.5 The Committee observes that the BE 2025-26 of Department of Health Research 
(DHR) at Rs 3900.69 crore is just 3.91 % of the Total Health Budget. Also, DHR got 
only 4.06% of the BE allocation of Department of Health & Family Welfare 
(DoH&FW) 2025-26, i.e., Rs 95,957.87 crore. Further, the Committee observes that 

14 
 
over the last five years, there has been no major change in the quantum of budgetary 
allocation for health research, which is still only 0.02% of the GDP. The Committee 
understands that public funding is the primary source of fund for meeting the 
expenditure on health research in India, therefore, the crucial role of healthcare 
research in advancing public health is undeniable.  The Committee expresses anguish 
over low budgetary allocation to health research as in the opinion of the Committee, for 
a country of almost 1.5 billion people, the existing trend of quantum of budgetary 
allocation over the years is abysmally low. 
 
2.2.6  Further, the Committee is given to understand that the Department, keeping 
the limited allocation in mind, is compelled to redefine its priorities like assigning 
preference to National Health Priority and high-impact research projects, adopting 
PPP mode for product development, regular monitoring, reviewing & reallocation 
funds for ongoing projects and essential programs, etc. The counter balancing 
measures of the Department points to the crunch of funds they are facing. In this 
regard, the Committee unanimously affirm that health research is fundamental to the 
future development of the country's healthcare system and should remain a priority 
sector. Hence, the Committee fully appreciates the efforts of DHR in their recalibration 
of projects and funds to attain optimal results and extends full in their efforts in 
securing additional fund. 
 
2.2.7  The Committee, in its 127th Report on Demand for Grants for 2021-22 of 
DHR had recommended that at least 5% of the budget of the DoH&FW should be 
allocated to DHR. The Committee also recommended the Department to set an aim to 
allocate 5% of the Total Health Budget for health research in the next two years. The 
Committee is displeased to note that even after a lapse of four years none of the above 
recommendations of the Committee has been complied with.Accordingly, the 
Committee expresses its disappointment and strongly reiterates its earlier 
recommendation and lends its support to the Department in its pursuance with Ministry 
of Finance in procuring enhanced allocation. 
 
2.2.8  Further, the Committee also found that no major financial documents of 
the Government of India like the Economic Survey outline the specific allocation of 
fund for Health Research in India. Hence, the lowly 3.91% of allocation for research 
in health sector, in comparison to the Total Health Budget, gets drowned in the larger, 
more projectable figures of DoH&FW. In the considered opinion of the Committee, 
the change in approach of the Government towards according more impetus to Health 
Research should begin from highlighting the money allocated over the years for 
Health Research prominently in important financial documents and indicators. Such 
indicators reflect the importance being accorded by the Government to the health 
sector and help in understanding the trajectory of growth in the health research. 
 
2.2.9 Considering global standards with respect to investment in health research, the 
Committee recommends that the Government must aim to invest at least 0.1% of the 
GDP in the next five years.

project/scheme/programme and ensuring successful implementation thereof.  Such 
reviews should take into account the emerging information, changing priorities or 
unforeseen circumstances, often requiring modifications to timelines, budgets, 
strategies, or resource allocations. The Committee is pleased to observe that the 
Department has oriented their activities to utilise their enhanced allocation. 
Accordingly, the Committee views the plans made by DHR positively and is optimistic 
about the results coming out in tune with the plans chalked out.  
 
2.3.6 The Committee, however, finds that under some schemes, the funds sought by 
DHR for the year 2025-26 have been curtailed citing the reason that only the 
remaining amount approved by the Standing Finance Committee (SFC) for the 15th 
Finance Commission period has been allocated. The Committee finds the given reason 
untenable as it comes in the way of much needed continuance of the beneficial 
activities of the schemes beyond the 15th Finance Commission period. In the 
Committee's view, such situations exemplify the classic case of 'red tape' causing 
financial constraints that hinder development. Accordingly, the Committee 
recommends that situations where genuine need for funds cannot be met due to 
procedural pre-requisites should be avoided in future. Further, the Committee wants 
to be apprised about the results of the recalibrated activities/targets under each 
scheme.

2.4.1 The DHR, has apprised that the Committee about the details of underutilization of 
allocated funds highlights that there have been savings of Rs. 342.89 crore in 2022-23 and 
‘savings’ of Rs. 35.36 crore in 2023-24. Again, in the FY 2024-25 against the RE allocation 
of Rs. 3391.64 crore the actual expenditure till 31.01.2025 is to the tune of Rs. 3118.26 crore, 
albeit, it has been stated that the since expenditure is still in progress and it is expected that 
full amount of RE will be utilized.  
 
2.4.2 On the underutilization of allocated funds, the Committee raised a query whether DHR 
has revisited the reasons for underutilization of funds, and the precautionary measures taken 
to ensure the rational and optimal utilization of allocated funds within the stipulated 
timeframe. In reply, it was submitted that the ‘savings’ primarily were attributed to the PM-
ABHIM Scheme. The funds earmarked for the procurement of COVID-19-related items 
remained unutilized due to improved COVID-19 conditions. Delays in the execution of 
tendering for construction activities for establishing four regional National Institutes of 
Virology and the National Institute of One Health contributed to the ‘savings’. Additionally, 
the establishment of Regional Research Platform were also not executed due to non-signing of 
MoUs with partnering countries. According to the Department, the reasons have been duly 
communicated and explained during the relevant year of appropriation of accounts. On the 
precautionary measures, it was informed that Monthly Budget Review meetings are held at 
the level of the Secretary &DG, ICMR foe specific review of pace of expenditure and 
utilization of funds incurred by the institute. 
 
2.4.3 The Committee observes that the utilisation of funds by the Department during 
2022-23, 2023-24 and 2024-25 has been 87.64%, 98.78% and 91.94%, respectively, 
compared to the RE funds, which is reasonably appreciative. Utilisation under 

35 
 
Secretariat head has been consistently lower than expected. Further, uptake of funds 
under International Cooperation has been abysmal. The Committee expects the 
Department to optimally utilized the earmarked budgetary allocation under full proof 
monitoring mechanism. 
 
2.4.4 The Committee takes into account the reasons stated by the Department for 
‘savings’ of funds in the last three years. On the delay in the execution of tendering for 
construction activities for establishing four regional National Institutes of Virology, the 
Committee finds that the expected date of completion is between December 2025 and 
July 2026. Regarding, the establishment of Regional Research Platform, the Committee 
observes that MoUs have been signed by ICMR with Nepal, Thailand and Myanmar. 
MoU on Cooperation in the Field of Health and Medicine has been renewed with 
Bangladesh in June 2024 and implementing agreement with MoH Maldives is under 
process. On both the issues, the Committee hold the Department to adhere to the 
deadline and not end up again surrendering the fund as ‘savings’ for the current 
financial year.  
 
2.4.5 The Committee is of the view that the underutilisation of allocated funds and 
indication of underspent funds under different heads as ‘Savings’ makes a reflection 
over the working of DHR. As per the Committee, savings happen only when an 
activity is curtailed than originally conceived plan.  The Committee, therefore, to do 
away the reflection mounting due to unutilised funds, recommends that DHR should 
enhance the implementing capability of the executing agency and the absorption 
capacity of the scheme/projects/programme to ensure its completion without time and 
cost overruns and achieving the set objectives as per plan. 
 
2.4.6 While analysing the demands of DHR, the Committee asked the Department 
whether they maintain any utilisation disciple of funds keeping in mind the Fiscal 
Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) limits on expenditure. In response, the 
Department informed that FRBM limits are observed at the level of Ministry of Finance. 
The allocation made for the Department of Health Research is done keeping in mind the 
FRBM limits.  
2.4.7 The Committee notes that allocation made for the Department of Health 
Research is done keeping in mind the FRBM limits. However, it has also been brought 
before the Committee that certain financial restrictions associated with last 
quarter/month of financial year hampers the progress of a research 
project/programme. Research involves organic development which cannot be shackled 
with financial stipulations. Hence, the Committee hopes the Department would seek 
their allocation management with Ministry of Finance, accordingly. In this regard, 
seeking the guidance of the good office of Principal Scientific Advisor would not be 
inappropriate.

2.5 The Committee observes that during FY 2023-24 & 2024-25, there have been a 
reduction of funds at RE stage under the Head - Secretariat and Actual Expenditure (AE) for 
FY 2023-24 reflects an even less utilization of funds. DHR was requested to submit the 
reasons for this variation in the budgetary allocation. As stated by DHR, the reasons for 
reduction in funds at the RE stage for FY 2023-24 and 2024-25 and actual expenditure 
during FY 2023-24, the DHR stated that the Department had kept a provision for the salary 
and remuneration of the vacant positions of regular/ contractual staff in anticipation of their 
being filled up. However, as the positions continued to be vacant, the reduced expenditure 
resulted in reduction in funds at the RE stage and Actual Expenditure. The low expenditure 
under heads such as Medical Treatment and Leave Travel Concession etc was due to less 
staff strength. Savings under Domestic Travel expenses was due to shifting of meetings 
from physical mode to online mode. Also, DHR functions from rented office premises of 
Indian Red Cross Society (IRCS) Building and the rent was paid at a reduced rate which 
resulted in savings under the head of Rent, Rates and Taxes. 
2.5.1 Further, for the FY 2025-26, the demand raised under the head is much less than the 
previous years. DHR was requested to explain the reasons and also state the impact of this 
reduction of funds. As per DHR, the overall budget allocation for RE 2024-25 and BE 2025-
26 for DHR has been reduced at RE stage seeing the trends for Secretariat expenditure till 
30.09.2024. The reduced demand during FY 2025-26 is primarily on account of freezing of 
the rent after increment of 3% from 2023-24 onwards in comparison to the earlier rate of 
increment @10% per annum. Any shortage of funds under the Secretariat head during the 
FY 2025-26 can be fulfilled at the RE stage. 
2.5.2 Regarding the Capital Expenditure in BE 2025-26, there is a capital expenditure of 
Rs. 1.15 crores under the Secretariat head.  DHR furnished that the capital expenditure of 
Rs.1.15 Crores is proposed under the heads of Information and Communication Technology 
(ICT) equipment (40 Lakhs), Machinery and Equipment (20 Lakhs), Furniture and Fixtures 
(50 Lakhs) and other fixed assets (5 Lakhs). DHR presently functions from the rented office 
premises located on 1st and 2nd floor of the IRCS Building. As there is shortage of office 
space, DHR is in the process of hiring part of the 4thfloor of the IRCS building on rent. This 
will require expenditure on capital assets such as Furniture, Desktops, IT equipment, Air 
Conditioners, etc. 
2.5.3 The Committee takes cognisance of the fact that there have been actual 
‘savings’ on account of rented office premises for DHR. Further, there has been 
unspent money initially kept to fill up vacant posts in the Department, which is an 
unpleasant and avoidable situation. The Committee understands the implications of 
key posts of Scientists remaining vacant, therefore, has already recommended for 
filling up the vacant posts at the earliest.  Further, the Committee is of the view that 
DHR should acquire an office premise of its own and shall take initiatives in this 
direction. Having own premises can save recurring expenditures and would perhaps 

37 
 
add to the stature and importance associated with the Department. For the meantime, 
the Committee expects that DHR would be utilising the fund allocated for capital 
assets in terms of office fixtures and equipment that are prerequisites for hassle-free 
concentration on the fulfilment of the critical roles assigned to DHR.

twice in 2017-18 and 2021-22, wherein both financial & physical targets and achievements

3.2.3 Earlier in its 152nd Action Taken Report on Demand for Grants (DFG) of DHR 2023-
24, the Committee had observed plateauing in the allocation and utilization of funds under the 
scheme since 2013-14. The Department has attributed various factors as reason which is as 
under: 
(i)  In the early years of the scheme, medical colleges and state authorities exhibited a 
lack of interest in establishing VRDL facilities. The budget was spent mainly on 
setting up new VRDLs and there were no recurring liabilities that led to lower initial 
fund utilization. Every possible effort was put forward to succeed the scheme. The 
first two years were spent generating awareness about the scheme’s importance and 
utility. 
(ii)  Now a network of 165 VRDLs (including 16 VRDLs - 1 Regional level, 3 state 
level, and 12 Medical college level in the east region) has been established across 26 
states and 5 UTs. The goal of setting up laboratories in every part of the country has 
been largely achieved, but VRDL could not be established in Sikkim, Nagaland, 
Lakshadweep, Ladakh, Daman & Diu, and Dadar & Nagar Haveli, due to the 
unavailability of Medical College or an eligible institution. 
(iii)  The funding requirement may not be increasing significantly as a large network has 
already been established in the country leading to stabilization in allocations. The 
network is now operational, and the focus have shifted from infrastructure expansion 
to operational sustainability as the Department wants to ensure quality diagnosis 
levelling the VRDLs at par with international standards, which requires consistent 
but not necessarily increasing funding. Thus, while the scheme is functioning well 
and is in a good pace towards meeting core objectives, further revisions may be 
required to upgrade the laboratory infrastructure and human resources.

epidemic, can also educate, warn and empower the person working on the ground and

recommendations of the NITI Ayog’ Pandemic Preparedness and Emergency Response

Resource Development for Health Research’ as an important initiative to foster talent in 
health research. Trainees are encouraged to develop and take up research projects for

capacity development programs. The Committee finds that the scheme has received the 
full quantum of funds as demanded by DHR since 2022-23. The Committee, however, 
expresses concerns that the funds has been underutilised, therefore, reduced at RE

note such reasons -as less viable proposal for funding research projects, non-completion 
of codal formalities required under the scheme guidelines for release of funds, no 
international fellowship was granted, etc. The Committee firmly believes that 
thesereasons indicate inadequate hand holding by DHR to the intended beneficiaries 
who could very well be the harbingers of India’s future in the health sector.

beneficiaries for such a bright scheme in India. The Committee considers it the duty and 
responsibility of DHR to educate and proactively handhold the beneficiaries to assist 
them to formulate viable proposals. The Committee shall be keen to know the efforts, 
other than the ordinary and customary steps, taken by DHR for facilitating the 
beneficiaries to submit viable proposals and to properly complete the requisite codal 
formalities. The Committee expects that avoidable procedural matters would be 
eliminated when the integration of the scheme with ICMR’s capacity development 
programs materialise.

important institutions like the National Institute of One Health, Zonal National

(iv) Develop protocols, tools and framework for integrated disease surveillance at 
the animal- human-environment interface for emerging diseases;

quality therapeutic monoclonal; and 
(vi) Develop analytic capability to derive better insights from the data and

Research/contribution/achievement of ICMR to Public Health Programmes/Policies 
4.6 As part of the discussion related to DFG 2025-26 of DHR, ICMR submitted 
instances whereinits research findings are translated into actionable public health 
programmes as well as instances when ICMR's research has influenced Government 
healthcare policies in India in the last decade. 
4.6.1 Translating Research into Actionable Public Health Programmes 
i. Identifying National Health Priorities – Research is aligned with the most 
pressing health challenges in India, including infectious diseases, non-
communicable diseases (NCDs), maternal and child health, and emerging health 
threats. 
ii. Evidence Generation through Multicentric Studies – ICMR conducts large-scale 
epidemiological and clinical studies to generate high-quality evidence that can 
inform policy and programmatic interventions. 
iii. Collaboration with Government and Stakeholders – Research findings are shared 
with policymakers, including the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare 
(MoHFW), state governments, and regulatory bodies to facilitate evidence-based 
decision-making. 
iv. Guideline Development and Capacity Building – ICMR translates research into 
practical guidance by developing Standard Treatment Workflows (STWs), 
Disease Management Guidelines, and Training Modules for healthcare providers.   
v. Policy Advocacy and Implementation Support – Findings are communicated 

72 
 
through policy briefs, white papers, and direct engagement with government 
agencies to ensure integration into public health programmes. 
vi. Real-World Demonstration Projects – ICMRimplements pilot studies and 
demonstration projects before scaling up interventions nationwide, ensuring 
feasibility and effectiveness in diverse settings. 
vii. Technology Transfer and Industry Partnerships – To accelerate the impact of 
research, ICMR facilitates collaborations with biotech firms, startups, and 
pharmaceutical companies for vaccine development, diagnostics, and medical 
innovations. 
viii. Public Awareness and Community Engagement – Through health communication 
campaigns, ICMR ensures that research findings reach the public, encouraging 
behavioural changes and better health outcomes. 
4.6.2 Research Influenced Government Healthcare Policies  
I. COVID-19 Response and Vaccine Development: – 
(a) ICMR played a pivotal role in India’s pandemic response by conducting 
Serosurveys, developing indigenous diagnostic kits, and supporting the 
development of Covaxin in partnership with Bharat Biotech and conducting bridge 
trials for Covishield in Indian population. 
(b) Research findings on variants, vaccine efficacy, and post-COVID complications 
directly influenced India's vaccination strategy and pandemic management policies. 
II. National TB elimination: – 
a) ICMR conducted a National TB Prevalence Survey in 20 States/group of States to 
assess burden of TB at sub-national levels. Based on the prevalence survey, the 
programme interventions were re-strategized to focus on vulnerable population to 
reduce TB incidence and mortality. ICMR’s studies on drug-resistant tuberculosis 
(DR-TB) led to the inclusion of newer drug regimens & newer diagnostics like 
TrueNAT, C-TB skin test etc in the National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP) 
III. Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) Policy: The ICMR AMR Network provided 
critical data on antibiotic resistance patterns, leading to the National Action Plan on 
AMR, which now guides antimicrobial stewardship and infection control 
programmes across India. 
IV. Hypertension Control Initiative: ICMR’s studies on the growing burden of 
hypertension and cardiovascular diseases informed the launch of the India 
Hypertension Control Initiative (IHCI), of which ICMR is also a part along with 
MoHFW& WHO, which integrates blood pressure management into primary 
healthcare settings. 
V. Vector-Borne Disease Control: ICMR’s research on VBDs transmission dynamics 
and vector control strategies contributed to different National Centre for Vector 

73 
 
Borne Disease Control (NCVBDC) guidelines like National Strategic Plan for 
Malaria, Manual on Integrated Vector management 2022, Common Protocol for 
Uniform Evaluation of Public Health Pesticides for use in Vector Control etc, 
including improved surveillance and early warning systems. Based on the 
evidence produced by ICMR, replacement of miltefosine 28 days regimen for VL 
with single dose liposomal amphotericin B was made & Combination regimen 
(LAmB + miltefosine): Adopted and recommended for VL-HIV treatment. 
VI. Revised Nutritional Guidelines and AnaemiaMukt Bharat: ICMR studies on 
malnutrition, anaemia prevalence, and dietary patterns influenced the 
AnaemiaMukt Bharat initiative, leading to policy changes in iron and folic acid 
supplementation programmes for children and pregnant women, Mandated Food 
fortification with Vitamin A and many more. 
VII. Cancer Policies: ICMR’s National Cancer Registry data has led to cancer being a 
notifiable disease in 15 states of India.  
VIII. HPV Vaccination: ICMR’s clinical trials and advocacy contributed to the phased 
introduction of the HPV vaccine into India’s Universal Immunization Programme 
(UIP) in 2022-23 to combat cervical cancer. 
IX. National One Health Mission: ICMR’s research on zoonotic diseases and 
antimicrobial resistance has significantly shaped India’s One Health approach, 
influencing policies for integrated human, animal, and environmental health 
surveillance. ICMR is also a crucial part of National One Health Mission, 
strengthening the future outbreak response and preparedness of the nation.  
X. Standard Treatment Workflows: The ICMR, and DHR receive the topics for 
developing STW from NHA and experts all over the country. So far, ICMR has 
released 125 Standard Treatment Workflows in 23 specialties. These workflows 
comprise symptoms, signs, diagnostics, treatment, etc. for concerned diseases. 
NHA is also using the STW as the clinical guidance document to prepare their 
reimbursement package under the Ayushman Bharat Scheme. 
4.6.3 The Committee takes note of the contribution/achievement of ICMR to public 
health programmes/policies and recommends that ICMR should continue to research 
projects of national health priorities and ultimately translating research projects into 
Actionable Public Health Programmes. The Committee recommends DHR to give 
incentives to ICMR so that ICMR undertake large scale epidemiological and clinical

guidance by developing Standard Treatment Workflows (STW) and formulating 
Disease Management Guidelines and Modern and Advanced Training Modules for 
healthcare providers.

Findings of ICMR on COVID effects  

75 
 
4.8 While discussing some of the major health concerns the country is currently facing, 
the Committee was curious to understand reasons for the rise in cases of sudden deaths due 
to myocardial infarctions post-COVID and the findings of ICMR regarding the subject. In 
reply, the Secretary, DHR, who is also the Director General of ICMR, stated that ICMR 
NIE conducted a study titled “Factors associated with unexplained sudden deaths among 
adults aged 18-45 years in India – A multicentric matched case–control study”. The study 
has been completed and the results of this study have been published in the Indian Journal 
of Medical Research.  
4.8.1 The study was conducted at 47 tertiary care hospitals located across 19 states/UT 
of India during May- August 2023. A multi centric matched case control study was 
conducted. Information was collected regarding data on COVID-19 vaccination /infection, 
post-COVID-19 conditions, family history of sudden death, smoking, recreational drug 
use, alcohol frequency, binge drinking and vigorous-intensity physical activity two days 
before death among the cases / interview among controls.Hence, the study observed that 
COVID-19 vaccination did not increase the risk of unexplained sudden death among 
young adults in India. Past COVID-19 hospitalization, family history of sudden death and 
certain lifestylebehaviours increased the likelihood of unexplained sudden death. 
 
4.8.2 During the Oral evidence of DHR, the Committee posed a question on the matter 
regarding apprehensions in the society that the anti-COVID 19 vaccines were behind some 
of the sudden deaths of young individuals reported across the country and the Secretary, 
DHR while explaining the issue further replied that the Covid vaccines, Covishield and 
Covaxin were found to be protective with respect to sudden death; they were protective 
rather than heightening the risk. 
 
4.8.3 The Committee feels that ICMR should proactively continue to play the role 
of dispelling misconceptions about health-related matters through their well-
documented research that may carry negative implications for the society at large. 
Studies of social relevance may be taken up suo motu and the research findings be 
published in lucid language discernible to the masses for their knowledge and faith. 
Dispelling such misconceived notionslike specific covid vaccines had increased the 
likelihood of unexplained sudden death among adults aged 15-25 years, should be the 
part of efforts towards building a well informed and properly guided population in 
matters of health.  
 
4.8.4 The Committee notes that the study about sudden deaths has been published 
in the Indian Journal of Medical Research. It is the suggestion of the Committee that 
DHR should give wider publicity to the outcomes of such studies in the public interest 
through social media platforms, community newsletters, blogs, etc., which would be 
the ideal use of these platforms to reach out to the whole population. On such 
platforms, medical esotericism can be replaced with clear and concise language which 
would help put the apprehensions/concerns of the masses to rest. 
  
Air pollution as major health risk factor 
 

76 
 
4.9 During the Oral evidence of DHR, members raised the concern of Air pollution 
emerging as a major risk factor for Cardio-vascular diseases, premature diabetes, low birth 
weights and impact on pregnant women’s health. The Committee wanted to know if ICMR 
was doing any research into these aspects and also on whether air pollution is causing 
sudden deaths in young people in the country. In their written submission about this, DHR 
informed that regarding occurrence of premature diabetes, a causal relationship is not 
established so far. Individuals’ risk for Type 2 Diabetes is shaped by lifestyle factors such 
as participation in physical activity. Some studies have suggested that rates of outdoor 
physical activity may be lower in areas where air pollution is getting heavier.  ICMR has 
not conducted any study in this area. 
 
4.9.1 ICMR launched a Centre for Advanced Research on Environmental Health (2010-
15): Air Pollution to examine the association between fine particulate matter (PM2.5) 
exposures and maternal, child and adult health outcomes in integrated rural –urban cohorts 
in which pregnant women, infants and adults were followed to assess chronic respiratory 
disease. Key findings of this study indicate that there is 4 gm decrease in birth weight, 
0.3% increase in longitudinal prevalence of ARI and 10% increase in prevalence of 
respiratory symptoms with 10mg/m3 change in household PM 2.5 concentrations. The 
Committee has further been informed that ICMR partnered with Public Health Foundation 
of India (PHFI)&Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) developed estimates 
based on modelling. Research findings titled “The impact of air pollution on deaths, 
disease burden, and life expectancy across the states of India: “The Global Burden of 
Disease Study 2017” was published in The Lancet Planetary Health 2018 on 6thDecember 
2018 (www.thelancet.com/planetary-health). 
 
4.9.2 The Committee reckons air pollution as a health hazard that has emerged as a 
major challenge.  The efforts initiated by ICMR to study the health implications of 
air pollution are taken note of.  However, it is apparent that we have rather 
unchartered paths to travel in this direction.  Earlier, air pollution was thought of as 
a threat in a handful of big cities like Delhi. But now, even small towns are affected. 
However, the Committee is aware that the control of air pollution warrants multi-
agency involvement. So, the Committee feels strongly that air pollution is a subject 
that needs intervention akin to the National One health Mission, where inter-
departmental/organisational coordination is ensured through an institutionalised 
structure. The Committee recommends that DHR-ICMR should come up withan 
effective plan to research more about the ill effects of air pollution and make 
available ways to counter its adverse effects. The action taken in this direction shall 
be intimated to the Committee. 
 
4.9.3 The Committee took into consideration the observation of the Emission Gap 
Report 2020 UN Environment Programme which has observed that India has seen 
over 6% more Green House Gas Emission than previous year. The Committee, 
therefore, feels that it is high time for India to establish an Environmental Health 
Regulatory Agency for Comprehensive and Cohesive Environmental Governance to 
control detrimental health effects of exposure to air, water and soil pollutants to 
prevent wide range of non-communicable diseases. The Committee, in this 

77 
 
connection, recommends DHR to undertake a detailed study of the Report and come 
forward with necessary course of research to overcome the challenges as highlighted 
in the Report.

research into correlation between air pollution and the diseases that is caused by

them altogether. By using artificial intelligence in healthcare, medical professionals can

nascent stage now. The Committee is also concerned to note that in case of cancer 
treatment the outcomes are not in sync with global standards as advanced targeted 
therapies by making use of genomics and proteomics is not widely done in India. The 
Committee, accordingly, advocates for cutting edge research in the field of genomics 
and proteomics and also suggests that the outcome of these studies be made available to 
common citizens so that early detection and cure of cancer reaches the common 
population. 
  
 
4.12.2 The Committee is given to understand that other than pure medical 
knowledge upskilling physicians & clinicians in areas like prompt engineering as 
such is quite a herculean task. Accordingly, the Committee recommends ICMR-

field of prevention, detection and treatment of Cancer.  The Committee further 
recommends that the DIAMOnDS Scheme may be recalibrated to include these

Patent-protection to Innovators  
4.14 During the oral evidence of DHR, the Committee posed a question on the 
possibility of reduction in the duration of patent-protection to innovators for affordable 
mass production of monoclonal antibodies. Replying to the question, the Department 
submitted that as per India Patent Act, 1970, Patents generally grant exclusive rights to 
innovators for a period of 20 years from the filing date. Hence, patent life available for 
exploitation of IP byinnovators including the innovators of monoclonal antibodies, may be 
increased by earlier grant of patent. To request an early grant of a patent under the Indian 
Patent Act, 1970, an applicant can file a request for ‘expedited examination’ which is done 
through Form 18A, allowing for a faster review process and potentially a quicker patent 
grant; this request should be accompanied by a request for early publication in Form 9 
along with the prescribed fee, enabling publication within a shorter timeframe than the 
standard 18 months. Early publication and expedited examination can significantly reduce 
the time taken to receive a patent grant.In India, the following entities can apply for 
expedited examination of a patent Application-Startups, Small entities, Female applicants, 
Government entities, Applicants in certain sectors, Applicants who have designated India 
as an International Solar Alliance (ISA) or International Preliminary Examination 
Authority (IPEA) in Patient Care Technician (PCT) application. 
 
4.14.1 The Committee has been given to understand that reducing the duration of 
patents is one of the options for making healthcare more affordable in India as once 
the duration of patents is over, Indian manufacturers can produce the drugs at a 
lowercost. So,the reduction of Patent duration can reduce the cost of treatment of 
diseases like cancer through cheaper drugs like antibody-based drugs which would 
certainly bring down the out-of-pocket expenditure of patients.  Since the subject 
matter of Patent and IP is under the Ministry of Commerce the Committee, therefore, 
recommends for an inter-ministerial consultation for a viable solution in the matter.  
The Committee desires that ICMR-DHR to look into the matter and have an inter-
ministerial discussion at the earliest. 
 
4.14.2 The Committee notes that as per India Patent Act, 1970, Patents generally 
grant exclusive rights to innovators for a period of 20 years from the filing date. 
Hence, patent life available for exploitation of IP by innovator including innovator of 
monoclonal antibodies, may be increased by earlier grant of patent.

III. National Antibiotic Policy 
 
5.3 The Committee raised the issue of the growing menace of anti-microbial resistance 
and wanted to know whether there is need for National Anti-microbial guidelines. The 
DHR stated that ICMR released guidelines for antimicrobial use in 2019 and for 
management for carbapenem resistant organisms in 2022. 
 
5.3.1 The Committee observes that there is rampant usage of antibiotics leading to 
Anti-microbial resistance. It is a matter of great concern that rapid/massive use of 
antibiotics has resulted in a countrywide problem of microbial/drug resistance. 
Nowadays, Antibiotics are misused, abused and overused. Immediate steps to control 
this trend need to be taken as the long-term effects of the drug resistance will cripple 
the health of the citizens of the country. To restore our natural immune system and 
our gut health indiscriminate usage of antibiotics needs to be stopped. Suitable 
interventions in the curriculum of medical colleges need to be done to sensitise our 
doctors on the ill effects of overuse of antibiotics. Therefore, the Committee 
recommends DHR, in tandem with Ministry/Department concerned to formulate 
National Anti-Biotic Policy covering all aspects of misuse of Antibiotics and its 
prevention and with the intent of restoring the Nations Immune Health.

VII. Vision for health security of next generation 
 
5.7 The Committee wanted to know the vision of DHR for health security of next 
generation. DHR responded that the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) under the 

90 
 
PM- Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission (PM-ABHIM) program has 
undertaken several key initiatives to enhance the nation's preparedness against future 
pandemics. The initiatives include: 
1. Upgradation of Virus Research and Diagnostic Laboratories (VRDLs): Upgradation 
of 80 Virus Research and Diagnostic Laboratories (VRDLs) across the country has 
been initiated by ICMR. This initiative will enable the early detection of pathogens 
during outbreaks, identifying case clusters early and facilitate complete outbreak 
investigations and efficient control. 
2. Establishment of BSL-3 laboratories: ICMR is upgrading five (5) Viral Disease 
Diagnostic Laboratories to Biosafety Level 3 (BSL-3) standards at locations viz 
Kota, Rishikesh, Raipur, Rajkot, and Bibinagar. This enhancement will enable the 
diagnosis of a broader range of pathogens, thereby expanding India's diagnostic 
capabilities even at the state levels. 
3. Deployment of mobile BSL-3 Units: Recognizing the need for rapid and flexible 
response capabilities, ICMR has deployed two mobile BSL-3 laboratories. These 
units will provide essential on-site diagnostic services during outbreaks, especially 
in remote and hard-to-reach areas. 
4. Establishment of Regional National Institutes of Virology: ICMR has established 4 
regional National Institutes of Virology at Jammu, Jabalpur, Dibrugarh and 
Bengaluru keeping in consideration of the regional priorities of different states. The 
establishment of these regional units will significantly strengthen and complement 
the existing system in efficiently countering the threats posed by 
pandemics/epidemics in the future. 
5. Establishment of the National Institute of One Health (NIOH):  ICMR is currently 
establishing the National Institute for One Health (NIOH) at Nagpur. For pandemic 
preparedness, the institute is mandated to undertake integrated and holistic research 
and development across human, animal, plant, and environmental health sectors.  
Embracing a 'One Health' approach, NIOH will be instrumental in the early 
detection and response to epidemics and pandemics. 
 
5.7.1 The Committee takes note that upgradation of a total of 80 VRDLs,

XII Impact of packaged foods on human health & Policy Measures to enhance 
informed food choices 
  
Impact of packaged foods on human health 
 
5.12 The Committee has been informed that the total market size of the packaged food 
sector was 2.8 billion U.S. dollars in India in 2023. The recent times in the context of the 
growing overweight obesity and diet related non-communicable diseases, (NCDs) there is a 
concern that the prepacked foods consumption might be a contributing factor. However, 
packaged foods can have both positive and negative impacts on human health depending on 
the extent of processing and their contents and how often they are consumed. The 
healthiness of a packaged food depends on various factors including the level of processing 
of the food and the extent of nutrients/ingredients of concern that are present in the food 
like refined flours, fats, added sugars, salt/sodium. Some of the Pre-packaged foods are 
likely to be highly processed and can become High in fats, salt and sugars. Many packaged 
foods, especially snacks, desserts, and ready-to-eat meals, are high in sugar, sodium, and 
unhealthy fats. Regular consumption of these can contribute to obesity, heart disease, 
diabetes, and high blood. Packaging materials, especially single-use plastics, can have 
harmful effects on the environment, indirectly affecting health by contributing to pollution 
and waste. 
 
5.12.2 Ultra-processed foods (UPFs) refer to food and beverage products that have 
undergone extensive industrial processing and contain a high number of additives such as 
preservatives, sweeteners, colourings, flavourings, emulsifiers, and other substances that 
are not commonly used in culinary preparations. Research suggests that a diet high in ultra-
processed foods may be associated with negative health outcomes NIN, 2024, Dietary 
Guidelines for Indians. The lack of fibre and poor micronutrient content make UPFs 
unhealthy.Consumption of UPFs is linked to overweight/ obesity and increased risks of 
coronary heart disease, stroke, and diabetes.  
 

99 
 
5.12.3 According to the Household Consumption Expenditure Survey (HCES, 2024) the 
monthly per capita expenditure on beverages and processed food has risen from 8.98 per 
cent and 7.9 per cent (2011-12) to 11.09 per cent and 9.84 per cent (2022-23) in urban and 
rural areas, respectively. A recent report by WHO and ICREAR which covered five 
popular categories of ultra-processed food in India, namely (a) chocolate and sugar 
confectionery, (b) salty snacks, (c) beverages, (d) ready-made and convenience food, and 
(e)breakfast cereals have reported that this sector grew at a compound annual growth rate 
(CAGR) of 13.37% in retail sales value between 2011 to 2021.

studies have shown that only over a fifth of all consumers use nutrition information for 
making food choices. The Food Safety Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) is taking 
steps to introduce a Front of Pack labelling System to indicate the healthiness of the pre-
packaged foods.

that becomes a contributing factor in the growing overweight obesity and diet related 
non-communicable diseases, (NCDs). The Committee takes note the findings of the

The Committee hopes that measures so undertaken will not only help the consumer

AT A GLANCE 
 
Mandate of DHR 
 
1. The Committee takes note of the allocation of a new Business to DHR in the 
form of Health Technology Assessment which will promote evidence-based decision 
making across the healthcare spectrum. An allocation of business suggests enhanced 
responsibility for managing the specific allocation, impacting its policy formulation, 
its implementation as well as coordination with other ministries. This also translates 
into additional financial implications like need for increased budgetary allocation to 
cover the new responsibilities, including staff recruitment, infrastructure 
development, etc. Accordingly, it is expected that DHR takes appropriate measures to 
continue to execute this crucial role and is also able to secure and utilise adequate 
allocation of funds for the work.  
(Para 1.2.3) 
Human Resource Management 
2. The Committee expresses displeasure that the posts of Scientists of various 
grades in DHR have been lying vacant now for an unacceptably long time. Though 
DHR makes continuing efforts to fill up these posts, but all have been in vain. It is 
understood that these posts were created in 2017 for specific roles within DHR but 
seem to have never been populated. The Committee has also been appraised in this 
context that contractual appointments of Scientists are being made in DHR which 
does affect the continuity of the implementation of the programmes on their sudden 
departure from the Department. In the considered opinion of the Committee, DHR 
has to walk the extra mile to fill up these posts on regular basis. One of the obvious 
ways to achieve is to make the conditions of service and/or remuneration more 
attractive to ensure that appointed scientists are to stay in DHR instead of deserting. 
Quicker/shortened recruitment process may be another avenue to be explored. 
Notwithstanding this, the Committee takes strong exception to the posts remaining 
vacant for so long and, therefore, the Committee recommends that urgent measures 
other than ordinary procedure to be taken to fill up the vacant posts. Further, 
Committee would like to put on record that adoption of stop gap management like 
contractual appointments to so significant posts of Scientists is totally unacceptable 
and ad-hoc approach and practice of contractual appointment should be 
discontinued. Contractual appointments to such posts that inherently warrant 
continuity as a critical prerequisite for their effectiveness would jeopardise the very 
success of the tasks for which the scientists are engaged.     
(Para 1.3.4) 
3. The Committee takes note of the program envisaged by the Department to 
attract Non-resident Indians (NRIs), Persons of Indian Origin (PIO), Overseas 
Citizens of India (OCI) serving abroad back to India. At the same time, the 
Committee expresses its concerns about continuing Brain Drain, the exodus of 
trained, proficient and talented Indian professionals to developed countries. India's 
brain drain is caused by a lack of higher education options, research funding and 
facilities, pay & perks that is lower than global standards in both the public and 
private sectors and fewer opportunities in terms of career progression, especially in 
specialized fields. Other facilitative factors like environment of equity, transparency, 
protection of ownership of genuine research outcomes, delayed systemic response, etc 
also add to contributing factors.   

101 
 
(Para 1.3.6) 
4. The Committee, even though aware of the funding limitations, is not fully 
convinced of the adequateness of a consolidated stipend of Rs.1.2 lakhs per month for 
3 years for a selected researcher under the Scheme to attract professionals from 
abroad. The Committee feels that the Department should consider keeping the 
window open to enhance the quantum of stipend, at least based on the project 
proposals presented and the remuneration the person is receiving in the foreign 
country. The same flexible approach should be adopted in case of the quantum of 
grant, the Committee desires.  Accordingly, to address the intricate issue of brain 
drain, India must adopt a comprehensive strategy that includes enhancing higher 
education, strengthening research infrastructure, and implementing policies to 
improve the standard of living. These measures would encourage skilled Indian 
professionals to return from abroad and undertake domestic health research projects. 
A unified and long-term approach is essential for India to retain and recover its most 
valuable asset—human capital.

5. Further, the Department should look into the possibility of involving private 
sector which can contribute through competitive pay packages, which would be well 
within their realm as promotion of PPP.
