achievement. The India Disease Burden Study, mentioned by the Department as a 
breakthrough initiative, provided crucial insights into the shifting burden of 
diseases in India, highlighting the growing prevalence of Non-Communicable 
diseases (NCDs). Going by the indicators provided by the Study, India’s efforts in 
the area of NCDs needs further impetus. 
(Para 1.4.1) 
7. Accordingly, the Committee observes that the policies, priorities and funding 
for health research in the country should be optimally aligned with its actual health 
needs rather than with the global research agenda. Hence, India should prioritise 
research on under-studied diseases in the country, such as cardiovascular, 
respiratory diseases, etc. along with research on public health, healthcare 
infrastructure/systems and implementation of clinical medicine. The Committee feels 
that alignment of health research with the National Health Policy & Priorities would 
be cardinal in this direction and hence recommends, accordingly. 
(Para 1.4.2) 
Role of public-private partnerships (PPPs) in Health Research Funding  
8. The Committee reckons that since the Government is always under 
compulsion to apportion the limited financial resources amongst the varied needs of 
the country, it would be prudent to leverage the financial resources, technological 
expertise and innovation capabilities of the Private sector in furthering the needs of 
the health sector, especially in research. The Committee holds the view that when 

102 
 
cutting edge research and innovation outcomes, produced in collaboration with the 
Private sector, are dovetailed with policy initiatives and wide access infrastructure 
of the Government, it can change the health care landscape of India. Taking into 
account the fact that promotion of public-private partnership is one of the 
businesses allocated to DHR as per the Allocation of Business Rules of the 
Government of India. The Committee recommends that the Department should 
consider adopting more measures to secure the participation of the Private sector in 
the health sector in the Country with tailor made collaborative and mutually 
beneficial outreach measures. 
(Para 1.5.1) 
9. The Committee notes that while on the one hand DHR acknowledges the 
importance of Public Private Partnerships (PPPs) for the development of innovations 
and informs that ICMR has successfully completed several projects under PPP 
mode,there is an absence of an institutional mechanism for PPP. In view of the 
submission of DHR and the fact that promotion of PPP is one of the businesses 
allocated to DHR as per the Allocation of Business Rules of the Government of India, 
the Committee recommends that DHR should come out with an institutionalised 
mechanism for promoting PPP.  
(Para 1.5.2) 
Emerging Technologies and Ethical Concerns related to Health Research 
10. The Committee recognises the importance of adoption of new technologies, 
innovation and constant endeavour for development of new drugs and treatment 
methods. Clinical trials are an inalienable data generating component of this 
continuing quest. The regulatory architecture now in place in the Country are taken 
note of, however, the Committee would like to emphasise the need to ensure 
‘informed’ consent of the participants of clinical trials which should invariably 
include sharing of information beforehand about how the data generated out of the 
trial would be used or shared. It is important to ensure that the participants fully 
understand the risks and benefits of a study, management of sensitive personal 
information and balancing the need for research advancement with individual 
privacy rights. Digitalization and sharing of patient information bears privacy 
implications that needs to be addressed and fixed with appropriate provisions.  
(Para 1.6.2) 
11. The Committee notes that the Government has taken a key step in setting up 
ICMR-National Institute for Research in Digital Health and Data Science and 
entrusting it with the task of developing India-specific AI-based solutions for 
strengthening the healthcare system with an overarching goal of achieving Universal 
Health Coverage. The Committee finds research in Digital Health and Data Sciences 
as one of the areas that can be prioritized for collaboration with domain leading 
private sector organizations. The Committee observes that the Department should 
explore the possibility to further augment the efforts in this direction. The 
Committee in this connection recommends that adequate money is allocated to 
ICMR-NIRDHDS for its new responsibility. In this regard, the Committee 
emphasizes the all-important need to protect data, personal as well as research 
based, while developing AI based solutions. 
(Para 1.6.4) 
Projected Demand and Actual Allocation  
 

103 
 
12. The Committee perceives research in health to be of pivotal importance. 
Solution based core research aligned with the goals associated with the national 
health priorities would be way forward of DHR. The Committee notes that DHR has 
taken cognisance of the Viksit Bharat aim and has accordingly established goals 
related to the field of Health Research. As part of which the Department has 
envisaged a structured approach towards the attainment 6 goals of specific activities 
in 5 year period of 2024-2029. However, the Committee notes with concern that the 
gap between the funds sought by DHR is getting widened since 2024-25. This gap 
between the projected demand and allocation of funds has increased from Rs. 575.09 
crore during 2024-25 to Rs. 1069.34 crore during 2025-26. From the submissions of 
the Department, it is but natural to infer that their activities, including the ones 
towards the attainment of the Viksit Bharat goals, are going to be adversely affected 
by the dearth of funds. The Committee notes in this regard that the fund utilisation 
by DHR reflects a decent percentage of 87 and above over the years, hence, it is 
imperative that DHR has enough justification to lay claim for higher budgetary 
allocation.  At the same time, the Committee appreciates the counter balancing 
efforts on the part of the Department to manage their project with the allocated 
funds. 
(Para 2.1.4) 
13. It is the firm view of the Committee that Health research has to be accorded 
higher priority by the Government than being given during recent years. 
Accordingly, the assurance of the Ministry of Finance to consider granting 
Rs.600.00 crore in RE for 2025-26 is not enough.  The Committee, accordingly, 
strongly recommends that the total funds as projected by DHR may be allocated as 
additional fund in the BE 2025-26 itself and if not so, surely atleast at RE stage. This 
is being recommended under the premise that DHR would continue to walk the talk 
and execute their schemes and programmes as per the book. The Committee desires 
that DHR should pursue with the Ministry of Finance with due diligence so that 
budgetary allocation to DHR must match with the projected demand.  
(Para 2.1.5) 
Health Research Funding 
14. The Committee observes that the BE 2025-26 of Department of Health Research 
(DHR) at Rs 3900.69 crore is just 3.91 % of the Total Health Budget. Also, DHR got 
only 4.06% of the BE allocation of Department of Health & Family Welfare 
(DoH&FW) 2025-26, i.e., Rs 95,957.87 crore. Further, the Committee observes that 
over the last five years, there has been no major change in the quantum of budgetary 
allocation for health research, which is still only 0.02% of the GDP. The Committee 
understands that public funding is the primary source of fund for meeting the 
expenditure on health research in India, therefore, the crucial role of healthcare 
research in advancing public health is undeniable.  The Committee expresses anguish 
over low budgetary allocation to health research as in the opinion of the Committee, 
for a country of almost 1.5 billion people, the existing trend of quantum of budgetary 
allocation over the years is abysmally low. 
(Para 2.2.5) 
15. Further, the Committee is given to understand that the Department, keeping the 
limited allocation in mind, are compelled to redefine their priorities like assigning 
preference to National Health Priority and high-impact research projects, adopting 
PPP mode for product development, regular monitoring, reviewing & reallocation 
funds for ongoing projects and essential programs, etc. The counter balancing 
measures of the Department points to the crunch of funds they are facing. In this 
regard, the Committee unanimously affirm that health research is fundamental to the 
future development of the country's healthcare system and should remain a priority 

104 
 
sector. Hence, the Committee fully appreciates the efforts of DHR in their 
recalibration of projects and funds to attain optimal results and extends full in their 
efforts in securing additional fund. 
(Para 2.2.6) 
 
16. The Committee, in its 127th Report on Demand for Grants for 2021-22 of DHR 
had recommended that at least 5% of the budget of the DoH&FW should be allocated 
to DHR. The Committee also recommended the Department to set an aim to allocate 
5% of the Total Health Budget for health research in the next two years. The 
Committee is displeased to note that even after a lapse of four years none of the above 
recommendations of the Committee has been complied with. Accordingly, the 
Committee expresses its disappointment and strongly reiterates its earlier 
recommendation and lends its support to the Department in its pursuance with 
Ministry of Finance in procuring enhanced allocation. 
(Para 2.2.7) 
17. Further, the Committee also found that no major financial documents of the 
Government of India like the Economic Survey outline the specific allocation of 
fund for Health Research in India. Hence, the lowly 3.91% of allocation for research 
in health sector, in comparison to the Total Health Budget, gets drowned in the 
larger, more projectable figures of DoH&FW. In the considered opinion of the 
Committee, the change in approach of the Government towards according more 
impetus to Health Research should begin from highlighting the money allocated 
over the years for Health Research prominently in important financial documents 
and indicators. Such indicators reflect the importance being accorded by the 
Government to the health sector and help in understanding the trajectory of growth 
in the health research. 
(Para 2.2.8) 
18. Considering global standards with respect to investment in health research, the 
Committee recommends that the Government must aim to invest at least 0.1% of the 
GDP in the next five years. 
(Para 2.2.9) 
Scheme-wise Projected Demand and Allocation (2025-26) 
19. The Committee finds that the demand for funds by DHR has mainly been 
under the heads (i) Health Technology Assessment – Attached Office, (ii) 
Establishment of Model Rural Health Research Units (MRHRUs), (iii) Development 
of Tools to prevent outbreaks of epidemics and (iv) ICMR. Since the lion’s share of 
the allocation to DHR goes to ICMR, the gap between the projected demand and 
allocated amount also is the widest under that head in terms of quantum of funds 
allocated, i.e, Rs 781.5 crore. For Development of Tools to prevent outbreaks of 
epidemics also the allocated funds are just about one third of the projected demand 
made. But for Health Technology Assessment– Attached Office, only Rs. 18.75 crore 
has been allocated against a projected demand made for Rs. 220.25 crore, which is 
less than 10% of the projected demand. HTA has been included as an Attached 
Office from last year but, to utmost surprise to the Committee, HTA is already 
being subjected to severe curtailment of funds.  
(Para 2.3.1) 
20. The Committee observes that drastic slashing of the funds as sought by the 
DHR is unacceptable in the absence of compelling reasons. Accordingly, the 
Committee recommends that DHR should make all efforts to convince the Ministry 
of Finance to secure funds for such game changing schemes. Further, as already 
recommended, it is the firm view of the Committee that the Government/Ministry of 

105 
 
Finance should attach more importance to health research. The Committee expects 
the Department to calibrate their Demands based on statics and expert opinion, 
straighten out all administrative infirmities associated with project submissions 
before approaching the Ministry of Finance for higher budgetary allocation under 
specific scheme. 
(Para 2.3.2) 
21. The Committee notes that DHR has got an increased allocation in BE to the 
tune of 509.05 crore in BE for 2025-26 compared to the RE of Rs. 3391.64 crore 
during 2024-25, which itself saw a hike compared to the BE for the year of Rs. 
3301.73 crore.  It is also noted that DHR has identified the activities on which the 
increased funding is to be utilised. Expanding the scope of MRU Scheme to cover 
Private Medical Colleges, upgradation of well performing MRUs to Centres of 
Research Excellence (CoREs), integration of ICMR’s Capacity Development 
Programme into DHR’s own HRD Scheme, revision of guidelines for Start-up 
Grant, increase in quantum of stipend/fellowship for Women Scientist Programme 
and Young Scientist Programme, strengthening of VRDLs, host of initiatives under 
PM-ABHIM, National One Health Mission activities, MedTech Mitra, 
implementation of DHR-ICMR strategic goals, etc, feature among the key areas 
where the enhanced funding is to be required for optimum utilisation to achieve the 
cherished output as per standard rate of return.  
(Para 2.3.4) 
22. The Committee considers the resilient monitoring mechanism and a periodic 
review a prudent strategy to have linkage amongst the scope, budget & timeline of 
any project/scheme/programme and ensuring successful implementation thereof.  
Such reviews should take into account the emerging information, changing priorities 
or unforeseen circumstances, often requiring modifications to timelines, budgets, 
strategies, or resource allocations. The Committee is pleased to observe that the 
Department has oriented their activities to utilise their enhanced allocation. 
Accordingly, the Committee views the plans made by DHR positively and is 
optimistic about the results coming out in tune with the plans chalked out.  
(Para 2.3.5) 
23. The Committee, however, finds that under some schemes, the funds sought 
by DHR for the year 2025-26 have been curtailed citing the reason that only the 
remaining amount approved by the Standing Finance Committee (SFC) for the 15th

reason untenable as it comes in the way of much needed continuance of the 
beneficial activities of the schemes beyond the 15th Finance Commission period. In 
the opinion of the Committee such situations would qualify as the cliched instance of 
‘red tape’ induced financial rigidity coming in the way of development. Accordingly, 
the Committee recommends that situations where genuine need for funds cannot be 
met due to procedural pre-requisites shall be avoided in future. Further, the 
Committee wants to be apprised about the results of the recalibrated 
activities/targets under each scheme.

during 2022-23, 2023-24 and 2024-25 has been 87.64%, 98.78% and 91.94%,

106 
 
Committee expects the Department to optimally utilized the earmarked budgetary 
allocation under full proof monitoring mechanism.

without time and cost overruns and achieving the set objectives as per plan.

27. The Committee notes that allocation made for the Department of Health 
Research is done keeping in mind the FRBM limits. However, it has also been

Establishment of Network of Laboratories for Managing Epidemics and National 
Calamities 
 Viral Research & Diagnostic Laboratories (VRDLs)  
 
33. The Committee notes that the VRDL Scheme to establish Viral Research & 
Diagnostic Laboratories (VRDLs) that began in 2013 has traversed well over time and 
now-a-days there is a network of 165 VRDLs in the country. The Committee 
appreciates the work done by DHR in this regard, especially during the initial years of 
the Scheme when the States and medical colleges were not showing the desired level of 
interest. However, when the time of reckoning came during the COVID pandemic and 
in case of other smaller out breaks like Monkeypox, Zika, and Nipah, the Government 
realised the importance of this diagnostic infrastructure which is the result of the 
tenacity exhibited by DHR in case of establishing VRDLs. The Committee 
appreciatesthe optimal utilisation of funds under the Scheme right since the year 
2013-14 despite the fact the scheme has never been allocated the estimated cost for a 
particular planned period. Further, the Scheme has been reviewed twice during the 
span of its existence till now, at an interval of about 4 years. Since the last review was 
in 2012-22, it is the time for next review. The Committee notes that new Standing 
Finance Committee (SFC) is being prepared for the 16th Finance Commission period 
with enlarged scope and the Committees hopes the VRDLs would emerge in new 
incarnation for extending infectious/Viral Research & Diagnostic Services of global 
standards. The Committee hopes that DHR would take concrete measures for 
strengthening of VRDLs that could not be taken up for support in Covid years and 
for converting 6 of them into Infectious Disease Research and Development Labs 
(IRDLs). 
(Para 3.2.5)

infrastructure, that should be taken further, is continued improvement in quality 
systems in public health laboratories for viral diagnosis, which has been added during 
the last review. Once the infrastructure is in place, their effective sustenance and 
relentless qualitative advancement becomes all important to reap the intended 
benefits. Accordingly, the Committee strongly recommends the continuation of the 
Scheme during the 16th Finance Commission period keeping such objectives like 
strengthening of existing VRDLs, their upgradation, prodigious ability to detect more 
pathogens, etc.  DHR, leveraging the excellent utilisation pattern of funds till now 
under the scheme, shall also seek adequate funds for the Scheme in tune with 
expanded scope for the period of 16th Finance Commission.

Colleges/Research Institutes could provide a cue in this direction.

HPV vaccines 
69. The Committee, like the majority of the people in the Country, is hopefully 
waiting for the results of the trial related to the development of single dose HPV 
Vaccine under the guidance of ICMR. The success of the trials could provide a major 
fillip to HPV immunisation in India as there is only multiple dose vaccines available at 
present which although provide protection. However, multiple doses have practical 
inconveniences, like keeping track of the dosage schedule, etc. The Committee is of the 
view that introduction of a single dose vaccine would considerably increase successful 
vaccination percentage as the vaccination schedule can be completed with one shot. 
This, in turn, will have a commensurate impact on the reduction of incidence of 
cervical cancer, which is a leading cause of cancer among women. Further, a 
homegrown vaccine can drastically bring down the cost of vaccination. This factor 
can accelerate the consolidation of the HPV vaccine in the Universal Immunization 
Programme. Hence, the Committee observes that the development of single dose HPV 
vaccine should be completed as per the set schedule. The Committee observes that 

118 
 
HPV vaccine can be a path breaker in breaking the vicious cycle of the cancer of the 
cervix. A countrywide campaign supported by the Central Government is needed to 
ensure that 100% administration of HPV vaccine is done among all girls with

vaccine so that the high price does not become a hindrance in this programme.

 Animal Labs 
82 As part of the evolution of medicines, vaccines, injectables, ointments and 
other pharma products animal trial has been a historically established global practise. 
Unfortunately, due to the approach adopted by animal right activist in setting up of 
testing labs with facilities of trials on animals has suffered immensely. The impact can 
be assessed when one compares the research and the outcome of the vaccine labs in 
Indonesia vis-a-vis CRI, Kasauli. Lack of proper animal testing facilities has resulted 
in a setback to research in India. The Committee advocates for a balanced approach 
so that the process of research and trials through animal testing labs is not adversely 
affected. The Committee also recommends that setting up of animal testing labs in 
India should be established more in number and made easier and rationally 
regulated, then and only then ICMR can develop these implants at cheaper rate. 
(para 5.2.1) 
 
National Antibiotic Policy 
83 The Committee observes that there is rampant usage of antibiotics leading to 
Anti-microbial resistance. It is a matter of great concern that rapid/massive use of 
antibiotics has resulted in a countrywide problem of microbial/drug resistance. 
Nowadays, Antibiotics are misused, abused and overused. Immediate steps to control 
this trend need to be taken as the long-term effects of the drug resistance will cripple 
the health of the citizens of the country. To restore our natural immune system and 
our gut health indiscriminate usage of antibiotics needs to be stopped. Suitable 
interventions in the curriculum of medical colleges need to be done to sensitise our 
doctors on the ill effects of overuse of antibiotics. Therefore, the Committee 
recommends DHR, in tandem with Ministry/Department concerned to formulate 
National Anti-Biotic Policy covering all aspects of misuse of Antibiotics and its 
prevention and with the intent of restoring the Nations Immune Health. 
(para 5.3.1)

84 The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that ICMR should oversee a 
countrywide screening programme to be done through portable x-ray machines to 
detect tuberculosis at an early stage in consultation with the State Governments. 
Suitable advisories need to be issued to all States so that scourge of TB is eliminated 
from India within a stipulated time.  
(para 5.4.1) 
 
Testing facilities for medical devices 
85 The Committee came across that India with its huge population needs to have 
its own indigenous medical devices industry. The Committee is of the opinion that 
adequate testing facilities for medical devices are not available within the country. As 
an example, ICMR even though it certifies radiological devices like x-rays etc. but 
lacks any testing laboratory for testing of such devices. Such laboratories to check 
radiological devices are available with the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB). 
The Committee recommends for an integrated and collaborative approach between 
CSIR, AERB, DBT, FSSAI Labs and other such institutions may be evolved so that 
their respective strength could be used instead of duplicating such facilities and at the 
same time facilitating industry.  
(para 5.5) 
 
86. Besides, the Committee also recommends that the procedure/protocol for 
registration of medical devices/drugs should be made more transparent, user-friendly 

122 
 
and time bound to facilitate the growth of Industry in these areas. The procedure 
should be clearly made evident on the website of the department concerned along with 
allocation of nodal officers to guide the medical devices/pharma industry. 
(para 5.5.1) 
 
 
 
Fresh areas of Research by ICMR 
 
87 The Committee takes note of the initiatives taken by ICMR to overcome the 
acute M.I. in young population, infertility, ageing problems, early puberty, refractive 
errors at early age, premature greying of hair, rare diseases like Duchenne Muscular 
Dystrophy, Rabies and Tetanus and the findings of its research in recent hair loss 
cases in Buldhana. The Committee understands that the research project and findings 
thereof would lead to policy/programme formulation that would prevent the 
identified aberrations. The Committee further hopes that AMR surveillance network 
and guidelines issued by ICMR would create awareness on rising levels of anti-
microbial resistance in Indian population.  
(para 5.6.1) 
 
Vision for health security of next generation 
 
88 The Committee takes note that upgradation of a total of 80 VRDLs, 
establishment of BSL-3 Laboratories by upgradation of 5 viral disease diagnostic 
laboratories to bio-safety level-3& deployment of 2 mobile BSL-3 laboratories and 
establishment of 4 regional national institute of virology and establishment of the 
National Institute of One Health (NIOH). The Committee believes that these 
arrangements would lead to early detection of pathogens during outbreak, expanding 
India’s diagnostic capabilities at the State levels, extending essential on-sight 
diagnostic services especially in remote and hard to reach areas, efficiently countering 
the threats posed by pandemics/epidemics in future and instrumental in early 
detection and response to epidemics and pandemics, respectively, provided the 
institutional mechanism work efficiently and effectively at the nick of the time.  
 
(para 5.7.1) 
Incentive to ASHAs 
 
89 The Committee is in agreement with DHR that ASHAs can be incentivized for 
contributing more towards health research, through activities like house-to-house 
surveys. The extensive grassroots presence makes ASHA ideal for bridging the gap 
between research and public health implementation, the Committee opines. 
Accordingly, the Committee recommends DHR to encourage and incentivise the 
ASHAs and peripheral health institutions to contribute more towards health research 
through activities like house-to-house surveys, disease surveillance, and community-
based data collection. The Committee also recommends that the ASHA workers 
should be incentivised from the allocation made to DHR and should be in addition to 
the regular remuneration of ASHAs. 
(para 5.8.1) 
Incentivizing CSR into Health Research Projects 
 

123 
 
90 The Committee takes note that ICMR has made revision in its Corporate 
Social Responsibility (CSR) Guidelines allowing CSR funds to be directed toward 
private sector partners for collaborative research projects. The Committee 
recommends ICMR to strive to secure alternative funding sources for critical 
healthcare research and development initiatives, thereby enhancing social impact. 
The Committee is in agreement with the DHR that establishment of a Section 8 
company, namely Medical Innovations Development Acceleration Company 
(MIDAC), will serve as a dedicated entity to accelerate R&D, facilitate funding, and 
drive commercialization of innovative healthcare solutions. The establishment of the 
MIDAC, which will serve as a dedicated platform for accelerating research 
translation, fostering public-private partnerships, and promoting the 
commercialization of innovative healthcare solutions. 
(para 5.9.1) 
 
Priority area in National Health Research Programme (NHRP) 
 
91 The Committee takes note of the funding details of various projects in priority 
area under NHRP and the timelines of the implementation. The Committee desires 
that each project under NHRP must be completed within the stipulated timeframe 
and serve the humankind as per originally conceived objectives. Moreover, the 
Committee would like to know the details of beneficiaries and organizations seeking 
the grant, the status of progress made towards the implementation of the health 
research projects and the outcome of the completed projects. DHR may submit 
quarterly report to the Committee about the progress of ongoing health projects 
under NHRP. The Committee also desires to know the quality assessment of the 
findings of the health projects report.  
(para 5.10.1) 
 
92 The Committee would further like to know the constitution of the decision-
making body granting fund for health research projects under NHRP. The 
Committee also wants to know whether the progress of health research projects or 
after the completion of the project under NHRP have ever been assessed/audited by 
the Third Party i.e. globally recognised scientists with domain experts in their 
respective field. 
(para 5.10.2) 
 
Effects of cell phone and mobile tower radiations on human health 
 
93 The Committee recommends DHR to undertake conclusive study on the 
linkage between exposure to radio frequency radiation and potential health effects 
including effect on cell growth, cell differentiation, DNA, immune system, hormonal 
effects, reproduction, neurological, cardiovascular systems, blood brain barrier, stress 
proteins, skin, sleep disorder etc. and the findings thereof may be furnished to the 
Committee for information. The Committee hopes that DHR would take concrete 
steps in the matter in the interest of humankind.  
(para 5.11.1) 
 
Impact of packaged foods on human health & Policy Measures to enhance informed 
food choices 
 
 94 The Committee expresses concern over pre-packed foods/UPFs consumption 
that becomes a contributing factor in the growing overweight obesity and diet related 

124 
 
non-communicable diseases, (NCDs). The Committee takes note the findings of the 
Household Consumption Expenditure Survey (HCES, 2024) concluding that the 
monthly per capita expenditure on beverages and processed food has risen from 8.98 
per cent and 7.9 per cent (2011-12) to 11.09 per cent and 9.84 per cent (2022-23) in 
urban and rural areas, respectively. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends 
the Government to resort to stricter guidelines on targeting marketing and 
advertising of unhealthy foods for children. The Committee takes into account that 
the Food Safety Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) is taking steps to introduce a 
Front of Pack labelling System to indicate the healthiness of the pre-packaged foods. 
The Committee hopes that measures so undertaken will not only help the consumer 
make informed food choices but also compel the food industry actors to reformulate 
their products to achieve better rating. 
(para 5.13.1)

CHAPTER I 
 
INTRODUCTION 
 
The Ministry of Ayush formed in 2014, evolved from the Department of Indian System of 
Medicine and Homoeopathy (ISM&H) formed in 1995. The Department was responsible for the 
development of ancient system of medicine prevalent in Indian subcontinent in times of yore. It 
was renamed as the Department of Ayurveda, Yoga, and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha and 
Homoeopathy (Ayush) in November 2003 with focused attention towards education and 
research in Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, and Homoeopathy. Sowa Rigpa, a 
traditional medicine system in many parts of Himalyan regions was also brought under the 
umbrella in year 2011.  
 
1.1 Ayurveda is a comprehensive traditional system of medicine evolved in India thousands of 
year ago in medieval and ancient times. Ayurveda emphasizes on holistic approach through 
health promotion, disease prevention and curative roles. Ayurveda considers health as a 
dynamic integration of environment, body, mind and soul and accordingly advocates 
personalized approach for prescribing diet, lifestyle or treatment regimen based on its 
fundamental concept that everyone has distinct psychosomatic constitution and health status. 
Homoeopathy, has also been in practice in India for around 100 years, provides long term 
palliative treatment in both acute and chronic cases owing to its effectiveness, lack of side 
effects and low cost of treatment. The National Health Policy (NHP-2017) advocates 
mainstreaming the potential of Ayush within a pluralistic system of integrated healthcare. In 
convergence with NHP and National Health Mission, the National Ayush Mission (NAM) 
envisages better access to Ayush Services, operationalization of Ayush Health and Wellness 
Centre, quality improvement of Ayush Education and Research in order to achieve Sustainable 
Development Goals and enhanced public health. 
 
1.1.1 The Ministry of Ayush works with the vision to position Ayush systems as the preferred 
systems of living and practice for attaining a healthy India. Such a vision has gradually emerged 
through the thought processes of experts concerned with health care provisioning in the country. 
The Ministry strives to promote these systems through robust policy frameworks, widespread 
awareness, and comprehensive educational initiatives. The core objectives include driving 
research and innovation, ensuring access to quality Ayush products, and fostering global 
acceptance of these practices. The Ministry is dedicated to developing skilled professionals, 
bolstering the medicinal plant sector, and ultimately, enhancing public health through 
sustainable and accessible Ayush solutions. 
 
 
 

2 
 
Thematic Areas of Ayush  
 
1.2 The Ministry envisages its Mission in terms of seven broad thematic areas of Ayush 
activities. The thematic areas are as follows: 
 
(i) Effective Human Resource Development 
(ii) Provision of Quality Ayush Services 
(iii) Information, Education and Communication 
(iv) Quality Research in Ayush 
(v) Growth of the Medicinal Plants Sector 
(vi) Drug Administration 
(vii) International Exchange Programme/Seminars/Workshops in Ayush sector 
 
 
FUNCTIONAL AREAS OF THE MINISTRY 
1.3 With an aim to position India as a Global Health care leader, the Ministry has identified the 
key areas of focus as Globalization and Market Share; Research; Technology; Policy Regulation 
and Standardizations; Manufacturing and Services; and Healthcare and Education. 
 
1.3.1 The Major Activities of Ministry of Ayush are carried out by several autonomous 
institutions, and various institutes/councils under direct control of the Ministry; Centre Sector 
Schemes and the Centrally Sponsored Schemes where grants are provided through National 
Ayush Mission (NAM) to States/UTs to take up Ayush Activities. 
 
1.3.2 The Ministry of Ayush executes its mandate through its 5 Research Councils, 12 National 
Institutes, the 2 Regulatory Commission (i.e. NCISM & NCH), its subordinate offices PCIM&H 
and the Public Sector Undertaking IMPCL.

institutional framework to achieve the objectives of those activities. The Committee 
desires that each and every institution must strive towards achieving the Mission

further observes that the broad thematic area of Ayush activities is the key to accomplish

Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha and Sowa-Rigpa (AUS&SR) & Homeopathy medical education,

Act, 1940 and rules there under, the compliance to this quality standards are mandatory for the 
production of ASU&H drugs being manufactured in India. So far, 2259 quality standards on raw 
materials (single drugs of plant/ animal/ mineral/ metal/ chemical origin) used in ASU&H

Microscopic & TLC Atlas on 351 single drugs incorporated in Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of 
India (API) has also published. Rule 160 A to J of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 
provides the regulatory guidelines for approval of Drug Testing Laboratory for carrying out 
such tests of identity, purity, quality and strength of Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani drugs. As on 
date, 34 State Drug Testing Laboratories have been supported for strengthening their 
infrastructural and functional capacity.  Further, 106 laboratories are approved or licensed under 
the provisions of Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 for quality testing of Ayurvedic, Siddha and

standard-setting processes under a single authoritative body viz. an independent drug 
controller of AYUSH, in alignment with the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, and its

mechanism that actively involves stakeholders in the development of pharmacopoeial 
standards, ensuring greater efficiency and uniformity. Additionally, the Committee 
emphasizes that PCIM&H and CCRAS may come together to coordinate and collaborate 
in this initiative to enhance the scientific testing and evaluation of a larger number of

equitable impetus to all sub-component of the Capacity Building and Continuing Medical 
Education (CME) in Ayush. Underlining the vital role of Research and innovation in 
Ayush Drugs for prioritized diseases, the Committee, recommends to collect data on 
safety, standardization and quality control for Ayush products and practices in order to 
develop evidence-based support on the efficacy of Ayush drugs and therapies. In order to 
inculcate scientific aptitude and expertise relating to Ayush systems, the Ministry should 
chalk out the strategy for development of potential human resource and its management 
in Ayush system. The Committee reiterates its recommendation that the outcome of the 
Research Scheme should successfully demonstrate the effectiveness of Ayush systems and 
the novel technology successfully developed out of such R&D must harness the potential of 
Ayush in the interest of public health delivery.

activities, training, Capacity Building etc.  The Committee, therefore, is of considered view 
that the Scheme is one of the most significant Schemes under AYUSH and accordingly,

UNIFORM &STANDARD LICENSING  
4.3 The Ministry has informed that it is working in coordination with Ayush Grid and state 
licensing Authority, Gujarat to make e-AUSHADHI portal more user-friendly and robust for 
online licensing of Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani and Homoeopathy drugs. 
4.3.1 The Drugs & Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Drugs Rules, 1945 have exclusive regulatory 
provisions for Ayurvedic, Siddha, Unani, and Homoeopathy drugs. Provisions relating to 
Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani Drugs are contained in Chapter IVA and Schedule- I of the Drugs 
and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and in Rules 151 to 169, Schedules E(I), T & TA of the Drugs and 
Cosmetics Rules, 1945. Further, second schedule (4A) of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 
provides standards for Homoeopathic drugs and  Rules 2dd, 30AA, 67 (C-H), 85 (A to I), 106-
A, Schedule K, Schedule M-I of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 pertain to Homoeopathic 
drugs. It is mandatory for the manufacturers to adhere to the prescribed requirements for 
licensing of manufacturing units & medicines including proof of safety & effectiveness, 
compliance with the Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) as per Schedule T & Schedule M-I 
of Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 and quality standards of drugs given in the respective 
pharmacopoeia. 
4.3.2 The matter related to uniform pattern of license was discussed in the meeting of 
Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani Drugs Consultative Committee (ASUDCC) held on 14/03/2024, 
wherein   Committee recommended that all the State Licensing Authorities (SLAs) should give 
uniform pattern of license numbers and to make necessary provisions under the rules to display 
manufacturing license number of the particular product in all the advertisements- electronic, 
social media or print media. The said recommendation was placed in ASUDTAB meeting held 
on 24/07/2024, wherein board recommended for draft notification for certain amendment in the 
Drug Rules for uniform license throughout the country. 

57 
 
4.3.3 The Committee is of view that the Ministry must have a standard licensing process 
based on uniform parameters across all the States so that drug formulations do not vary 
from State to State. A standardized approach will eliminate variations in drug 
formulations from state to state, thereby enhancing the quality, safety, and efficacy of 
AYUSH medicines. This will prevent discrepancies in ingredient composition, dosage, and 
therapeutic claims, ensuring that AYUSH drugs meet the same regulatory and scientific 
benchmarks nationwide. It will also strengthen consumer confidence by guaranteeing that 
all licensed AYUSH drugs adhere to nationally recognized quality standards, ultimately 
fostering wider acceptance and integration of AYUSH medicines in mainstream 
healthcare. 
4.3.4 The Committee, keeping in view the obscure and diverse pattern of licensing that 
creates hurdles for the manufactures for seeking license for production of Ayush products. 
The Committee therefore recommends that arrangement be made to have simplified 
procedure for seeking uniform and standard license that will ensure ease of doing business 
for Ayush manufacturers thereby seeking the objective of AtmaNirbhar Bharat and Make 
in India mission. Moreover, the manufacturers will be encouraged to setup AYUSH 
industry in the country for production of AYUSH products that will ultimately promote 
AYUSH sector in domestic as well as the global market. 
 
Clinical Trials Registry- India (CTRI) 
4.4 The Clinical Trials Registry- India (CTRI), hosted at the ICMR’s National Institute of 
Medical Statistics is a free and online public record system for registration of clinical trials 
being conducted in India that was launched on 20th July 2007. The CTRI also has data sets 
specific to the AYUSH system of medicine where AYUSH-specific information is being 
captured during the trial registration process.  The Committee has been apprised that the 
information pertaining to R&D protocol, approval and subsequent outcomes is maintained 
separately at respective institutes, research councils and other autonomous bodies etc. Clinical 
Trial of CCRAS is being monitored through an elaborated mechanism “Electronic Data 
Capture(EDC)” which is scrutinized at the headquarters level. CCRH is registering all its 
clinical trials on Clinical trial Registry of India before initiation of its research project. NIA has 
established the PMU (Project management Unit) to develop a robust CTMS and also launched 
IMR(Intra Mural Research) Policy for better R&D outcomes. NIA has also developed DDDU ( 
Drug development and Discovery Unit) for development of New Drugs. 
 
4.4.1 The Committee is of considered view that implementing a robust Clinical Trial 
Management System (CTMS) will significantly improve documentation, efficiency, and 
compliance in AYUSH clinical research. All the research councils, institutes and other 
autonomous bodies engaged in R&D, clinic trials and related activities should be brought 
onto to this single platform. Automation of key trial processes, including patient 
recruitment, randomization, monitoring, adverse event reporting, and regulatory 
submissions, will enhance efficiency. By automating workflows, it will reduce manual 
errors, enhance regulatory transparency, and accelerate trial approvals. Standardizing 
research protocols with ICMR/GCP guidelines will ensure uniformity across AYUSH 

58 
 
disciplines, strengthening the scientific validation of traditional medicine. AI-driven 
analytics will support data-driven decision-making, enabling better tracking of adverse 
events and treatment outcomes. Furthermore, a well-integrated CTMS will allow multi-
center trials, facilitating global acceptance of AYUSH-based interventions and positioning 
India as a leader in integrative medicine research. 
4.4.2 The Committee further desires that information on reported claims regarding Ayush 
treatment for controlling cholesterol levels using tablets or injections, supported by 
research-based evidence, if available, may be provided.

4.13 The issues relating to integrative approaches and differences of opinion on public

implementation of health welfare schemes and policies. The Committee therefore feels that

common platform. The Committee desires that through this institutional mechanism,

resolve the issues affecting health policy formulation and implementation strategies. The

Allopathy so that integrated and coordinated efforts may be made for treatment of

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE-  
AT A GLANCE 
 
 
 
FUNCTIONAL AREAS OF THE MINISTRY 
The Committee takes into account the thematic areas of Ayush activities and the 
institutional framework to achieve the objectives of those activities. The Committee 
desires that each and every institution must strive towards achieving the Mission 
Objective of the Ministry of Ayush within the specified time framework. The Committee 
further observes that the broad thematic area of Ayush activities is the key to accomplish 
the mission objectives of the Ministry i.e., improve access to high quality and affordable 
Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha and Sowa-Rigpa (AUS&SR) & Homeopathy medical education, 
availability of adequate and high quality AUS&SR & Homeopathy medical professionals 
in all parts of the country, promote equitable and universal healthcare that encourages 
community health perspective. The thematic area of Quality research in Ayush is 
undertaken through pioneer research councils under MoA such as CCRAS, CCRUM, 
CCRS, CCRH and CCRYN. The Committee, however, feels that in order to address 
emerging challenges of healthcare, there is a need for functional integration of Ayurveda 
and conventional medicine with its affordable and evidence based use to boost Ayurveda 
in the paradigm of contemporary scientific, technological and medical parameters. 
( Para 1.3.3) 
Staff strength of the Ministry  
 
The Committee observes that against the sanctioned strength of 78 posts in various levels a 
total of 53 officers are in-position thereby there is a vacancy in 25 posts, especially at 
middle and lower level, which must be hampering the operational efficiency of the 
Ministry. The Committee, therefore, desires that recruitment process should be expedited 
to fill up the vacant posts at the earliest for efficient working of the Ministry.  
( Para 1.4.1) 
 
PROPOSED INITIATIVES TO BE TAKEN DURING THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2025-26 
 
The Committee appreciates the milestones achieved by the Ministry in year 2023-24 & 
2024-25 and takes note of initiatives proposed for the coming FY 2025-26. Given the 
operational efficiency, professional pursuit and proper & adequate institutional support 
for research councils, educational institutes, regulatory bodies, etc., the Committee 
observes that the Ayush system is striving towards establishing itself an alternative system 
of medicine. The Committee desires that the Ministry should make concerted efforts for 
optimal utilization of the potential of available AYUSH resources and establish the 
Ayushsystem within a pluralistic system of Integrative healthcare and re-emphasizing the 
need for integrating AYUSH in the National Health Mission/National Health Priorities, 
research and education in convergence with the objectives of National Health Policy 
(NHP) 2017. The Committee recommends the Ministry to lay focus on the implementation 
of its schemes, maintaining high standards of education and research and strengthen its 
monitoring mechanism vide its institutional statutory and regulatory bodies to have 

72 
 
Always  Better Control (ABC) over quality and safety of AYUSH drugs. The Committee 
appreciates the new initiatives for the coming year and is of the view that Ayurveda and 
Yoga should reach every household for a Healthy and Fit India. 
( Para 1.8) 
 
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
 
The Committee takes note of the variations between projected demand and allocated BE 
and the budget utilization trend of the Ministry of Ayush. Given the Ministry’s larger 
vision to position Ayush systems as a preferred system of attaining a healthy India the 
Committee expects the Ministry to fully utilize the RE in actual expenditure and make 
necessary plans/policies that should justify for getting a higher share of the Projected 
Demand in the forth-coming financial years.  
( Para 2.1.2) 
 
The Committee observes that there is a recurrent occurrence of reduction of budget 
allocation at RE stage. The Committee recommends that the Ministry make necessary to 
oversee the execution and implementation of plans as per Annual Action Plan and 
Output/Outcome Framework each year. The Committee suggests that an appropriate 
number of staff should be present to meet the needs of the Govt. work, thereby meeting 
the short-term goals and long-term vision of the Ministry.  
( Para 2.3) 
 
 
The Committee observes that the projected demand of the Ministry for the year 2025-26 is 
Rs. 5408.48 crore against which an amount of Rs. 3992.90 crore has been allocated in BE 
2025-26 thus there is a shortfall of Rs. 1415.58 crore.  The Committee expresses its 
concern that reduced budgetary allocation to the Ministry of Ayush in comparison to the 
projected demand would have an adverse impact on the implementation of originally 
conceived projects/schemes/programmes. The Committee, therefore, recommends the 
Ministry of Ayush to approach the Ministry of Finance to seek higher budgetary 
allocation at the supplementary demand stage to ensure that no undertaken 
project/scheme gets suffered for want of requisite fund. 
( Para 2.3.1) 
 
 
The Committee in its 108th Report and 128th Report has recommended allocation of 5% 
and 10% of total health budget, yet the budget allocation is been slowly reduced from year 
2023-24, 2024-25 and 2025-26 in comparison to that of Dept. of Health and Family 
Welfare. The Committee recommends the Ministry to place strong proposals before the 
Ministry of Finance backed by visionary schemes/programmes that would warrant a 
higher budgetary allocation. The Committee expects the Ministry to reach the 10% mark 
in the ensuing financial years.  
    ( Para 2.4.1 ) 
 
 

73 
 
OUTPUT-OUTCOME MONITORING FRAMEWORK (2025-26) 
 
The Committee takes notes of the various details of Output-Outcome Framework of the 
schemes of Ministry of Ayush to be executed during 2025-26. The Committee recommends 
the Ministry of Ayush to have resilient and alert mode of monitoring mechanism to 
oversee the execution of the Schemes/Projects to ensure that the physical targets as set in 
the Output-Outcome Framework is achieved without time and cost overruns. The 
Committee, in this regard, recommends the Ministry to undertake midterm performance 
evaluation of each scheme and projects through Cost Benefit Analysis, targets set vs 
targets achieved. The ministry may publish such analysis in public domain to increase the 
faith of public in the Minstry’s on ground performance. The Committee strongly believes 
that the Output-Outcome Framework will enrich the enabling environment of the 
Ministry of Ayush and bring forth the catalytic changes in providing Ayurvedic and 
Homeopathic mode of treatment to all.  
( Para 2.6.1) 
  
 
MINISTRY’S PROPOSAL TO 15TH FINANCE COMMISSION 
The Committee notes the Ministry aims to enhance AYUSH services, particularly in 
underserved and remote areas, but lacks the resources to do so effectively. The need to 
establish integrated AYUSH hospitals in many districts, has a high financial requirement. 
The Committee also observes that the Ministry is not fully utilizing the funds allocated to 
it.  It's crucial to optimize resource utilization by implementing strategies that improve the 
efficiency and effectiveness of existing programs, focusing on high-impact interventions in 
priority areas, and establishing robust tracking systems to monitor spending and identify 
the most effective resource allocation. Simultaneously, a strategic approach to 
infrastructure expansion is necessary, prioritizing the establishment of integrated AYUSH 
hospitals in underserved districts through a phased approach that aligns with available 
resources, while also exploring cost-effective models for hospital establishment and 
operation.  
( Para 2.7.1) 
The National Ayush Mission (NAM), being a centrally sponsored scheme where Center 
and States have fund share like 60% and 40%. The Committee was apprised that some 
States/ UTs express their inability to contribute their share. Due to the resource crunch, 
the Mission is not effective in achieving goals. The Committee, therefore, recommends the 
Ministry to provide financial assistance schemes for on-boarding the States/UTs on NAM. 
The Ministry may also explore the possibility with the MoF to change the contribution 
ratio of the Centre and State to 70:30 for encouraging the states to get onboard NAM. 
( Para 2.7.2) 
The 15th Finance Commission is till the 31.3.2026. The Committee observes that the M/o 
Ayush must strive hard to integrate Ayush into mainstream healthcare. Besides providing 
Ayush services through PHCs, CHCs and DHs, significant efforts are required in quality 

74 
 
improvement, research and regulatory framework in Ayush healthcare, global 
collaboration, AYUSH market expansion, sustainable development of medicinal plants etc. 
All this would not be possible without adequate development of skilled Health Human 
Resource in the Ayush sector. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry 
should come up with mega schemes in mission mode. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry take proactive steps for correspondence with 16th Finance Commission and 
accordingly chalk out plan for adequate fund allocation and timely release of the same for 
the five years thence for accelerated growth of AYUSH.  
( Para 2.7.3 ) 
 
NATIONAL MEDICINAL PLANTS BOARD 
 
The medicinal plants form the major resource base of our indigenous health care 
traditions. The Committee takes note of the export of Medicinal plants as recorded under 
Ch-12 of HS-Code 1211 valued around US $ 486.78 million in the year 2023-24. The 
Committee appreciates the performance achieved in regard to digital platform namely e-
CHARAK. The Committee suggests to further enhance the reach of the online portal cum 
android based application “e-CHARAK 2.0” for trading of medicinal plants amongst 
various stakeholders involved. The Committee further recommends NMPB to organize 
frequent ‘Buyer-Seller Meet among the Farmer Bodies, Industries and State/UT 
Government. The stakeholders should be encouraged to engage in conclusive buying 
selling business exchanges, discussion on challenges faced in the sector of Medicinal Plants 
Cultivation and Supply Chain Management and the way forward thereon. 
( Para 3.2.6) 
 
The Committee, in view of the crucial role played by the medicinal plants in the overall 
growth of the Ayush Sector, recommends the Ministry to explore the possibility of setting 
up Special Export Zones and more Regional Centers to optimize the strategic reach of the 
Ayush Systems. The Committee further recommends that the NMPB may focus more on 
R&D in all aspects of medicinal plants, development of Agro-techniques, post-harvest 
management, storage and processing, developing molecular characterization tools etc. 
( Para 3.2.7 ) 
 
 
The Committee feels that the role of NMPB in overall growth of Ayush market and 
economic development is very crucial. The Committee therefore recommends the NMPB 
to formulate innovative schemes to attract the cultivators and entrepreneurs in the 
medicinal plants industry and devise ways to enhance the livelihood systems based on 
medicinal plants for farmers, collectors and other stakeholders. 
( Para 3.2.8)

PHARMACOPOEIA COMMISSION FOR INDIAN MEDICINE AND 
HOMOEOPATHY 
The Committee strongly recommends the consolidation of all AYUSH drug-related 
standard-setting processes under a single authoritative body viz. an independent drug 
controller of AYUSH, in alignment with the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, and its 
associated rules. To achieve this, the Ministry should establish a streamlined and inclusive 
mechanism that actively involves stakeholders in the development of pharmacopoeial 
standards, ensuring greater efficiency and uniformity. Additionally, the Committee 
emphasizes that PCIM&H and CCRAS may come together to coordinate and collaborate 
in this initiative to enhance the scientific testing and evaluation of a larger number of 
ASU&H drug samples to ensure safety, efficacy, and quality strengthening the foundation 
of research and standardization in the sector. 
( Para 3.3.5) 
INFORMATION, EDUCATION AND COMMUNICATION (IEC) 
 
The Committee observes that the State-wise reach of Arogya Fair/Ayurveda Parv is less 
compared the size of India comprising of 28 states and 8 UTs. The Committee 
recommends that the reach should cover 50% of the Indian states in coming year and 
eventually should cover all over India in near future to propagate the potentiality of 
Ayush System in prevention and treatment of common ailments. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends the Ministry to leave no stone unturned in efficiently and 
effectively implementing IEC Scheme, thus generating awareness amongst the common 
masses especially in rural, urban slums, hilly & tribal area.  
( Para 3.4.4) 
 
 
PROMOTION OF INTERNATIONAL CO-OPERATION 
 
The Committee takes note of financial and physical performance made under 
International co-operation Scheme vis-à-vis budgetary allocation and set objectives. The 
Committee recommends that going forward communication should be made with first 
world countries like UK and USA for promoting AYUSH among the Indian diaspora as 
well as their native citizens. The Committee realizes the potential in promoting AYUSH 
related healthcare travel to India, accordingly, the Ministry has to chalk out strategies to 
vigorously promote AYUSH system of medicine in international markets support 
investment, exchange of exports to boost Ayush products in global market. The Ministry 
should keep the consideration that Ayush Vision@2047 has target to enhance contribution 
of Ayush Sector upto 7.7% of GDP. The Committee feels that the strategic course of 
action viz. Road shows abroad, CMEs for foreign audience, Familiarization trips, 
Strategic Marketing-Communication through a professional agency, Collateral, Audio 
Video Content, Social Media Marketing can further be taken up by the Ministry for 
achievement of the Mission Objective of the Scheme.  
( Para 3.5.5)

namely AYURVEDA-BIOLOGY INTEGRATED HEALTH RESEARCH (ABIHR) under

impetus to all sub-component of the Capacity Building and Continuing Medical Education 
(CME) in Ayush. Underlining the vital role of Research and innovation in Ayush Drugs 
for prioritized diseases, the Committee, recommends to collect data on safety, 
standardization and quality control for Ayush products and practices in order to develop 
evidence-based support on the efficacy of Ayush drugs and therapies. In order to inculcate 
scientific aptitude and expertise relating to Ayush systems, the Ministry should chalk out 
the strategy for development of potential human resource and its management in Ayush 
system. The Committee reiterates its recommendation that the outcome of the Research 
Scheme should successfully demonstrate the effectiveness of Ayush systems and the novel 
technology successfully developed out of such R&D must harness the potential of Ayush in

AYURSWASTHAY YOJANA

objectives. The Committee observes with concern that the CoE scheme has suffered in the 
year 2024-25, therefore the Committee recommends the Ministry to create awareness 
among stakeholders, establishing a digital platform for application entry, examinations

STATUS OF UTILIZATION CERTIFICATES 
The Committee understands that Utilization Certificate (UC) in government systems is a 
crucial document that verifies how funds allocated for a specific project or scheme have 
been spent. Moreover, UC ensures transparency and accountability by demonstrating that 
the fund allocation has been used for its intended purpose and not misappropriated, and 
that the project achieved its desired outcomes. In this light the Committee has observed 
and recommended time and again regarding the delay in clearing pending UCs. The 
Committee expresses concern over pending UCs to number of 1549 involving Rs. 1608.29 
during 2023-24 and a total number of 1521 pending UCs involving an amount to the tune 
of Rs. 1765.85 in 2024-25. The Committee observes that the largest share in pending UCs 
is that of NAM with 897 UCs worth Rs 1592.09 crores. Timely submission of UCs is very 
crucial in scheme monitoring, subsequent release of funds and successful implementation 
of the scheme. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Ministry must 
expedite its efforts in liquidating UCs as per standard timeline set for the activity. 
States/Uts may be persuaded and encouraged to use the NAM portal efficiently for the 
submitting UCs, SAAPs etc.  
( Para  4.2.2) 
 
UNIFORM &STANDARD LICENSING  
The Committee is of view that the Ministry must have a standard licensing process based 
on uniform parameters across all the States so that drug formulations do not vary from 
State to State. A standardized approach will eliminate variations in drug formulations 
from state to state, thereby enhancing the quality, safety, and efficacy of AYUSH 
medicines. This will prevent discrepancies in ingredient composition, dosage, and 
therapeutic claims, ensuring that AYUSH drugs meet the same regulatory and scientific 
benchmarks nationwide. It will also strengthen consumer confidence by guaranteeing that 
all licensed AYUSH drugs adhere to nationally recognized quality standards, ultimately 
fostering wider acceptance and integration of AYUSH medicines in mainstream 
healthcare. 

89 
 
( Para 4.3.3) 
The Committee, keeping in view the obscure and diverse pattern of licensing that creates 
hurdles for the manufactures for seeking license for production of Ayush products. The 
Committee therefore recommends that arrangement be made to have simplified 
procedure for seeking uniform and standard license that will ensure ease of doing business 
for Ayush manufacturers thereby seeking the objective of AtmaNirbhar Bharat and Make 
in India misson. Moreover, the manufacturers will be encouraged to setup AYUSH 
industry in the country for production of AYUSH products that will ultimately promote 
AYUSH sector in domestic as well as the global market. 
( Para 4.3.4) 
Clinical Trials Registry- India (CTRI) 
The Committee is of considered view that implementing a robust Clinical Trial 
Management System (CTMS) will significantly improve documentation, efficiency, and 
compliance in AYUSH clinical research. All the research councils, institutes and other 
autonomous bodies engaged in R&D, clinic trials and related activities should be brought 
onto to this single platform. Automation of key trial processes, including patient 
recruitment, randomization, monitoring, adverse event reporting, and regulatory 
submissions, will enhance efficiency. By automating workflows, it will reduce manual 
errors, enhance regulatory transparency, and accelerate trial approvals. Standardizing 
research protocols with ICMR/GCP guidelines will ensure uniformity across AYUSH 
disciplines, strengthening the scientific validation of traditional medicine. AI-driven 
analytics will support data-driven decision-making, enabling better tracking of adverse 
events and treatment outcomes. Furthermore, a well-integrated CTMS will allow multi-
center trials, facilitating global acceptance of AYUSH-based interventions and positioning 
India as a leader in integrative medicine research. 
( Para 4.4.1) 
The Committee further desires that information on reported claims regarding Ayush 
treatment for controlling cholesterol levels using tablets or injections, supported by 
research-based evidence, if available, may be provided.

Cosmetics Act to check such malpractices.  
( Para 4.11) 
 
 
The Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry is working on 20,000 students at 
Eklavya Residential Model Schools to focus on TB, Anemia, Haemoglobinopathies and 
malnutrition among those children, in collaboration with M/o Tribal Affairs. The 
Committee is of the opinion that the Ministry must explore such activities including Sickel 
Cell Anemia in the Tribal areas and in the northeastern regions and widen the scope of 

93 
 
collaboration with M/o Tribal Affairs. The Committee has also been apprised of the 
coming proposals for 50 bedded hospitals in every district and 100 bedded hospitals in all 
tier-2 cities. The Committee expects the Ministry to expedite the process ensuring priority 
is given to areas where the AYUSH healthcare is less developed. 
( Para 4.12) 
 
Cooperative and Collaborative Approach between Ayush and Allopathy 
 
The issues relating to integrative approaches and differences of opinion on public health, 
medical education and research, policy formulation and implementation etc. between 
traditional medicine and modern medicine have come up before the Committee time and 
again. The Committee is of the view that these differences affect the implementation of 
health welfare schemes and policies. The Committee therefore feels that there should be 
an institutional mechanism to bring the two systems of medicines on a common platform. 
The Committee desires that through this institutional mechanism, regular joint meetings 
between the M/o Ayush and M/o Health & Family Welfare, NMC and NCISM, NCH and 
Ayush Research Councils may be held to settle the grey areas and resolve the issues 
affecting health policy formulation and implementation strategies. The Committee 
strongly recommends that instead of antagonistic relationship, there should be cooperative 
and collaborative approach and cohesive equilibrium between the Ayush and Allopathy so 
that integrated and coordinated efforts may be made for treatment of various diseases.  
( Para 4.13) 
 
Promotion of Yoga and Naturopathy 
 
The role of Yoga and Naturopathy in health promotion and preventive health is 
undeniable. Awareness of Yoga and its significance has reached international dimensions 
as evident in the celebrations of International Day of Yoga and Yoga parvs/camps being 
organized everywhere in the country. The Committee, however, observes that there is an 
unequal distribution of national institutes of Yoga and Naturopathy across the States and 
UTs, particularly in rural and backward areas. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that national institutes for Yoga and Naturopathy may be opened in states like Bihar, 
Uttar Pradesh, Jharkhand and in NER. The Committee further recommends that Yoga 
camps may be organized not just for jubilation but be organized regularly at Block and 
village levels with the real intention to imbibe attitude and commitment to Yoga and 
Naturopathy by heart. The Committee also desires that Yoga classes may be held 
mandatorily in all primary schools and Yoga instructors in each school may also be 
appointed for this purpose.  
( Para 4.14) 
 
Equitable distribution of Ayush Centres 
 
The Committee has been apprised that there is unequal distribution of Ayush healthcare 
in the country. There are states like Punjab and Maharashtra where there is relatively less 
development of integrated Ayush hospitals and functional Ayush Centres. The Committee 
would like to know how many Ayush Centres and Ayush Grams are functional in all 
states/UTs and recommends that the Ministry of Ayush must ensure equitable 
development of Ayush healthcare and ecosystem across the geographical area of the 

94 
 
country, including setting up of Ayush Centre at the places where these centres are in 
scarce, keeping in view the region-specific requirements and potential in Ayush industry. 
The Committee has also been apprised of the coming proposals for 50 bedded hospitals in 
every district and 100 bedded hospitals in all tier-2 cities. The Committee expects the 
Ministry to expedite the process ensuring priority is given to areas where the AYUSH 
healthcare is less developed. 
( Para 4.15) 
 
  
 Ayush Vision @2047 
 
The Committee, after perusal of the goals, strategies and roadmap of the Ministry for 
reaching the goal of Ayush@2047, the Committee observes that the Ministry is on the 
right course of action. The setting up of GTMC, increase in export of medicinal plants, 
setting up of 12273 plus AAMs etc. would enrich Ayush Eco-system. The Committee 
desires that the Ministry of Ayush should leave no stone unturned in achieving the set 
targets set in Ayush Vision @2047. The Committee desires the work done so far by the 
Ministry in line with the larger vision of the Ministry. The Committee, however, observes 
with concern a general trend in under-utilization of the allocated funds to the Ministry for 
various schemes that may halt progress of Ayush Mission. The Committee recommends 
that the Ministry enhance the monitoring mechanism in place for overseeing the optimal 
utilization of the funds allocated. The Committee desires the Ministry to be more effective 
in timely utilization of budgetary allocation. The Committee is of considered view that 
timely development of infrastructure and capital assets will put in place a strong 
foundation for the growth of AYUSH. 
( Para 5.1.1) 
The Committee takes note of various components of Ayush Vision@2047 that inter-alia 
cover Strategic Areas (Research, Education & Capacity Building, Healthcare, 
Manufacturing& Services) opportunities (Governance & Innovation Governance, Global 
Value Chain) that would pave the way of maximum promotion and popularization of 
Ayush Sector in domestic market and global fora. The Committee is of the considered 
view that application of Ayush in Clinical healthcare, biochemistry, lifestyle illness would 
lead to standardization of Ayush research & medicine system and thus contributing to 
evidence based solution, thereby boosting the new paradigm shift in Ayush sphere. The 
Committee believes that identification of strategic course of action education & capacity 
building healthcare and manufacturing & services would go a long in furtherance of 
Ayush Sector. The Committee strongly visualize that a lot of opportunities are awaiting in 
areas of governance of tariff lines, formulation and standardization & quality of Ayush 
Sector. Needless to say, quality certification and labs & healthcare NABL Accreditation of 
all labs would stamp Ayush Sector is the global market. 
( Para 5.1.2) 
 
The Committee, however, cautions the Ministry of Ayush against any dilly dallying 
approach and reluctance over its strategic & proactive course of action, otherwise 
achievement of set targets under Vision Ayush@2047 would remain a distant dream. 
( Para 5.1.3) 

95 
 
 
The Committee is also of the considered view that since Ayush Vision@2047 is a long 
distant drawn Roadmap, it is but natural that the Ministry should draw short-term plan 
for certain achievement of set target and must have provision of mid-term evaluation of 
progress made and if required modify the course of action to achieve the target set. The 
Committee reposes faith in Ministry of Ayush for achieving the goals set in Vision 
Ayush@2047 provided there are adequate budgetary allocation of each of its 
scheme/project, optimum utilization of fund under a resilient monitoring mechanism &co-
ordinating and controlling the factors of deviance. 
( Para 5.1.4) 
 
As deposed by the Secretary, M/o Ayush before the Committee, the Ayush manufacturing 
and services command about US$ 50 billion market size at present and the ambitious plan 
is to reach US$ 200 billion market size in the next 5 years.  While the Committee is 
delighted to note the rapid increase in the size of the Indian Ayush industry, with 
budgetary allocation of 0.012 percent of GDP, the Committee is quite apprehensive of the 
ambitions of the ministry to grow and develop Ayush as per its expectations. The 
Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Ayush needs to come up with more new 
schemes and strategies for growth and development of Ayush activities and claim for a 
much more enhanced budgetary allocation in comparison to the Department of Health & 
Family Welfare. 
( Para 5.1.5) 
 
FUTURE PLANS 
The Committee appreciates the larger vision of Ayush @2047 and the future plans of 
making AYUSH a multi-billion dollar market, yet the Committee is wary about the 
present situation of the healthcare in the country and observes that yearly short term 
goals be given a priority and direction to provide best AYUSH healthcare to the public by 
establishing PHCs/CHCs at district level etc. The Committee is in agreement of the 
Ministry of Ayush that the target of 30 lakh Ayush professionals in country by 2047, 
setting up one Ayush HQ in every district with at least one Ayush College, creation of over 
50 lakh new jobs, increasing contribution of Ayush to up to 7.7% of GDP etc. by the 2047 
is achievable by converting the long duration ambitious targets into short-term plan with 
smaller objective & goals and having co-ordinating and controlling monitoring 
mechanism over the implementation progress of projects/schemes/programmes ensuring 
achievement of set targets/goals/objectives. The Committee, in this regard, recommends 
the Ministry to make concerted efforts to implement the projects/schemes/programme 
through development of botanical drugs, entering into Free Trade Agreements (FTA) with 
favourable countries for enlarging global markets & enhancing exports level to a new 
height, establishing global hub of traditional medicine alongside WHO GTMC, production 
& promotion standard & quality drugs, ensuring widespread availability of 
AyushAushadi Kendra etc.  
( Para 5.2.1) 

96 
 
The Committee understand that the Global Footprint of Yoga needs to be further 
enhanced to tap into the global market and globalization of Yoga and Ayurveda training 
under Yoga Certification Board, Ayurveda Training Accreditation Board(ATAB)  may be 
promoted internationally for highest global participation in receiving and propagating the 
ancient form of knowledge rechristened in Ayush System i.e. Ayurveda, Yoga & 
Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Rigpa-Sowa and Homeopathy for alternative mode of 
treatment of diseases and  healthy living. 
( Para 5.2.2)

1.1.1 The Committee observes that the delay in the cons truction work was mainly due to 
non-performance by the selected construction agencies along with improper planning and 
ineffective monitoring. Though the construction status is near completion in the first three 
Packages, under Package IV only 60% of the w ork is complete. It is high time that the 
Institute should strengthen the existing infrastructure and strive to complete the remaining 
work within the stipulated time limits as it has been six years since the Institute has been 
operationalized and the cons truction work is still incomplete. The Committee is inclined to 
observe that the selection of construction agencies was devoid of merit and transparency 
resulting in substantial time and cost overrun. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
stringent monitoring mechanism should be put in place to ensure timely completion of work

necessary steps to take possession of the area which is under encroachment. The Committee is

1.6 Budgetary Allocation 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.6.1 The Committee is anguished to observe there has been underutilization of funds till 
the year 2016 -17 in AIIMS, Rishikesh. The Committee notes that out of a total budget 
estimate of Rs. 426.50 crores during 2018-19, only Rs. 165 crores of funds have been released 
till 15th October, 2018. The Committee also notes that under GIA (CCA) alloca tion has been 
slashed to Rs 250 crores from the projected demand of Rs 1186.96 crores in BE 2018 -19. The 
Committee is of the opinion that AIIMS, Rishikesh has set up over ambitious  targets for itself 
and therefore, needs to reconsider these demands. A cost  benefit analysis also needs to be 
done vis-à-vis availability of other tertiary care services in the adjoining area. The Committee 
recommends that a common criterion along with a rational approach towards utilization of 
financial allocation for each AIIMS  needs to be done. The Committee is not convinced with 
the justification for overall projected demand to the tune of 1363.46 crores which is far above 
the expenditure incurred in other similar tertiary care center with much higher OPD/IPD load. 
Needless to say the Committee is concerned at the audacious projection which alone is almost 
equal to the sum total of all the remaining five regional AIIMS under study. The Committee 
recommends that suitable benchmark for AIIMS standards be formulated by the Central  
Institute Body (CIB) so that fiscal discipline and prudence in the utilization of the resources is 
done under all circumstances. The Committee recommends that AIIMS, Rishikesh should 
review its projections to a more realistic level. 
(Para 3.9 of the report) 
 
1.6.2 The Committee observes that in -principle approval of many important centers like 
Cardiac Science Center, Neuroscience Center, Ad vance Eye Center, Lung Center  with 
estimated expenditure to the tune of Rs. 100 crores each has been given by the Gov erning 
Body but the construction work could not be started due to unavailability of funds. Besides, 
the Committee is concerned to note that when there has already been a construction of a full -
fledged hospital to seek Rs. 97.61 crore for Administrative blo ck, Rs. 100 crore for the 
academic block, Rs. 100 crore for research block and Rs. 383 crore for residential 
accommodation gives an impression that there is no need for optimum/rational utilization of 
scarce resources. The Committee, therefore, recommends to the Ministry to monitor the 
utilization of funds given to AIIMS, Rishikesh with utmost caution and justification. The 
Committee also recommends for a comparative cost -benefit analysis of AIIMS, Rishikesh 
with other regional AIIMS specifically AIIMS, Bhubaneswar in this regard, as the Committee 
finds it to be the better managed in terms of investment outcome scale and rational utilization 
of limited resources. The Committee is of the opinion that regional AIIMS should provide 
tertiary health care in the n eglected region but should not merely duplicate the facilities 
available with AIIMS Delhi. The Committee recommends that setting up of advanced centers 
should be done only when AIIMS Rishikesh achieves at least 50% of the OPD footfall of 
AIIMS Delhi and th e existing infrastructure is put to optimum usage. Availability of
