Recommendation 
1.2.5 Further, the Department should look into the possibility of involving private sector which 
can contribute through competitive pay packages, which would be well within t heir realm as 
promotion of PPP. 
(Para 1.3.8 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.2.6 As part of this effort, DHR is in the process of establishing the Medical Innovation 
Development Acceleration Council (MIDAC): a special purpose vehicle envisioned as a strategic 
institutional mechanism to drive biomedical innov ation through effective public -private 
collaboration. Through this proposed section 8 company, we plan to engage Indian talent in 
Health Research in the private sector in contributing to the national health priorities of India.   
1.3 Landmarks in Health Research in India 
Recommendation 
1.3.1 While going through the major landmarks in Health Research in India in the last decade, 
the Committee notices that the India has done considerably well in the field of Communicable 
Diseases, commensurate to its own needs as well as to contributing the global knowledge pool. 
The Committee is appreciative of this achievement. The India Disease Burden Study, mentioned 
by the Department as a breakthrough initiative, provided  crucial insights into the shifting burden 
of diseases in India, highlighting the growing prevalence of Non -Communicable diseases 
(NCDs). Going by the indicators provided by the Study, India‘s efforts in the area of NCDs needs 
further impetus. 
(Para 1.4.1of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.3.2 ICMR research in NCD continued to expand and strengthen its diverse portfolio, 
addressing critical and contemporary health challenges. The primary focus remains on the 
prevention, diagnosis, and management of chronic condi tions, including Oncology, 
Cardiovascular Diseases, Mental Health, Neurological Sciences, Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolic 
Syndrome, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Diseases, Gastroenterology, Geriatrics, Oral Health, 
Orthopedics, and Nephrology & Urology, wi th efforts directed toward the prevention, diagnosis, 
and management of chronic health conditions. 
1.3.3 Additionally, research activities have continued in the fields of Otorhinolaryngology , 
Hematology, Anesthesiology, and Disability, Rehabilitation, and Assistive Technology. Other 
key areas of focus included Trauma, Accidents and Injuries, Environmental and Occupational 
Health, Climate Change, Tobacco, and Chronic Disease Health Research. M ultidisciplinary 

4 
 
studies in Toxicology, Anatomy, Anthropology, Nanomedicine, and Traditional Medicine also 
highlighted ICMR‘ commitment to advancing innovation in healthcare and biomedicalsciences. 
1.3.4 Some of the achievements i.e. Initiatives of the Nat ional importance of the past year may 
be highlighted as: 
(i) Cancer care: 
a.  CARE-Clinical Pharmacology –ICMR‘s CARE- Clinical Pharmacology initiative 
focused on therapeutic monitoring of anti -cancer drugs such as sunitinib and 
docetaxel, showing that dru g monitoring improved patients‘ quality of life (QOL) 
and reduced treatment costs.  
b.  PFOS (PREVALL): ICMR, in collaboration with Tata Memorial Center -
ACTREC, developed a powder for oral suspension (PFOS) of 6 -mercaptopurine 
(PREVALL), which helps in acc urate dosing for children undergoing treatment 
for Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia (ALL). Since children aged 1 –10 often face 
difficulties swallowing tablets, this liquid formulation of 6 -MP helps in 
overcoming this issue and ensures better treatment outcome s. The product, 
expected to benefit approximately 10,000 children annually, was patented and 
launched on November 25, 2023. 
(ii) Cardiovascular Disease 
a. PACT-HF Trial – This trial, aimed at preventing repeat hospital admissions and 
death in Heart Failure patients, recruited 1,693 patients, with a 97% follow-up rate 
and a 9% mortality rate at six months. 
b. The India Hypertension Control Initiative (IHCI) – IHCI has successfully 
expanded to 154 districts, enrolling over 5.1 million hypertensive patients ac ross 
22,000 health facilities, including 16,000 Health & Wellness Centers. Nearly half 
(47%) of the registered patients have achieved BP control. 
c. STEMI Care Pathway: Implemented in districts of Himachal Pradesh, Punjab, 
Uttar Pradesh and Andhra Pradesh,  this initiative demonstrated that STEMI 
patients can be diagnosed at CHC level via tele -ECG and  receive life saving 
thrombolytic therapy. The model has since been upscaled to the entire state of 
Himachal Pradesh, Punjab and 4 districts of Andhra Pradesh. 
(iii) Stroke and Neurological Research 
a. INSTRuCT Clinical Trials – The Indian Stroke Clinical Trial Network 
(INSTRuCT) was established to create a cutting -edge stroke clinical trial 
infrastructure in India. Initially, INSTRuCT Phase I undertook two clini cal 
trials across 30 centers. The network expanded in Phase II, encompassing 

5 
 
58 centers. Currently, four clinical trials are ongoing under this network, 
each addressing distinct aspects of stroke care and treatment. 
b. FeSSH Trial – (Fever, hyperglycemia, swallowing and hypertension  
management in acute stroke: Stepped wedged cluster randomized trial with 
cross-sectional data collection): Baseline data were collected across 20 
centers, with 12 centers transitioning to the intervention phase. A total of 
3,022 eligible patients were identified from a screened population of 4,818. 
c. SMRUTHI India – The Strategic Multimodal Intervention in At -Risk 
Elderly Indians for the Prevention of Dementia (SMRUTHI India) aims to 
establish a prospective longitudinal cohort o f elderly individuals with 
multiple risk factors (CAIDE ≥ 6) and develop a validated multimodal ―care 
bundle‖ intervention in four MRHRU field areas. 
(iv) Diabetes Research 
a. Indian Diabetic Risk Score: The Indian Diabetic Risk Score was evaluated 
and found to be a cost-effective tool for screening diabetes in Asian Indians. 
b. INDIAB Study: The INDIAB study provided state -specific obesity 
prevalence data for better policy planning of the nationalprogram and 
suggested age -specific HbA1c cut -offs to minimiz e over -diagnosis of 
diabetes, especially in elderly individuals. The survey was completed in 30 
states/ UTs, with follow -up studies completed in  Arunachal Pradesh and 
Tamil Nadu and the data is being analyzed. The study in the Union 
Territories has also been completed. 
c. Dietary Recommendations: ICMR‘s research also highlighted the 
importance of dietary changes for diabetes management. The data 
recommended reducing carbohydrates and increasing protein intake for 
Type 2 diabetes (T2D) remission and preventi ng progression from pre -
diabetes to T2D. 
d. Young Diabetes Registry: ICMR‘s Young Diabetes Registry reported 
critical data on the prevalence of Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes, along with 
complications such as retinopathy, neuropathy, and nephropathy. This 
registry also documented a high incidence of co -morbidities such as 
autoimmune thyroid disease and hypertension in diabetic patients.

1.5 Emerging Technologies and Ethical Concerns related to Health Research  
Recommendation 
1.5.1 The Committee recognises the importance of adoption of new technologies, innovation 
and constant endeavour for development of new drugs and treatment methods. Clinical trials are 
an inalienable data generating component of this continuing quest. The regulatory architecture 
now in place in the Country are taken note of, however, the Committee would like to emph asise 
the need to ensure ‗informed‘ consent of the participants of clinical trials which should invariably 
include sharing of information beforehand about how the data generated out of the trial would be 
used or shared. It is important to ensure that the p articipants fully understand the risks and 
benefits of a study, management of sensitive personal information and balancing the need for 
research advancement with individual privacy rights. Digitalization and sharing of patient 
information bears privacy imp lications that needs to be addressed and fixed with appropriate 
provisions. 
(Para 1.6.2 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.5.2 ICMR emphasizes the primacy of informed consent, underscoring that the rights, safety, 
and well-being of research participants must remain the highest priority. This principle is clearly 
articulated in the National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Hea lth Research involving 
Human Participants, 2017 published by ICMR. The New Drugs and Clinical Trials (NDCT) 
rules, 2019 also gives a format of preparing informed consent documents. In case of clinical 
trials, ethics approval is provided only after scrutinizing the informed consent documents; both in 
English and the relevant regional language. Funds released by ICMR for the research project are 
conditional to the valid ethics approval documents.  
1.5.3 In alignment with these guidelines, it is standard resea rch practice that the Principal 
Investigator (PI) and the designated study staff responsible for obtaining informed consent are 
adequately trained prior to the initiation of any study. Patient information sheets are prepared in 
languages that are comprehen sible to potential participants and they are given ample 
opportunities to clarify the doubts, if any. The patient information sheet clearly describes the 
risks and benefits of participating in the study, the voluntariness of participation and that there 
will be no negative impact of non-participation or withdrawal from the trial.   
1.5.4 It is ensured that all the clinical trials that are conducted and coordinated by ICMR follow 
the principles of ethics and written informed consent is appropriately obtained . It is also ensured 
that confidentiality of data is maintained by the study team. Data collected digitally is always 
anonymized and personal identifiers such as name are not collected.

1.23 AI for early detection of cancers 
Recommendation 
1.23.1  The  Committee, while acknowledging AI as a viable technique in the arena of early 
cancer detection, is apprehensive about its possible drawbacks. To make AI a success the basic 
requirement is large amount of quality data, algorithms to examine the voluminous data with 
precision & accuracy for efficient diagnosis and last but not the least comes the ethical concerns. 

28 
 
To overcome these impediments, the Committee feels that Government needs to invest in R&D, 
requires active collaboration across disciplines, formu lation of standards guidelines, capacity 
building of clinicians and researchers to make successful use of technology of AI in medical 
field, which is at a nascent stage now. The Committee is also concerned to note that in case of 
cancer treatment the outco mes are not in sync with global standards as advanced targeted 
therapies by making use of genomics and proteomics is not widely done in India. The 
Committee, accordingly, advocates for cutting edge research in the field of genomics and 
proteomics and also suggests that the outcome of these studies be made available to common 
citizens so that early detection and cure of cancer reaches the common population.  
(Para 4.12.1 of the Report)

products/findings. Regulatory frameworks, a technology/product has to g o through during 
developmental stages, has been put in place to ensure the quality, safety and effectiveness of the 
product. However, many a times, innovators find traversing this labyrinth more difficult than 
discovering the product itself. Hence, it is o nly appropriate that the developmental stages, a new 

30 
 
technology/product has to go through, before it can be commercially made available, are 
christened as ‗Valley of Death‖.  
(Para 4.13.2 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.24.2  In response to the Hon‘ble  Committee's recommendations, the Department of Health 
Research has envisioned several focused interventions under MIDAC, including the MedTech 
Mitra initiative, to directly address the challenges faced by healthcare innovators: 
i)   Establishment of MIDAC as a Section 8 Company: MIDAC is proposed to be 
established as a not -for-profit corporate entity under the Companies Act, 2013, 
with the core mandate to facilitate the translation of research into commercially 
viable products. MIDAC will act as a central platform to address barriers in 
clinical validation, intellectual property management, regulatory navigation and 
technology transfer. 
ii)  Bridging the "Valley of Death": Recognizing the developmental void many 
innovations face, MIDAC will provide structur ed handholding, grant support and 
validation infrastructure. Through dedicated sub -schemes like Validation and 
Evaluation Support to Medical Innovations (VESMI)  and Biomedical Product 
Development and Management (BPDM) , MIDAC will fund innovations from 
early-stage concept through to regulatory-ready status. 
iii) MedTech Mitra Platform Operationalization: Under MIDAC, the MedTech Mitra 
platform will be scaled up to assist startups, SMEs and academic innovators by 
providing expert guidance on regulatory pathwa ys, clinical trials and IP filing. It 
will facilitate access to ICMR‘s trial networks and regulatory support from 
CDSCO and engages in capacity building to empower innovators in navigating 
technical and legal requirements. 
iv) Support for Regulatory Compli ance and Risk De -Risking: MIDAC enables 
accelerated clinical validation and performance evaluation, especially for 
diagnostics, therapeutics and vaccines, which often stagnate due to lack of 
regulatory clarity or infrastructural support. The platform will also assist in pre -
submission regulatory guidance and post -market surveillance studies, enhancing 
trust and product quality. 
v) Enhancing Public -Private Partnerships: MIDAC has formalized collaborations 
with industry and research organizations to promote t ranslational research through 
Public-Private Partnerships (PPP), a key mechanism to bridge resource and 
expertise gaps. 

31 
 
1.24.3  The establishment of MIDAC and the expansion of MedTech Mitra will represent a direct 
and comprehensive response to the Committee's observations. These initiatives are strategically 
designed to de -risk innovation, overcome regulatory hurdles and enable faster access of 
indigenous medical technologies to the market; thereby transforming the ―Valley of Death‖ into a 
bridge to success for Indian healthcare innovators. 
Recommendation 
1.24.4  The Committee endorses the importance of setting up a dedicated entity to handhold the 
healthcare innovators in their research to market journey. The choice of a Section 8 company also 
prima facie looks apt to the Committee as the elimination of profit motive helps in concentrating 
on the goals effectively, though there are other statutory benefits as well. The Committee desires 
the DHR to furnish the details of the rationale for setting up of MIDAC as a Section 8 Company. 
(Para 4.13.3 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.24.5 In alignment with the Hon‘ble  Committee's endorsement, the Department of Health 
Research (DHR) has strategically proposed establishment of the Medical Innovations 
Development Acceleration Council (MIDAC) as a Section 8 Company under the Companies Act, 
2013, for the following key reasons: 
a) Non-Profit Mandate Aligned with Public Health Goals: MIDAC is envisioned not 
as a revenue -generating enterprise but as a mission -driven enabler to bridge the 
gap between biomedical research and public access to affordable technologies. A 
Section 8 structure ensures legal and institutional alignment with public health 
imperatives, free from commercial pressures, thus maintaining scientific integrity, 
equity and transparency. 
b) Flexibility and Operational Autonomy:  As a Section 8 Company, MIDAC can 
function with greater agility and efficiency than traditional government 
departments, allowing quick decision -making in areas such as IP licensing, 
contract execution, hiring technical experts and fund mobilization. It offers a 
suitable legal platform to form multi-sectoral partnerships with academia, industry 
and international donors; critical for translational research. 
c) Statutory and Financial Advantages: MIDAC can receive grants, donations, CSR 
funds and equity -free investments and is eligible for tax exemptions under 
Sections 12AA and 80G of the Income Tax Act. These benefits make MIDAC an 
attractive and credible partner for private stakeholders and philanthropic 
institutions seeking to invest in public health innovation. 

32 
 
d) Precedents from Other Strat egic Government Initiatives: Successful Section 8 
entities such as BIRAC (DBT), iDEX (Defence)and IN -SPACe (ISRO) 
demonstrate the effectiveness of this model in driving sectoral innovation.MIDAC 
draws inspiration from these to address the unique challenges of India‘s healthcare 
innovation ecosystem; particularly for technologies with limited immediate 
commercial demand but high national health value. 
e) Institutional Synergy and IP Stewardship:  Operating under the aegis of DHR, 
MIDAC complements ICMR‘s rese arch mandate by facilitating clinical 
validation, IP protection and technology transfer —functions which require an 
independent but closely aligned organizational entity.It allows the management of 
IP rights, royalties and industry licensing with profession al autonomy, enabling 
reinvestment into innovation and ecosystem development. 
f) Accountability and Governance: MIDAC will be governed by a Board of 
Directors, including senior officials from DHR, MoHFW and independent experts, 
ensuring transparency, accountability and strategic alignment with national health 
priorities. 
1.24.6 Establishing MIDAC as a Section 8 Company allows the Department of Health Research 
to institutionalize a mission -oriented, flexible and collaborative platform dedicated to advancing 
health innovations. This model ensures the focus remains on public good rather than profit, 
aligning perfectly with the goals endorsed by the Committee and ensuring effective 
implementation of India‘s biomedical innovation strategy. 
Recommendation 
1.24.7  The Committee notes that proposal for MIDAC has got in -principle by DHR approval of 
Department of Expenditure, M/oFinance. Though Rs 200.00 cr. was sought for MIDAC in BE 
2025-26, but the fund was not allocated as the final approval for MIDAC is yet to be received. 
The Committee is of the firm opinion that if MIDAC is incorporated with the stated objective, as 
presented before the Committee by Secretary, DHR, it would be a path breaking measure. 
Accordingly, the Committee strongly recommends that DHR shall pursue the final approvals for 
MIDAC fervently and that the M/o Finance should allocate the required funds for the company 
on high priority. 
(Para 4.13.4 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.24.8   We thank the Hon‘ble Committee for its support.

1.28 Elimination of Tuberculosis  
Recommendation 
1.28.1 The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that ICMR should oversee a 
countrywide screening programme to be done through portable x -ray machines to detect 

37 
 
tuberculosis at an early stage in consultation with the State Governments. Suitable advisories 
need to be issued to all States so that scourge of TB is eliminated from India within a stipulated 
time.  
(Para 5.4.1 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.28.2 In reference to Para 5.4.1, regarding the recommendation of ICMR to oversee a 
countrywide TB screening pro gram through portable X -ray machines in consultation with State 
Governments, the following points are submitted: 
1.28.3 Despite achieving the highest -ever case notifications with 26.07 lakh TB cases reported 
under national program, approximately 10% cases (2.5 lakh cases) are still missed, continuing the 
chain of transmission in the community. The National TB Prevalence Survey revealed that 
nearly1/3rd of TB patients identified were asymptomatics, underscoring the limitations of 
symptom-based screening alon e.  Also, during the recent 100 -Day TB Elimination Campaign, 
39.6% of TB cases (2.85 lakh out of 7.19) were asymptomatics who were primarily identified 
through increased use of upfront chest X -ray examination coupled with molecular testing. This  
has reaffirmed the crucial role of chest X -ray imaging in systematic TB screening. The WHO 
also recommends the systematic screening of high risk individuals using mobile handheld X -ray 
integrated with artificial intelligence (AI) tools. 
1.28.4 In this regard, ICMR has been actively validating the portable handheld X -ray devices 
and has encouraged domestic manufacturing to enhance supply, promote competitiveness and 
reduce costs. To date, five such devices have been validated by ICMR and are being used in field 
settings. Additionally, DHR -ICMR has recommended three AI -based tools for real -time 
interpretation of chest X -rays in settings where expert radiological opinion is scarce. 
Complementing these advances, ICMR has also validated and recommended cost -effective, true 
point-of-care molecular tests, providing an opportunity to scale up molecular diagnostics 
enabling faster and reliable confirmation of TB cases. 
1.28.5 Building on these developments and the success of the 100 -Day Intensified TB 
Elimination Campaign across 347 districts in 33 states using the portable handheld X -rays (n=84) 
provided by the ICMR, the MoH&FW is now expanding community -based Active Case Finding 
(ACF) initiatives to all districts in the country where systematic screening of high -risk and  
vulnerable populations is prioritized. These portable devices have been found acceptable in 
communities and easy to operate in remote and hard -to-reach areas. Active community 
engagement, with the involvement of local health workers such as ASHA workers i n the ACF 
strategy, will significantly aid in the early detection of TB cases and identification of missed 
cases, effectively breaking the chain of transmission. 
1.28.6 A continuous ACF monitoring mechanism, data management system, and periodic review 
at both State and Central levels through the national TB program are essential to ensure robust 
oversight, accountability, and progress towards the country‘s TB elimination goals. 

38

Recommendation 
1.29.1 The Committee came across that India with its huge population needs to have its own 
indigenous medical devices industry. The Committee is of the opinion that adequate testing

Recommendation 
2.6.1 The Committee has been given to understand that reducing the duration of patents is one 
of the options for making healthcare more affordable in India as once the duration of patents is 
over, Indian manufacturers can produce the drugs at a lower cost. So th e reduction of Patent 
duration can reduce the cost of treatment of diseases like cancer through cheaper drugs like 
antibody-based drugs which would certainly bring down the out of pocket expenditure of 
patients.  Since the subject matter of Patent and IP i s under the Ministry of Commerce the 
Committee, therefore, recommends for an inter -ministerial consultation for a viable solution in 
the matter.  The Committee desires that ICMR -DHR to look into the matter and have an 
interministerial discussion at the earliest. 
(Para 4.14.1 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
2.6.2 Based on the recommendations of the Hon‘ble  Committee regarding decreasing the 
duration of patents as a strategy to make healthcare technologies affordable and accessible in 
India, it may please be noted that the patent terms are governed by The World Trade 
Organization (WTO), by the Trade -Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS) 

48 
 
agreement. This agreement sets out minimum requirements for the protection of intellectual 
property rights including a patent term of 20 years that all WTO member countries are obligated 
to incorporate into their national legislation. India has been a member of the WTO since 1995 and 
has been committed to aligning its laws with its provisions and therefore decreasing the patent 
duration for making healthcare affordable and accessible may not be feasible in lig ht of the 
national laws and international treaties. However, other suitable mechanisms as recommended by 
the Committee are noted for exploring suitable avenues for making the healthcare technologies 
affordable and accessible.

3.11 HPV vaccines 
Recommendation 
3.11.1 The Committee, like the majority of the people in the Country, is hopefully waiting for 
the results of the trial related to the development of single dose HPV Vaccine under the guidance 
of ICMR. The success of the trials could provide a major fillip to HPV  immunisation in India as 
there is only multiple dose vaccines available at present which although provide protection. 
However, multiple doses have practical inconveniences, like keeping track of the dosage 
schedule, etc. The Committee is of the view that introduction of a single dose vaccine would 
considerably increase successful vaccination percentage as the vaccination schedule can be 
completed with one shot. This, in turn, will have a commensurate impact on the reduction of 
incidence of cervical cancer,  which is a leading cause of cancer among women. Further, a 
homegrown vaccine can drastically bring down the cost of vaccination. This factor can accelerate 
the consolidation of the HPV vaccine in the Universal Immunization Programme. Hence, the 
Committee observes that the development of single dose HPV vaccine should be completed as 
per the set schedule. The Committee observes that HPV vaccine can be a path breaker in breaking 
the vicious cycle of the cancer of the cervix. A countrywide campaign supported by the Central 
Government is needed to ensure that 100% administration of HPV vaccine is done among all 

64 
 
girls with monitoring by ICMR. Steps be also taken to substantially reduce the price of the 
vaccine so that the high price does not become a hindrance in this programme.  
(Para 4.11.1 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
3.11.2 In order to address these issues, ICMR is conducting a study titled "Antibody Response 
following One Dose of Cervavac® as compared to One Dose of Gardasil  ® Vaccine in Healthy 
Girls Aged 9 -14 Years: A Non -inferiority, Multicenter, Double -blind, Randomized Controlled 
Trial" across three sites in India - Noida, Pune and Kolkata. Enrollment of trial participants has 
been completed (504 participants) and follow ups are currently ongoing. Expected date of 
completion of two year follow up is March 2027, following which the results of the trial will be 
made available. 
Further Recommendation 
3.11.3 Though the Committee appreciates the sharing of information about trials of single 
dose HPV Vaccine being carried out in the country, it does not find the reply of the 
Government to have adequately addressed  all the issues highlighted in the 
recommendation. Need for a country wide campaign promoting HPV Vaccine  and the cost

is also important for the successful completion of vaccination schedule as it would be less 
challenging logistically in our  administrative and infrastructure milieu. In view of this, the 
Committee reiterates its recommendation and wants a complete answer on all facets of the

4.1 Role of public-private partnerships (PPPs) in Health Research Funding 
Recommendation  
4.1.1 The Committee notes that while on the one hand DHR acknowledges the importance of 
Public Private Partnerships (PPPs) for the development of innovations and informs that ICMR 
has successfully completed several projects under PPP mode, there is an absence o f an 
institutional mechanism for PPP. In view of the submission of DHR and the fact that promotion 
of PPP is one of the businesses allocated to DHR as per the Allocation of Business Rules of the 
Government of India, the Committee recommends that DHR should  come out with an 
institutionalised mechanism for promoting PPP. 
 (Para 1.5.2 of the Report) 
Action Taken  
4.1.2 Department of Health Research (DHR) acknowledges and appreciates the Hon'ble 
Committee's observation regarding the need for an institutional me chanism to strengthen Public -
Private Partnerships (PPPs) in health research. While DHR and ICMR have successfully engaged 
with the private sector through project -specific collaborations (MDMS, HTAIn etc.), the 
Department concurs that a dedicated, structure d, and sustainable framework is essential for 
scaling and systematizing PPP initiatives across the health research ecosystem. 
4.1.3 As part of this effort, DHR is in the process of establishing the Medical Innovation 
Development Acceleration Council (MIDAC): a special purpose vehicle envisioned as a 
strategic institutional mechanism to drive biomedical innovation through effective public -private 
collaboration. 
4.1.4 Vision and Institutional Role of MIDAC 
4.1.5 MIDAC is conceived as a flagship initiati ve under DHR to foster translational biomedical 
research, accelerate product development, and enable commercialization of indigenous 
technologies. It directly aligns with DHR's mandate under the Allocation of Business Rules 
(1961), which includes inter -sectoral coordination and the promotion of PPPs in health and 
biomedical research. 
4.1.6 MIDAC's vision is to leverage the collective strengths of government, academia, industry, 
and startups to address India's pressing public health challenges through innova tion and 
indigenous product development. Its mission is to systematically support the transformation of 

67 
 
research leads -originating from ICMR, academia, and industry -into validated, market -ready 
health technologies through an institutionalized PPP model. 
4.1.7 Role of MIDAC in Promoting PPP in Biomedical Innovation 
4.1.8 MIDAC's institutional framework will operationalize PPPs across four interlinked 
domains: 
1. Translational Research and Product Development 
MIDAC will identify promising innovations, originating from ICMR and the 
broader research ecosystem, and forge PPPs to co -develop these into diagnostics, 
therapeutics, vaccines, and medical devices. PPPs will help bridge resource gaps, provide 
technical expertise, and ensure scalability of innovations for public health deployment. 
2. Intellectual Property and Technology Transfer 
MIDAC will serve as a centralized hub for managing ICMR's intellectual assets, 
facilitating patent filing, licensing, and royalty management. It will foster strategic 
collaborations with industry partners for the commercialization of public -funded 
innovations-thus creating a strong innovation-to-market pipeline under a PPP framework. 
3. Pre-Clinical and Clinical Validation 
To address critical bottlenecks in biomedical R&D, MI DAC will support 
validation infrastructure (labs, networks, panels), performance evaluation protocols, and 
field feasibility studies. It will enable industry partners, startups, and government agencies 
to jointly conduct evaluations required for regulatory  approvals and programmatic 
adoption. 
4. MedTech Mitra Platform 
MIDAC will also operationalize the MedTech Mitra platform, developed in 
collaboration with NITI Aayog, ICMR, and CDSCO, to provide comprehensive 
handholding to innovators. Through targeted PPP s, the platform will support startups and 
SMEs in navigating product development, clinical trials, and regulatory pathways, 
thereby enhancing market readiness and reducing import dependency 
4.1.9 National Impact and Forward Path 
4.1.10 As the nodal entity for biomedical innovation and translational research under DHR, 
MIDAC will be central to realizing the vision of a Viksit Bharat by 2047. It will: 
1.  Institutionalize PPPs as a core mechanism to drive health innovation; 
2.  Maximize returns from ICMR's annual investment of over 3,000 crore Rs; 

68 
 
3.  Advance the goals of the One Health Mission by supporting rapid development of 
countermeasures for emerging infectious threats; 
4.  Promote self-reliance in medical technologies and reduce import dependency. 
 
4.1.11 DHR is currently in the advanced planning stage for the operationalization of MIDAC 
and is actively consulting with relevant stakeholders to finalize its governance, funding structure, 
and implementation roadmap.

4.10 National Antibiotic Policy   
Recommendation 
4.10.1 The Committee observes that there is rampant usage of antibiotics leading to Anti -

Action Taken 
4.10.2 The Centre for Evidence‑Based Guidelines at the DHR in collaboration with DGHS, 
NHSRC and DoHFW has initiated the evidence‑based guidelines for the empirical use of 
antibiotics to reduce antibiotic misuse and overuse. 
4.10.3 In May 2024, the Steering Group  assigned the development of evidence -based guidelines 
for the country across twelve priority disease conditions, with a well‑defined scope for each 
syndrome: 
a)      When to initiate empirical therapy 
b)      Choice of empirical agent(s) 
c)      Duration of therapy 
d)      When to change the antibiotic 
 
4.10.4 The guidelines will harmonize prescribing practices by delineating precise criteria for 
therapy initiation, antimicrobial selection, treatment duration and subsequent modification, 
thereby obviating empiric uncertainty and unwarranted administration. By mandating predefined 
junctures for de‑escalation or discontinuation, anchored in clinical response and microbiological 
data, the framework will avert unnecessarily protracted courses driven by conventi on rather than 

75 
 
clinical necessity. In aggregate, these interventions are anticipated to attenuate empirical 
overprescriptionand safeguard the long‑term efficacy of antimicrobials.

4.14 Impact of packaged foods on human health & Policy  Measures to enhance 
informed food choices 
Recommendation 
4.14.1 The Committee expresses concern over pre -packed foods/UPFs consumption that 
becomes a contributing factor in the growing overweight obesity and diet related non -
communicable diseases, (NCDs). The Committee takes note the findings of the Household 
Consumption Expenditure Survey (HCES, 2024) concluding that the monthly per capita 
expenditure on beverages and processed food has risen from 8.98 per cent and 7.9 per cent (2011-
12) to 11.09 per cent and 9.84 per cent (2022 -23) in urban and rural areas, respective ly. The 
Committee, therefore, strongly recommends the Government to resort to stricter guidelines on 
targeting marketing and advertising of unhealthy foods for children. The Committee takes into 
account that the Food Safety Standards Authority of India (FS SAI) is taking steps to introduce a 
Front of Pack labelling System to indicate the healthiness of the pre -packaged foods. The 
Committee hopes that measures so undertaken will not only help the consumer make informed 
food choices but also compel the food in dustry actors to reformulate their products to achieve 
better rating. 
(Para 5.13.1  of the Report) 
Action Taken 
4.14.2 As the Hon‘ble Committee has observed, India is witnessing a surge in 
overweight/obesity and diet related non -communicable diseases. Alth ough obesity and NCDs 
have a multi -factorial aetiology, unhealthy diets and low physical activity remain the main 
modifiable risk factors. India is witnessing a worrying shift in its food habits, with ultra -
processed foods (UPFs) becoming a regular part of  daily diets, not only in urban areas but also in 
rural areas. A 2024 policy brief by ICRIER and WHO revealed that spending on UPFs surged 
from $900 million in 2006 to nearly $38 billion in 2019. 
(https://icrier.org/pdf/Ultra%20Processed%20Food%20-Policy-brief.pdf) 
4.14.3 And the Household Consumption Expenditure Survey (2022 –23) shows processed foods 
now make up about 10% of food spending in both rural and urban households  
(https://mospi.gov.in/sites/default/files/publication_reports/HCES%20FactSheet%202023-24.pdf 
) 
4.14.4 This growing reliance on processed packaged, nutrient -poor foods is one of the causes 
that is fuelling an alarming rise in obesity, diabetes, and heart disease. The Indian Council of 
Medical Research–National Institute of Nutrition (ICMR –NIN) in its recent ly released Dietary 
Guidelines for Indians has introduced two important guidelines – ‗Minimize the consumption of 
high fat, sugar, salt (HFSS) and ultra -processed foods (UPFs)‘ and for the first time, include 
reading food label as an important guideline to  promote healthy food choices 
(https://www.nin.res.in/dietaryguidelines2024.html). 

78 
 
4.14.5 ICMR-NIN also supports introduction of strong, mandatory Front -of-Pack Nutrition 
Labelling (FOPNL) system, backed by allied regulations such as strict limits on salt, sugar, and 
fat content in foods, marketing restrictions for unhealthy foods (especially those targeted at 
children), and better public awareness. 
4.14.6 The Food Safety and Standards Autho rity of India (FSSAI) has been working on 
introducing FOPNL, aimed at helping consumers make healthier food choices. After wide 
stakeholder consultations, FSSAI launched a study by Indian Institute of Management (IIM), 
Ahmedabad on Consumer Preferences for  Different Nutrition Front of Pack Labels in India 
(https://www.fssai.gov.in/upload/uploadfiles/files/IIMA_FoPL_Report_22_02_2022.pdf). Based 
on this report, FSSAI launched a draft regulation on the Indian Nutrition Rating (INR) in 2022 —
a star -based system that rates the overall nutritional quality of packaged foods 
(https://comments.fssai.gov.in/Bestviewwl.aspx?NOTIFICATION_ID=4123). It was placed in 
public domain and received several comments from various stakeholder groups. A committee 
was constituted by FSSAI including a few ICMR_NIN scientists. The committee reviewed the 
comments and submitted a report.  In addition, NIN also conducted a study on acceptability, use 
and ability of various formats of food labels to influence the consumer food choices. The same 
was shared with FSSAI and presented to the CEO, FSSAI in 2023 
(https://www.nin.res.in/survey_reports/fopnl_report.pdf). 
4.14.7 Other recent efforts under the ‗Let‘s Fix Our Food‘ Initiative – a consortium of several 
scientific, policy, professional an d multi-lateral organizations being led by ICMR -NIN has been 
strongly advocating for initiatives like immediate introduction of FOPNL systems, placing 
restrictions on marketing and advertising of unhealthy foods to children and adolescents, 
simultaneously intensifying nutrition education and food literacy and taxation of HFSS foods.

researchers for securing  grants, fellowships and other support under the HRD Scheme. It 
does not mention since when these measures  have been employed. The Committee is the 
opinion that if they have been operational for some  time now, then their effectiveness needs 
to be explained . The recommendations of the Committee in this regard were made taking 
into account the perennial underutilization of funds under HRD Scheme and were intended 
to attract more talented researchers to take benefit of the Scheme  and contribute to 
nation’s progress . Accordingly, considering the importance of the outcomes the HRD 
scheme, the Committee wants DHR to furnish a more cogent reply in this regard clearly 
indicating measures taken/planned to improve the existing underutilization of funds for the 
Scheme understanding the inadequacies of the extant measures. In the considered opinion 
of the Committee, a n out of the box thought process coupled with robust mechanisms to 
gather feedback primarily from the beneficiaries and also other stakeholders may produce 
better results. 
(Para 3.8.7) 
13. The Committee reiterates its prior recommendation, underscoring the critical 
objectives of the HRD Scheme, and urges DHR to provide a more comprehensive response. 
The response should explicitly outline the steps not already taken or in place but tangible 
proposals to address the persistent underutilization of funds, based on a clear assessment of 
shortcomings in the current measures. From the Committee's perspective, embracing 
innovative approaches paired with strong feedback mechanisms that prioritize input f rom 
beneficiaries and incorporate views from other stakeholders may hold the potential to 
deliver significantly improved results. 
(Para 3.8.14) 

83 
 
RESEARCH GOVERNANCE – HEALTH TECHNOLOGY ASSESSMENT 
 
14. The Committee is pleased to note that a new separate HTA Scheme is in the works. 
However, the Committee would like to be inter alia  appraised of the specific action 
taken/proposed with respect to its recommendation for setting up more research hubs in 
the underserved and remote areas of the Co unty as well as the expected time by which the 
new HTA Scheme will be operational.  The Committee would also like to be apprised of 
response of the Ministry of Finance (Department of Expenditure) to the new Concept Note 
drafted for a new separate HTA Scheme. 
(Para 3.9.3) 
PRIME MINISTER'S AYUSHMAN BHARAT HEALTH INFRASTRUCTURE MISSION 
(PM- ABHIM) BIO-SECURITY PREPAREDNESS 
15. The Committee does not find the reply to be as comprehensive as it should have been 
on its recommendation on (PM -ABHIM) Bio-Security preparedness. The action taken on 
the aspect of civil construction including that of critical national Institutes has been 
mentioned as a one liner response as if the construction agencies have the sole responsibility 
in this regard and in case if the y falter again, as in the past, DHR should be prepared for 
delays in the implementation of PM -ABHIM Scheme. Further, the reply does not clearly 
mention about how many more  MBSL-3 laboratories are planned to be increased. The 
Committee is not convinced whether 0 2 more mobile labs would be sufficient to cater to all 
the currently underserved and remote areas of the country. Accordingly, the Committee 
reiterates its recommendation and wants a comprehensive answer from DHR touching 
upon all aspects of the recommendation. 
(Para 3.10.5) 
HPV VACCINES 
16. Though the Committee appreciates the sharing of information about trials of single 
dose HPV Vaccine being carried out in the country, it does not find the reply of the 
Government to have adequately addressed all the iss ues highlighted in the 
recommendation. Need for a country wide campaign promoting HPV Vaccine and the cost 
aspects should have been addressed in the reply. Though the Committee comprehends that 
cost of the vaccine may also depend upon the path the trials t ake, it would remain a vital 
factor that would decide the acceptance of the vaccine in India ; may be even its full-fledged 
inclusion in the Universal Immunisation Programme of the Government. Being single dose 
is also important for the successful completio n of vaccination schedule as it would be less 
challenging logistically in our administrative and infrastructure milieu. In view of this, the 
Committee reiterates its recommendation and wants a complete answer on all facets of the 
recommendation. 
(Para 3.11.3)

involved in granting exclusive rights to innovate for a period of 20 years from the filing date 
in a quicker manner as an important measure. The action taken by the DHR in this regard 
is to be intimated in a comprehensive manner and hence the Committee reiterates its 
recommendation.

AYUSH
 
I.         INTRODUCTION
1.1       Ever since independence in 1947, there has been state patronage and policy support to the Indian systems of
Medicine but its institutionalized development started when the Department of Indian Systems of Medicines and
Homoeopathy (ISM&H) was set up by the Government of India as an independent department in March, 1995, under
the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.  It was renamed as Department of Ayurveda, Yoga & Naturopathy, Unani,
Siddha and Homoeopathy (AYUSH) in November, 2003.   The main objective of this full- fledged Department headed
by a Secretary, is to provide focussed attention for the proper development and propagation of Ayurveda, Siddha,
Unani, Homoeopathy, Yoga and Naturopathy and to fully utilize the potentials of these systems.
1.2       Thrust areas of the Department are: -
i)
                    Improvement and up-gradation of standards of education in AYUSH;
ii)                   Quality Control and Standardization of drugs;
iii)                 Ensuring sustained availability of raw materials, i.e. medicinal plants, metals, minerals and materials of
animal origin etc;
iv)                 Research & Development on the efficacy of the systems;
v)                  Participation of AYUSH in the National Health Care Delivery System & National Health & Family Welfare
Programme;
vi)                 Information, Education and Communication.
 
1.3       Over the years, there has been a steady growth in infrastructure of AYUSH. At present, the number of
practitioners of AYUSH are 7.18 lakhs, out of which 5.17 lakhs are institutionally qualified. The number of non-
institutionally qualified practitioners is 2.01 lakhs. There are 549 teaching institutions which include 450 undergraduate
colleges and 99 post graduate colleges. Number of drug manufacturing units both in Government and private sector in
the country is 9493. The number of GMP complaint manufacturing units is 3973 and the number of Government drug
testing laboratories is 21. There are 1,355 hospitals with total bed strength of 53296 and 22,635 dispensaries, out of
which maximum numbers of hospitals and dispensaries provide Ayurveda system of treatment. Total number of
Ayurveda hospitals and dispensaries in the country are 753 and 15,193 respectively. The population coverage through
AYUSH system is 7  doctors per 10,000 population.
1.4       The Secretary, during the course of his presentation before the Committee, stated that the Department started
playing a vital role in strengthening, upgrading and popularization of the AYUSH systems during the 10
th five year plan
with the introduction of a number of Central Sector and Centrally Sponsored  Schemes aimed at development of
educational institutions, mainstreaming of AYUSH speciality clinics/OPDs in the existing allopathic hospitals, research
and quality control. Achievements made during the year 2005-06 include:-
Ø
      Setting up of AYUSH wings in 139 District Hospitals, opening of 299 AYUSH speciality clinics, 44
OPD/polyclinics and supply of essential AYUSH drugs to 13,273 AYUSH dispensaries in rural and backward
areas throughout the country
Ø      133 AYUSH educational institutions have been assisted under various schemes relating to upgradation of
UG/PG colleges and reorientation training programme or continuing  medical education.
Ø      29 AYUSH colleges (Ayurveda-15, Siddha-1, Unani-5, Homoeopathy-8) including 12 during the year have been
sanctioned financial assistance for development as a model institute on the norms of developing one model
college per system per State. Now this scheme is proposed to be modified to assist more than one college per
system per State in view of the fact that some systems like Siddha and Unani are widely prevalent only in
particular areas and also that some States are very large.

Ø      Financial assistance provided to 25 States Drug Testing Laboratories and 43 State pharmacies for upgrading
their infrastructure.
Ø      Enforcement of Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP)  to ensure the safety and efficacy of Ayurveda, Siddha
and Unani drugs manufacturing units in 3973 units in 14 States.
Ø      Launching of a major collaborative research initiative by the AYUSH Research Councils in collaboration with
the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) and Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR)
called the Golden Triangle Project.
Ø      Setting up of two pharmacopoeial  laboratories by the Central Government  at Ghaziabad, namely,
Pharmacopoeial Laboratory for Indian Medicine and Homoeopathy Pharmacopoeial Laboratory with the
objective of laying down Pharmacopoeial standards for purity, quality and strength of Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha
and Homoeopathy drugs and for testing of drug samples received from State Drug Inspectors, samples taken on
the directions of courts and samples sent by consumers.
Ø      Creation of Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL), an original proprietary database developed by the
Department of AYUSH and the National Institute of Science Communication and Information Resources
(NISCAIR). It includes a search interface providing full text search and retrieval of traditional knowledge
information (IPC) and keywords in multiple language.
 
Ø
      Inauguration of National Institute of Siddha, Chennai in November, 2005 and Unani Institute of Medicine
Bangalore.
 
II.        BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
 
2.1       The Committee observes that there has been massive enhancement in the allocation of plan funds for the
Department.   As compared to Ninth Plan allocation of Rs. 364.43 crores, funds provided to the Department in the Tenth
Plan were Rs. 1194.60 crores.   Department has   managed optimum utilisation of funds during both the plan periods,
massive enhancement of funds notwithstanding.   The Committee notes that the trend of allocation and utilisation of
funds during the last two years of both Ninth and Tenth Plan indicates interesting similarity.   The Department could not
match the substantive increase  in allocation of plan funds in 2000-01 and 2001-02,  the last two years of Ninth Plan. 
Committee notices the same position in 2005-06 where funds had to be reduced at the RE stage.  The Committee
apprehends the same position during 2006-07 also.
2.2       The Plan Allocation of the Department for the year 2006-07 is Rs. 381.60 crores, showing an increase of Rs.
81.60 crores when compared to RE allocation of  Rs. 300.00 crores in 2005-06.   Expenditure  reported by the end of 
the year is Rs. 292.35 crores.   The Committee has taken note of the fact that plan allocation of Rs. 345.00 crores of the
Department at BE stage of 2005-06 was reduced to Rs. 300.00 crores at RE stage. Reason given is delay in
administrative and financial sanctions in respect of the North-East institute of Ayurveda and Homoeopathy and All
India Institute of Ayurveda, New Delhi.    Clarifying that the situation was beyond their control, the Secretary assured
the Committee that the Department would make earnest efforts to obtain the required sanctions for the two projects and
optimum utilisation of the allocated funds.   
2.3       The Committee is not fully convinced by the justification given by the Department.   The Committee would like
to point out that during 2005-06, expenditure reported upto 15.1.2006 was Rs.223.27 crores which went upto Rs.292.35
crores by the end of the financial year.  This clearly shows that the last quarter of the year reported higher rate of
expenditure as compared to the remaining three quarters of the year. 
2.4       Committee’s attention has been drawn by another disturbing trend in the utilisation of allocated funds.   As
reported in the Performance Budget  (2005-06) , as on 31
st March, 2004 there were as many as 373 pending Utilisation
Certificates amounting to Rs.107.02 crores.   As per the latest information made available to the Committee, number of

-                     Reorientation training programme for AYUSH personnel.
-                     Renovation and strengthening of hospital wards of teaching hospitals of AYUSH.

3.2       The Committee notes that   against an allocation of Rs. 37.56 crores in 2005-06, expenditure reported upto 7th
March, 2006 is Rs.27.82 crores.  Receipt of less proposals due to pending UCs of previous years has been cited as the
main factor responsible for underutilization of allocated funds.  The Committee notes that level of overall expenditure
under the scheme has been more or less satisfactory during 2003-04 and 2004-05.   However, the Committee would like
to point that status of some components indicate a different position.   Funds meant for development/assistance of
UG/PG AYUSH colleges remained under utilised during 2003-04 and 2004-05 due to revision of the component and
receipt of less number of feasible proposals.  The Committee observes that during 2005-06, the physical targets set
under these components could not be achieved fully.   Under ROTP/CME for AYUSH personnel, the Committee notes
that against a target of 105-110 colleges to be benefited, achievement level is restricted to 64 colleges only.   The
Committee understands that the component in its revised form is being closely monitored.    The Committee would like
to know about the number of beneficiaries (institution and statewise) during 2005-06.  
3.3       The physical targets set for establishment of computer labs for selected colleges could not be met during 2005-
06 as central assistance of Rs.20 lakhs could be provided to only two colleges against a target of 7-8 colleges.  The
Committee finds that the scheme, very much required under the present scenario has not been getting due impetus.  
While there was nil achievement during 2003-04, performance level during 2004-05 showed noticeable improvement.    
Status of this component during 2005-06 is again discouraging.   The Committee strongly feels that this component
needs to be focussed more.  
3.4       The Committee takes a serious view of the pendency level of Utilisation Certificates   pertaining to all the

HOSPITALS AND DISPENSARIES
4.1       Budget allocation of Rs.90 crores for the two schemes of AYUSH hospitals and dispensaries in 2005-06

Rs.85.02 crores.  In contrast provision for AYUSH dispensaries was reduced from Rs. 45 crores to Rs.33.17
crores and the actual expenditure was only Rs.32.32 crores.   
4.2       The Committee observes that there are about 21000 AYUSH dispensaries in the country and the scheme
calls for financial assistance @Rs.25000 per dispensary per annum.  The Committee notes that during 2003-04
and 2004-05,  utilisation was optimum and the funds were not found sufficient for the projected requirements of
the existing dispensaries.    The Committee is not aware about the reason for the reduction in the allocated funds
for AYUSH dispensaries during 2005-06.   The Committee would however like to point out that the core
strategy of mainstreaming of AYUSH under NRHM is to make available AYUSH services at the PHC/CHC
level, either by reallocation of AYUSH doctors from existing dispensaries or by hiring of additional doctors on
contract basis for which funds will be provided under NRHM.  The Committee apprehends that  on the plea of
providing  AYUSH doctors at PHC/CHC with  the funds being provided therefor under NRHM, AYUSH
dispensaries  spread across the country may perhaps  not continue to provide the services as being done uptil
now.  Out of the 10000 AYUSH dispensaries and units located in rural and backward areas, only 7936
dispensaries could be covered for improving the supply position of essential AYUSH drugs during the year
2005-06.  The Committee would, therefore, like to emphasize that every effort should be made for effective
functioning of the existing AYUSH dispensaries.

5.3       The Committee has been given to understand that fund constraint if any in the provision of Rs.11 crores

Keeping in view increasing number of cases of spurious and fake drugs available in the market, the Committee
feels that there is a need for   increasing the quantum of financial assistance under this component.   This would
enable individual units or a group of units to set up a joint quality control lab and acquire requisite equipment for

 6.1.3   Maintenance of Central Register of Homoeopathy is the responsibility of CCH.  However, the

VIII  NATIONAL MEDICAL PLANT BOARD  
8.1       An enhanced allocation of Rs. 38.00 crore has been made for the Board for 2006-07 against an allocation of Rs.
30.00 crore in 2005-06. The Committee observes that there has been optimum utilization of funds allocated for the
Board during the Tenth Plan period.
8.2       The Board was set up in November 2001 with the objective of development of medicinal plants used in AYUSH
medicines for sustained availability. The Committee observes that the Board was set up on the recommendation of a
Task Force constituted by the Planning Commission. Quite a few achievements could be credited in the name of the
Board.  So far, 32 State Medicinal Plant Boards have been set up. 32 medicinal plants have been identified at national
level for cultivation, conservation and development.
8.3
              The Committee has observed that the Board has not been provided with the required manpower. Perhaps this
issue has neither been emphasized enough nor seen in the proper perspective. Only one post of Chief Executive Officer
was created at the time of setting up of the Board. Since then, the Department has made attempts to get the required staff
but without any success so far. The only activity worth mentioning has been circulation of a Cabinet note on 20.01.2005
for creation of 30 posts and grant of status of a registered society to the Board to the concerned Departments.
Subsequently, a memorandum for EFC be has also been circulated to all concerned on 18.07.2005.
8.4       The Committee is surprised to note that the proposal and projected requirements did not find favour with the
Department of Expenditure and the Planning Commission. Instead it was suggested that 5 posts including 2 posts on
outsourcing basis suggested by the Department of Expenditure would serve the purpose and accordingly there was no
justification for creation of 30 additional posts.
8.5       The Committee finds that the final outcome of this whole exercise has been the proposed study for restructuring
of the Board for which preparatory exercise has already begun. The Committee is not happy with the turn of events. Six
years have gone since the setting up of the Board and the basic decision about its objective and infrastructure required
therefor remains undecided. One plan period would be over soon and perhaps the next plan would also be nearing its
end before a final view on the setting up of the Board is taken. The Committee expresses its deep sense of
dissatisfaction on this turn of events. The Committee, accordingly, reiterates once again to expedite the decision about
the mandate and structure of the Board acceptable to all concerned. The Committee is afraid that continuance of an air
of indecisiveness about this vital Body would lead to our endangered medicinal plants reaching the brink of extinction.

XII.     Use of Animal and Marine Products in Ayurveda, Sidha and Unani Drugs.
 
12.1     The Committee observes that some of these animal products namely Praval (coral), Shankha (conch shell),
Kapardika (cowrie) and Mrigashringa (stag horn and deer horn), tiger nails, musk, discharge of civet cat have been
banned under Wild Life                  ( Protection) Act, 1972. The Committee was informed that the Department has taken
up with the Ministry of Environment and Forest who are exploring the possibility of providing some of these items to
the Ayurveda drug industry without causing and harm to the environment. 
12.2     The Committee strongly feels that the Department has to play a more pro-active rote in this sensitive area by
banning all animal products and wild honey in all preparation. Pig and cow products are likely to take on communal
colour. Other items like Ambrgris and elephant parts are internationally banned. Earthworm, animal teeth, peacock
feathers have no medicinal value and reduce the medicine to a placebo.   
 
XIII. Standardization of Naturopathy Courses
13.1     The Committee observes that naturopathy centers, purporting to be medical centers have sprung up all over the

COMMITTEE ON HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE

country.   Inspite of the fact that the Department of AYUSH has a naturopathy wing which gives naturopathy legitimacy
as a medical science, the Committee attention has been drawn by the following disturbing ground realities: -
(a)                There is no naturopathy council to decide norms.
(b)               No norms have been decided.
(c)                Quack treatments have not been banned.
(d)               No licensing is required.
(e)                No courses have been decided for colleges or syllabuses regulated or standardized.
(f)                 There is total confusion in the regulation of medicines that purport to be treatments in naturopathy.
(g)                There is no degree. People who have studied it by correspondence for less then a week have become
practitioners. In fact, degrees have been gotten by mail.
13.2     The Committee is not inclined to agree with the contention of the department that it is not feasible to constitute a
separate Central Council for regulation of Yoga & Naturopathy. States have therefore been advised to set up their own
mechanism for regulation of  Yoga & Naturopathy in states. The Committee was given to understand that few steps
have been taken by the Department to regulate the naturopathy courses. WHO draft guidelines on Naturopathy are being
examined for adoption in Indian context. 13.3            The Committee was given to understand that a Morarji Dasai
National Institute of Yoga has already started work on preparation of draft curriculum for various courses and norms for
accreditation of yoga institutions. The National Institute of Naturopathy, Pune has also been asked to prepare similar
guidelines. These guidelines will be circulated to states for their guidance and enforcement.
13.4     The Committee strongly feels that there is an urgent need for regulation of education of naturopathy. There are
ten degree colleges of naturopathy in the country. But in the absence of any council having the power to regulate the
education of naturopathy, such colleges are running courses in a haphazard way, without any Central Standardization or
and any accountability whatsoever. The Committee is of the firm view that the Department should initiate immediate
action so that people are not put to any trouble. The Committee is happy to note that Department is reviewing the status
of both education and treatment aspects of naturopathy and would be coming out with a proper regulatory system in this
regard within a period of three months. The Committee would like to be apprised of the same.

textbooks and manuscript which are to be acquired should also be given. 
 XVI.   Miscellaneous
            Tibetan Medicine has become quite popular amongst the people although it is not a recognized system in India. 
In states like Himachal Pradesh, Amchis are the medical practitioners in the Tibetan system of medicine.  There have
also been reports about violations concerning wildlife and usage of huge amount of bone material in this system of
medicine. The Committee has been given to understand that the Tibetan Medicine does not find any mention in our
existing legislation.  The Drugs and Cosmetic Act 1940 has a chapter on Indian Medicine but it does not mention
anything about the Tibetan medicine.  The Committee is of the opinion that the Tibetan system of medicine should be
brought within the ambit of law.  The Committee urges the Department to consider the inclusion of Tibetan system of
medicine in the legislation so as to regulate and recognize it for the benefit of the people.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS AT A GLANCE
 
II.        BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
 
  The Committee apprehends the same position during 2006-07 also. (Para 2.1)
2.3       The Committee is not fully convinced by the justification given by the Department.   The Committee would like
to point out that during 2005-06, expenditure reported upto 15.1.2006 was Rs.223.27 crores which went upto Rs.292.35
crores by the end of the financial year.  This clearly shows that the last quarter of the year reported higher rate of
expenditure as compared to the remaining three quarters of the year.  (Para 2.3)
While appreciating the efforts made by the Department, the Committee is constrained to observe that these UCs
date back to 1976.   It seems that the Department has initiated corrective measures only during the last year or so.   The
Committee would like to have an idea about the pending UCs (State and Scheme wise). (Para 2.4)

  III.     CENTRALLY SPONSORED SCHEMES
The Committee notes that level of overall expenditure under the scheme has been more or less satisfactory
during 2003-04 and 2004-05.   However, the Committee would like to point that status of some components indicate a
different position.   Funds meant for development/assistance of UG/PG AYUSH colleges remained under utilised during
2003-04 and 2004-05 due to revision of the component and receipt of less number of feasible proposals.  The
Committee observes that during 2005-06, the physical targets set under these components could not be achieved fully.  
Under ROTP/CME for AYUSH personnel, the Committee notes that against a target of 105-110 colleges to be
benefited, achievement level is restricted to 64 colleges only.   The Committee understands that the component in its
revised form is being closely monitored.    The Committee would like to know about the number of beneficiaries
(institution and statewise) during 2005-06.      (Para 3.2)
The Committee finds that the scheme, very much required under the present scenario has not been getting due
impetus.   While there was nil achievement during 2003-04, performance level during 2004-05 showed noticeable
improvement.     Status of this component during 2005-06 is again discouraging.   The Committee strongly feels that this
component needs to be focussed more.   (Para 3.3)
            The Committee was informed that the matter of pending UCs was being vigorously followed up with the
concerned States.  It was proposed to impress upon the States that release of further funds would be dependent on the
clearance of pending UCs.   The Committee   feels that this is the right decision taken which was long overdue and
hopes that   there would be judicious utilisation of funds by the State Govts. in future. (Para 3.6)
 
IV.          HOSPITALS AND DISPENSARIES
   The Committee is not aware about the reason for the reduction in the allocated funds for AYUSH dispensaries
during 2005-06.   The Committee would however like to point out that the core strategy of mainstreaming of AYUSH
under NRHM is to make available AYUSH services at the PHC/CHC level, either by reallocation of AYUSH doctors
from existing dispensaries or by hiring of additional doctors on contract basis for which funds will be provided under
NRHM.  The Committee apprehends that on the plea of providing AYUSH doctors at PHC/CHC with the funds being
provided therefor under NRHM, AYUSH dispensaries spread across the country may perhaps not continue to provide
the services as being done uptil now.  Out of the 10000 AYUSH dispensaries and units located in rural and backward
areas, only 7936 dispensaries could be covered for improving the supply position of essential AYUSH drugs during the
year 2005-06.  The Committee would, therefore, like to emphasize that every effort should be made for effective
functioning of the existing AYUSH dispensaries.    (Para 4.2)
V.        DRUGS QUALITY CONTROL
            The Committee strongly feels that quality control of AYUSH drugs   is required to be maintained in view of the
increasing demand for such drugs and also for checking circulation of spurious drugs in the market.  (Para 5.3)
The Committee strongly recommends that a decision for enhancing the funding for units obtaining GMP
certificates should be taken well before the beginning of XIth Plan. (Para 5.5)
   The Committee would, however, like to emphasize that there is an urgent need for the Department for taking a
pro-active role by making persistent efforts for strengthening of drug testing labs and the other allied controlling
authorities. (Para 5.6)       
VI.     CENTRAL SECTOR SCHEMES STATUTORY INSTITUTIONS
6.1       Central Council of Homoeopathy
The Committee is of the view that the Department and the Council both have to take the responsibility for
getting expedited the publication of Central Register of Homoeopathy.   (Para 6.1.3)

6.2 Central Council of Indian Medicine
The Committee apprehends that availability of unspent balances might have been the factor responsible for
initialization of allocated funds. (Para 6.2.2)
The Committee is of the view that in the event of non-submission of required information by any state council, a
mechanism needs to be evolved so as to ensure that the updation of Central Register does not get unduly delayed.  In the
event of the AYUSH practitioners of a particular state being deprived of the opportunity of getting registered in the state
council, the fault should lie with that council.  (Para 6.2.3)
The Committee is not fully satisfied with the justification given by the Department.  The Committee hopes that
the Govt. would be bringing forward the amended Bill relating to the CCIM before Parliament which would take care of
these anomalies. (Para 6.2.4) 
VII.         HOSPITALS AND DISPENSARIES
7.1   All India Institute of Ayurveda, New Delhi
The Committee apprehends that not much progress would be made during 2006 also as the planning for the
project of building continues to be under consideration.  The Committee is not aware of the original estimate approved
for the construction of the building for the hospital.  However, as things stand, it would be definitely on a enhanced
level when completed. (Para 7.1)
7.2       Ayurveda Hospital, New Delhi
The Committee strongly feels that in order to expand the services of the hospital, required number of permanent
posts need to be created. The Department should once again approach the Ministry of Finance in this regard. (Para 7.2)
7.3      Expansion of AYUSH Dispensaries in CGHS
            The Committee does not appreciate this kind of approach. Implementation of SIU Report needs to be given
priority so that dispensaries already set up can become fully functional. The Committee would, accordingly, recommend
the creation of additional posts for AYUSH dispensaries without any further delay. (Para 7.3)
VIII.   NATIONAL MEDICAL PLANT BOARD  
            The Committee is surprised to note that the proposal and projected requirements did not find favour with the
Department of Expenditure and the Planning Commission. Instead it was suggested that 5 posts including 2 posts on
outsourcing basis suggested by the Department of Expenditure would serve the purpose and accordingly there was no
justification for creation of 30 additional posts. (Para 8.4)
The Committee, accordingly, reiterates once again to expedite the decision about the mandate and structure of
the Board acceptable to all concerned. The Committee is afraid that continuance of an air of indecisiveness about this
vital Body would lead to our endangered medicinal plants reaching the brink of extinction. (Par 8.5)
            The Committee observes that the existing monitoring mechanism has perhaps not proved to be effective enough.
Basis for this assessment made by the Committee is the alarming increase in the number of pending Utilization
Certificates under both the schemes. (Para 8.8)
The Committee apprehends that the pendency is likely to arise further in view of sanctioning of as many as 1233
projects worth Rs. 32.10 crore and 233 projects worth Rs. 25.65 crore under the Contractual Farming Scheme and
Promotional Scheme respectively during 2005-06 alone. (Para 8.10)
The Committee observes that both pendency rate of UCs involved therein is very high. During the course of
discussion with the representatives of the Department as well as the National Medicinal Plant Board, it was

categorically stated that amount involved in pending UCs would be negligible. However, the following information
forwarded by the Department proves the contention to be wrong and misleading. The Committee takes strong exception
to this.
            The Committee is not convinced by the justification given by the Department that pending UCs was a common
problem with all Ministries administering Centrally Sponsored Schemes on account of delay in release of CHS grants by
the states to implementing agencies and consequent delay in submission of UCs. The plea of the Department that the
requirement of vetting by Chartered Accountants under the Contractual Farming Scheme was difficult to be complied
with by farmers is also not acceptable to the Committee. The Committee would like to emphasize that the pendency is
bound to increase keeping in view the level of central assistance released under both the schemes during 2004-05 and
2005-06. (Para 8.11)
The Committee hopes that reports of these studies would provide critical input to the Board to modify and recast
the scheme accordingly. The Committee has a suggestion to make in this regard. Involvement of Forest Department will
not be helpful simply because they do not have any expertise in growing trees. The Committee is of the firm opinion
that agriculture universities like Pant Nagar need to be involved in the implementation of schemes like Promotional and
Contractual Farming. The Committee fails to understand the reason for not initiating the provision of recovery of funds
provided in the terms and conditions of both the schemes. The Committee strongly feels that a review of the functioning
of state Boards also needs to be done. They need to be strengthened and made accountable for the drawbacks being
noticed in the two schemes.   (Para 8.12)
IX.          STRENGTHENING OF PHARMACOPOEIAL LABORATORIES
The Committee is constrained to observe that the post of Director, PLIM, still remains to be filled up.   The
Committee has been given to understand that the post had to be readvertised under the directions of UPSC. The
Committee does not have much hope of further progress in the matter during the last year of the Tenth Plan. (Para 9.2) 
The physical targets and the achievement level during 2005-06 with regard to various activities undertaken by
the lab also indicate a good track record.           (Para 9.3)
The Committee finds that the building of PLIM although completed structurally is yet to be handed over by the
CPWD.   At present, the matter is being pursued vigorously with the CPWD engineers.     Statement of the Department
that the building for HPL is reportedly complete indicates that there may be some formalities to be completed in respect
of this project also.   The Committee is not aware whether the buildings for both the labs were handed over on 10 th
April, 2006 after fulfilling all mandatory requirements as assured by the CPWD.   The Committee would like to be
apprised about the final position.  The Committee would also like to know about the original estimate and the actual
expenditure of both the projects.  (Para 9.4)
X.        DEVELOPMENT OF NORTH-EAST UNDER PLAN SCHEMES OF THE DEPARTMENT
The Committee has been observing the progress of this project for quite some time.  In the beginning of every
year, nominal provision for this project is being religiously made.  The proposed allocation for the entire Tenth plan was
Rs. 5 lakhs and the beginning of last year has started without any progress whatsoever being made.  As per the latest
information furnished by the Department, the matter has been reviewed by the Minister on 4 th October 2005 in the light
of observations made by the Ministry of Finance, Department of Expenditure about the viability of   the project.  The
Committee is surprised to note that a decision has now been made to locate the Institute of Health and Medical Sciences
at Shillong and allotment of land  for the Institute has also been made.   At present, approval of CCEA is awaited.  The
Committee is not very happy with the way the project of Institute  to be set up for the benefit of NE region has been

apprehends that another plan period would perhaps be over in taking a final decision and starting the preparatory
exercise for this much needed institute.  The Committee can only emphasize that the Department should vigorously
pursue this matter with all concerned authorities.   (Para 10.2)
XI.    PERFORMANCE AUDIT OF DEPTT. OF AYUSH FOR THE PERIOD OF 2000-01 TO 2004 – 05 BY
CAG
 
The Committee notes that a number of areas which deserve to be seriously viewed have been raised in the CAG
Report.  The Secretary of the Department admitted before the Committee that most of the observations made by the
CAG were valid and exercise has been started at the Department level to take the corrective measures.  The Committee
would like to be apprised about the full details of follow up action to taken by the Department.   (Para 11.2)
XII.     USE OF ANIMAL AND MARINE PRODUCTS IN AYURVEDA, SIDHA AND UNANI DRUGS.
 
            The Committee strongly feels that the Department has to play a more pro-active rote in this sensitive area by
banning all animal products and wild honey in all preparation. Pig and cow products are likely to take on communal
colour. Other items like Ambrgris and elephant parts are internationally banned. Earthworm, animal teeth, peacock
feathers have no medicinal value and reduce the medicine to a placebo.    (Para 12.2)
XIII.    STANDARDIZATION OF NATUROPATHY COURSES
 
            The Committee strongly feels that there is an urgent need for regulation of education of naturopathy. There are
ten-degree colleges of naturopathy in the country. But in the absence of any council having the power to regulate the
education of naturopathy, such colleges are running courses in a haphazard way, without any Central Standardization or
and any accountability whatsoever. The Committee is of the firm view that the Department should initiate immediate
action so that people are not put to any trouble. The Committee is happy to note that Department is reviewing the status
of both education and treatment aspects of naturopathy and would be coming out with a proper regulatory system in this
regard within a period of three months. The Committee would like to be apprised of the same. (Para 13.4)
XIV.            INTERNATIONAL EXCHANGE PROGRAMME
The Committee would like to have an idea about the contributions of AYUSH made by such Exchange Programme /
Conferences.  (Para 14.3)
 The Committee would like to have full details in this regard, amount of sanction, expenditure (industry-wise) users.
