6.9 Research Achievements and Impact of AIIMS New Delhi  
 
6.9.1 Over the five-year period from 2020 to 2025, AIIMS New Delhi has made substantial 
contributions to medical research and public health, emerging as one of the foremost centres 
for innovation in diagnostics, therapeutics and healthcare systems research. Supported by a 
wide range of national and international extramural grants, the Institute’s work has advanced 
critical areas including oncology, neurology, infectious diseases and digital health 
technologies. A major part of this period was defined by the COVID-19 pandemic, during 
which AIIMS played a central role in shaping India’s national response. Experts from the 
Institute were integral to government advisory bodies such as the National Task Force, where 
they contributed to the formulation of treatment protocols, testing strategies, clinical 
management guidelines and telemedicine policies. AIIMS also guided oxygen allocation 

 
32 
 
during the national crisis and participated in vaccine trials while contributing significantly to 
vaccine safety datasets. The Institute operated major vaccination centres that inoculated over 
five lakh beneficiaries, including healthcare workers and the general public. Through 
initiatives such as the AIIMS COVID Portal, dedicated helplines, media engagements and 
community outreach, the Institute undertook extensive public communication efforts aimed at 
addressing misinformation, providing mental health support and enhancing public awareness. 
 
6.9.2 Between 2022 and 2025, AIIMS researchers achieved several notable breakthroughs 
across clinical and translational research. Collaborative projects with Wadhwani AI led to the 
development of artificial intelligence–based screening tools for diabetic retinopathy, 
pulmonary tuberculosis and skin cancers. These Smartphone-enabled applications achieved 
diagnostic accuracies exceeding 90 percent, offering scalable, cost-effective solutions for 
early detection, particularly in low-resource environments. In 2024, researchers developed a 
blood-based biomarker test for early detection of Alzheimer’s disease, providing a 
significantly more affordable alternative to high-cost imaging techniques. In the same period, 
a new CAR-T cell therapy targeting the BCMA antigen was developed for the treatment of 
multiple myeloma, demonstrating promising preclinical outcomes in reducing tumour burden. 
Most recently, in 2025, the Institute introduced a diagnostic platform using transmission 
electron microscopy for rare genetic disorders such as Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia, enabling 
more precise identification of ultra-structural ciliary defects and improving timely clinical 
intervention. 
 
6.9.3 The Committee notes the research contributions made by AIIMS New Delhi 
between 2020 and 2025, particularly in the areas of diagnostics, oncology, neurology, 
artificial intelligence and infectious disease management. While these achievements have 
strengthened India’s healthcare capacity, the Committee observes that sustained 
advancement in such high-impact research will require dedicated institutional support, 
enhanced infrastructure and structured collaborations. Accordingly, the Committee 
recommends that AIIMS New Delhi institutionalize a minimum of 20 percent protected 
time for faculty engaged in research, ensuring that clinical responsibilities do not 
impede scientific productivity. The Committee further recommends the establishment of 
Institute-wide innovation and incubation centres to promote translational research, 
foster start-ups and accelerate the development of technologies with public health 
relevance. 
 
6.9.4 The Committee observes that AIIMS, New Delhi has established a vibrant 
research ecosystem supported by substantial extramural and intramural funding, 
advanced facilities and strong national and international collaborations. The Committee 
recommends that the Institute’s research wing must make notable contributions to 
national health programs and policies. The Committee is of the considered view that 
AIIMS research, in addition to pure research must become part and parcel of doing the 
research having implications for the policy and advocacy of national healthcare 
priorities and plans.  
 
6.9.5 AIIMS has also made important contributions through the creation of standardised 
best-practice guidelines for research across diverse domains. Technical resource centres 

 
33 
 
established at the Institute have developed evidence-based frameworks to enhance 
methodological rigour, ethical compliance and reproducibility in basic science, as well as to 
support structured, high-quality clinical research. These research achievements have had a 
far-reaching impact on the Indian healthcare landscape. Advances in diagnostics have reduced 
dependence on expensive imaging modalities and significantly shortened diagnostic timelines 
for conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease and Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia, enabling wider 
access and timely care. Innovations in cancer treatment, particularly affordable CAR-T 
therapy, have expanded access to advanced care for low-income patients and improved 
survival outcomes in multiple myeloma. AI-driven diagnostic tools have substantially 
increased screening coverage in a country managing approximately 1.4 million new cancer 
cases annually. In the realm of infectious diseases, AIIMS’ contributions during the COVID-
19 pandemic accelerated vaccine deployment, strengthened variant surveillance and informed 
national policies that helped reduce mortality among high-risk populations. 
 
6.9.6 The Committee observes that the creation of standardised best practices 
guidelines for medical research across diverse domain in AIIMS have generated 
broader systemic benefits. The Committee believes that AI-led healthcare solutions 
would contribute to more efficient diagnostics nationwide, expanded telemedicine 
adoption and reduced disparities between urban and rural health system through 
proliferation of research outcome at peripheral ground level. Moreover, the growth of 
medical technology innovation linked to the modern and scientific advanced initiatives 
would produce additional economic and employment benefits in the healthcare sector. 
The Committee recommends for an outcome based analysis of the research outcomes by 
AIIMS. The Committee also recommends that AIIMS should actively collaborate with 
other Scientific Institutions like CSIR, DBT, IITs, ICMR etc to develop an integrated

academic and research activities at AIIMS New Delhi that inter-alia include instituting 
protected research time, establishing innovation incubators across the Institute and

need for further strengthening of research infrastructure, including the creation of AI-

Additionally, deeper international collaborations through joint PhD programmes, long-
term research fellowships, student and faculty exchange initiatives are expected to

6.9.8 The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that AIIMS strengthen its

6.10 Key Concern Areas and Opportunities of Research Wing 
 
6.10.1 The Research Wing at AIIMS New Delhi serves as the central coordinating body for 
fostering and managing biomedical research across all departments of the Institute. Its 
responsibilities span a wide range of functions that are essential for maintaining scientific 
quality and supporting the advancement of medical knowledge.  
 
6.10.2 Another major area of attention is the development of infrastructure and capacity 
building. This includes upgrading laboratory facilities, expanding the use of digital research 
platforms such as REDCap and strengthening training resources for faculty, residents and 
research staff. The Research Wing also prioritizes collaboration and networking, working to 
strengthen institutional ties with national and international research organizations to promote 
joint academic and scientific initiatives. 
 
6.10.3 Maintaining high standards of research quality and integrity is an overarching priority. 
The Wing actively promotes principles of reproducibility, methodological transparency and 
adherence to ethical standards in both basic and clinical research. Alongside this, improving 
digital data management, meta-analysis capabilities and systematic review methodologies has 
emerged as a critical need to support evidence-based practice and robust scientific output. The 
Wing also seeks to enhance the visibility of AIIMS research through increased publication in 
high-impact journals and strengthened dissemination mechanisms. 
6.10.4  To further strengthen the Research Wing and enhance the Institute’s overall 
research output, several measures have been identified. Encouraging multidisciplinary and 
cross-institutional research collaborations can broaden scientific perspectives and accelerate 
innovation. Leveraging artificial intelligence and big data analytics will support advances in 
predictive modelling, diagnostics, and personalized medicine. Regular training workshops in 
research methodology, ethics and publication strategies can improve the competence and 
confidence of early-career researchers. Streamlining grant application and approval processes 
through centralized digital platforms will reduce administrative burden and improve 
efficiency. 
 
6.10.5 In addition, promoting open access to global scientific literature, particularly through 
national initiatives such as One Nation One Subscription, can democratize knowledge and 
improve the quality of research. Strengthening partnerships with biotechnology and 
pharmaceutical industries will facilitate translational research and foster innovation in 
therapeutics and diagnostics.  
 
6.10.6 The Committee notes the wide-ranging responsibilities of the Research Wing at 
AIIMS New Delhi and the critical role it plays in managing research funding, ensuring 
regulatory compliance, maintaining research quality and supporting collaborative 
scientific work. While the Institute has made commendable progress, the Committee is 
of the view that further strengthening of the Research Wing is essential to enhance 
research productivity and promote innovation at par with global standards. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that AIIMS New Delhi expand and institutionalize 
multidisciplinary and cross-institutional research programmes, particularly in emerging 
areas such as artificial intelligence, big data analytics and personalized medicine. The

7.3.2 The Committee was informed that 22 new AIIMS have been set up under the Pradhan 
Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojna in various States and are in different stages of operation, 
which will considerably help in easing the patient load in AIIMS, New Delhi. 
 
7.3.3 The Committee notes with concern the disproportionately high patient load at 
the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi leading to 
congestion/long waiting time for patients not just inside the hospital but wobbling 
queues outside too. The OPD data for the period January to December 2024 reveals that 
a significant proportion of patients hailed from neighbouring and distant States viz. 
Delhi (39.72%), UP (23.45%), Haryana (13.29%), Bihar (12.64%), Uttrakhand (3.45%) 
and remaining from other States.  The Committee observes that such overwhelming 
reliance on AIIMS, New Delhi indicates not only the pre-eminent status of the Institute 
but also the lack of comparable facilities in other parts of the country. Such excessive 
concentration of patients in one institution has led to overburdened facilities, longer 
waiting times and strains on both infrastructure and manpower, ultimately 
compromising the quality of patient care and academic training. 
 
7.3.4 Under the Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana (PMSSY), 22 new 
AIIMS, established in various States across the country are at different stages of 
operationalisation. The Committee understands that these institutions were envisioned 
precisely to reduce the patient load at AIIMS Delhi by providing high-quality tertiary 
care closer to the population in their respective regions. The Committee, in this 
connection, recommends that urgent steps be taken to strengthen the infrastructure, 
faculty, diagnostic facilities and overall patient care standards in all 22 new AIIMS so 
that the AIIMS like other Institutes  may emerge as credible and reliable alternatives to 
AIIMS, New Delhi. Additionally, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare should 
ensure time-bound recruitment of faculty and non-faculty staff, expedite the 
commissioning of super-specialty departments and provide adequate budgetary support 
for state-of-the-art diagnostic and treatment facilities in such institutes. The Committee 
desires that the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare should furnish the details of 
updated status of the operations of these 22 AIIMS to enable the Committee to obtain a 
real picture and to assess the time by when the problem of overcrowding in AIIMS, 
Delhi will be resolved.  The Committee also recommends for setting up of AIIMS like 
institution in each state, including Karnataka, as patients from all over the country 
cannot make access for treatment of diseases from far flung areas.  The Committee 
further recommends for strengthening of all AIIMS like institutions in the states, like 
Telangana and Andhra Pradesh to be strengthened, as well equipped and manpowered 
as AIIMS, New Delhi to seek treatment of diseases at par to reduce the dependency of 
patients on AIIMS, New Delhi and thus reducing the overcrowding. 
 
7.3.5 The Committee further recommends that effective referral mechanisms be 
developed in coordination with other AIIMS like institutions in various States, so that 
patients requiring tertiary care can be guided towards the nearest functional AIIMS 
rather than converging disproportionately on AIIMS, New Delhi. Public awareness 
campaigns should also be undertaken to build confidence in the quality of services being 
provided at these new AIIMS in various States.

7.4 STEPS TO ADDRESS OVERCROWDING AND LONG WAITING TIME  
 
7.4.1 Upon enquiring about the measures taken to address overcrowding and long waiting 
time, the Committee was informed that the appointment system at AIIMS, New Delhi permits 
patients to book appointments with a maximum waiting period of one month for new cases 
and three months for follow-up consultations. It was further stated that, in order to reduce 
waiting time, the Institute has expanded its facilities through the commissioning of new 
specialty centres and blocks such as the National Cancer Institute, the Surgical Block, the 
New RAK OPD Block, the Mother & Child Block and the National Centre for Ageing. These 
additions, inter alia, had contributed to a substantial increase in the number of OPD 
consultations. 
 
7.4.2 The Committee took into consideration the action taken by AIIMS, New Delhi to 
reduce overcrowding and long waiting times through the new specialty centres, the 
Online Registration System (ORS) and token-based walk-ins. The Committee 
appreciates the introduction of online appointments through the Online Registration 
System (ORS) portal, along with a token system designed to regulate walk-in patients on 
a first-come, first-served basis. The distribution of OPD slots as 50 per cent allocated for 
online appointments, 30 per cent reserved for walk-ins and the remaining 20 per cent 
earmarked for cross-referrals is a rational approach. However, the Committee is of the 
view that despite these measures, the demand for services at AIIMS continues to exceed 
its capacity. The Committee therefore recommends that AIIMS, New Delhi further 
strengthen its digital appointment management system by making it mobile-friendly, 
multilingual and integrated with centralized electronic medical records, real-time 
updates, automated reminders and referral linkages with other AIIMS and regional 
institutions. These measures, along with physical patient-support mechanisms, would 
streamline patient flow, reduce unnecessary congestion from routine follow-ups and 
ensure equitable access. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry of 
Health and Family Welfare replicate the ORS and token-based model across all AIIMS 
and major central hospitals for greater efficiency and transparency nationwide. 
 
7.4.3 The Committee also recommends that a structured two-way referral system be 
established between AIIMS institutions and other medical colleges in order to ensure 
effective distribution of patients across healthcare facilities. The Committee is of the 
considered view that the adoption of a hub-and-spoke model, linking Primary Health 
Centres (PHCs), Community Health Centres (CHCs), district hospitals, medical colleges 
and AIIMS institutions, would facilitate seamless integration of services across different 
levels of care. The Committee also strongly recommends that the Government should 
seriously consider setting up the ‘Hub and Spoke’ model to address the problem of 
overcrowding in the hospitals in metropolitan cities. Such a system would enable 
patients to be directed to the most appropriate facility based on the nature and severity 
of their medical needs, thereby enhancing efficiency, reducing overcrowding at apex 
centres and improving outcomes.  
 

 
47 
 
7.4.4 The Committee further recommends that the Ministry of Health and Family 
Welfare, in consultation with AIIMS, explore the possibility of establishment of satellite 
centres of AIIMS around Delhi for all time given treatment and emergency, particularly 
in four part of Delhi viz. East Delhi, West Delhi, North Delhi and South Delhi and other 
suitable locations in the National Capital Region with just 100 to 150 bedded centres 
with estimated cost of Rs. 150 crore to Rs. 200 crore and search centres may be called as 
AIIMS Satellite Centre.   The Committee thinks once these satellite centres are tagged 
with AIIMS, there would be a lot of public acceptability.  Since in Delhi, the travel 
radius is almost 50-60 KM there is also the need to have cardiology, neurology and 
trauma centres of AIIMS, New Delhi in different parts of Delhi/NCR viz. Gurugram, 
Sonipat, Baghpat, Faridabad, Ghaziabad/Noida or at other suitable location because 
time is a crucial factor in the treatment of the heart attack, brain stroke and road 
accidents where the medical treatment is to be given within the golden hour.  Resident 
doctors may be posted on rotation basis in these centres, functioning as extensions of 
AIIMS, New Delhi, could provide outpatient consultations, diagnostics and follow-up 
care, thereby decongesting the main campus and ensuring easier access to patients 
residing in surrounding regions. Such decentralisation would not only improve patient 
convenience & timely treatment but also allow AIIMS, New Delhi to focus its core 
capacity on complex tertiary care, research and advanced training. 
 
7.5 EXPANSION OF TELEMEDICINE SERVICES 
 
7.5.1 Responding to the Committee’s query about the approach of the Institute with regard 
to the adoption/expansion of telemedicine to address the issue of overcrowding and whether 
the telemedicine be seen as a viable alternative to in person consultation in the long run while 
providing the same level of care and quality provided to in-person consultation, AIIMS New 
Delhi management in their written submission, stated that Telemedicine can not be taken as 
the same level of care and quality as in-person consultation in any way. However, as far as 
AIIMS-like tertiary hospitals are concerned, this facility should be provided for doctor-to-
doctor consultation for very complex cases, keeping in mind the telemedicine prescription 
guidelines by the National Medical Commission (NMC). In addition, AIIMS, trying to set up 
a system for chronic disease cases where the patient requires long-term follow-up from the 
same doctor/unit for specific diseases. However, during the course of the presentation on the 
subject, the Director, AIIMS stated that the Institute is utilizing telemedicine facilities as the 
institute wants that all the patient should not visit the institute, therefore, if the patient can 
have tele-consultation and skip the physical visit to the AIIMS. The AIIMS management 
encourages such patients who seek telemedicine services.

7.6.6 The Committee understands that AIIMS, New Delhi remains committed to

7.7 MECHANISM TO ADDRESS THE MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT 
REFERENCES 
 
7.7.1 AIIMS, New Delhi, notwithstanding the fact that the institute being pioneer in the 
healthcare delivery in the country, issues related to problems faced by the public while 
assessing and availing treatment in the institute, have cropped up time and again before the 
Chairman, and Members of the Committee on Health and Family Welfare during its 
meetings. As a whole not only the general public but even Hon’ble Members of Parliament 
usually have to face a lot of problems including long waiting time and other hurdles while 
willing to seek treatment at AIIMS. During the Committee’s meeting held on 13th May, 2025 
several members shared inconvenience faced by them while seeking one’s treatment or 
treatment of kith and kin or persons on their reference. The sorry state of the fact is that some 
members of the Committee pin-pointed that there are no takers of their calls and references

7.7.3 The Committee also recommends the AIIMS management to guide the staff 
deployed during night hours to take additional responsibility and care towards patient 
to ensure to access the institute in night hours and guide the patients responsibly and

Such guidelines should be implemented in letter and spirit.    
 
7.8 ALLIED SERVICES PROVIDED TO PATIENTS 
 
7.8.1 AIIMS has undertaken several initiatives to enhance patient care and support services 
across its campus. A key example is ASHRAY, a facility managed by retired CRPF 
personnel, where patients waiting outside AIIMS, New Delhi after 9 P.M. are escorted and 

 
53 
 
provided with food, shelter, hygienic toilets and drinking water. The next morning, they are

the large campus, AIIMS has installed multilingual signage, introduced accessible e-shuttle 
services with multiple pick-up and drop-off points and deployed trained Patient Care 
Coordinators along with sensitized security guards to assist patients. An intra-hospital 
navigation system is also being implemented to ensure easy access to care areas. Recognizing 
the challenges faced by patients and their attendants, the Institute has expanded sheltered 
waiting areas, particularly near the Masjid Moth Campus and created covered waiting halls. 
Affordable dormitory-style accommodations such as ‘Vishram Sadans’ have been developed.  
 
7.8.2 The Committee is pleased to note that as in terms of affordability of treatment, AIIMS 
has strengthened the supply of generic drugs through six AMRIT Pharmacy outlets and one 
Jan Aushadhi counter across the campus. All inpatients holding valid BPL cards, or certified 
as needy by their treating doctors, are provided with necessary medicines free of cost, even if 
these are not included in the regular hospital supply list. Patients covered under various 
Government schemes are also fully supported in this regard and the Institute is actively 
evaluating the list of essential drugs to be provided free of cost to all inpatients. 
 
7.8.3 The Committee appreciates the comprehensive patient support systems 
introduced by AIIMS, including the establishment of ASHRAY, patient-friendly 
navigation initiatives, expansion of sheltered waiting areas, provision of affordable 
accommodations and strengthening availability of affordable drug. These measures 
reflect a patient-centric approach and have significantly enhanced accessibility, comfort 
and equity in care delivery. The Committee, at the same time, underscores the need for 
further strengthening patient guidance and navigation within the campus, particularly 
for patients referred to various specialties/faculties/departments. 
 
7.8.4 The Committee understands that night shelter ashrams have been arranged for 
stay of patients during the night, however, there is urgent need to enhance the capacity 
of such night shelter as many of the patients does not get the shelter for the night stay. 
Therefore, the Committee strongly recommends that AIIMS, New Delhi management 
should seek the capacity of night shelter enlarged under Corporate Social Responsibility 
from all possible PSUs viz.  BEL, NTPC, SAIL, REC, GAIL etc.   
 
7.8.5 The Committee further recommends the establishment of multiple dedicated 
Help Desks strategically located across the campus. All such Help Desks should be 
manned by trained staff and linked with Patient Care Coordinators who can personally 
escort patients from one specialty or department to another, ensuring that no patient or 
attendant is left confused or disoriented in accessing critical services, especially during 
night hours.  
 
7.8.6 The Committee also recommends continuous monitoring of existing 
mechanism/systems to ensure timely assistance, integration of digital navigation tools 
with physical guidance and adequate staffing to meet the high patient volume. Such 
measures will not only enhance the overall patient experience but also reduce delays in 

 
54 
 
accessing consultations and treatments, thereby reinforcing its role as a model of

7.10 WAITING TIME FOR TEST AND INVESTIGATIONS  
 
7.10.1 AIIMS, New Delhi manages an extraordinary diagnostic load on a daily basis, with 
more than 3,000 radiology procedures and over two lakh laboratory tests being carried out. In 
keeping with its mandate of providing affordable healthcare, all investigations and laboratory 
tests up to ₹300 are offered free of cost to patients. It was, however, informed that the sheer 
volume of demand often leads to long waiting times for tests and investigations, posing 
challenges to timely diagnosis and treatment. 
 
7.10.2 Taking into account an extraordinary investigation and laboratory loads on 
AIIMS, New Delhi on a daily basis (3000 Radiology procedure and over 2 Lakh 
laboratory tests), the Committee recommends that AIIMS, New Delhi, in collaboration 
with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, take immediate steps to reduce the 
pressure on its diagnostic services. In this regard, the feasibility and practicality of 
decentralization of laboratory and diagnostic services by strengthening such services at 
regional and district hospitals to manage routine and high-volume investigations closer 
to patients’ homes may be explored.  
 
7.10.3 The Committee further recommends that the Government should consider 
adopting a Public–Private Partnership (PPP) model by empanelling and compensating 
accredited private hospitals and diagnostic facilities at fixed standard rates. The 
Committee is of the view that such a system would allow insured patients, whether 
under public or private insurance, to access diagnostic services at private centres 
without additional financial burden.  
 
7.10.4 Keeping in view the submission of the Director AIIMS that two lakh tests are 
being done per day in AIIMS, New Delhi, the Committee would like to be apprised of 
the types of tests conducted frequently and the percentage & the frequency of tests done 
free under Rs. 300.00. The Committee would further like to know the percentage & the 
frequency of cancer markers, immunohistochemistry, flow cytometry tests being done in 
AIIMS

7.12 WAITING TIME OF SURGICAL PROCEDURES (OT details verbatim + 
background note) 
 
7.12.1 AIIMS, New Delhi manages one of the highest surgical and procedural workloads in 
the country and the scale of demand is reflected in the waiting times across departments. 
Emergency, life-threatening, and research-related cases are attended to without delay, but 
elective and non-urgent procedures often involve significant waiting periods. In some 
specialties, these ranges from a few weeks to several months, while in complex disciplines 
such as neurosurgery, the waiting period may extend up to five years. Burns and Plastic 
Surgery, Gastrointestinal Surgery, ENT, Ophthalmology, Paediatric Surgery and Obstetrics & 
Gynaecology, in particular, report long waiting time for routine and elective cases, 
underscoring the pressure on existing infrastructure.  
 
7.12.2 To address this challenge, AIIMS has initiated several steps. A comprehensive master 
plan is being implemented to expand bed capacity and strengthen inpatient facilities, with a 
special focus on augmenting high-dependency units required for post-operative care. 
Diagnostic services such as CT scan, MRI and laboratory investigations have been made 
functional round-the-clock to facilitate quicker pre and post-surgical assessments. The 
Institute has also increased the number of recovery rooms, while developing post-operative 
step-down units to ensure smoother patient transitions and reduce pressure on intensive care 
beds. Alongside this, greater efficiency in operation theatre utilization through pre-procedure 
planning and case selection is helping to improve patient turnover and reduce surgical 
backlogs. 
 
7.12.3 The Committee has been given to understand about the highest surgical and 
procedural workloads on AIIMS, New Delhi and the scale of demand is reflected in the 

 
56 
 
waiting time across department ranging from a few weeks to several months viz. 
Neurosurgery waiting time extends upto 5 years and Burns and Plastic Surgery, 
Gastrointestinal Surgery, ENT, Ophthalmology, Paediatric Surgery and Obstetrics & 
Gynaecology, in particular, report long waiting time for routine and elective cases, 
underscoring the pressure on existing infrastructure. The Committee is of the view that 
in order to reduce the waiting time of laboratory investigation there is urgent need for 
further strengthening the Diagnostic services by adding more MRIs and CTs under PPP 
Model.  Now a days super speciality hospitals have a lot of tele-radiology systems that 
can be replicated at least for laboratory investigations. 
 
7.12.4 The Committee is of the view that the Government should decentralize the Lab 
services into regional district hospitals and even compensating private hospitals to carry 
out test at a fixed rate by the Government and using PPP model wherein the insurance 
patients, both under public insurance as well as private insurance can use private 
diagnostic facilities at standard rates. 
 
7.12.5 The Committee also understands the need for strengthening the peripheral 
AIIMS in each states, District Hospitals and State Hospitals besides strengthening the 
infrastructure at Taluk, District, medical college level in all states for accessible and 
affordable treatment not only to combat the problem of overcrowding in AIIMS, New 
Delhi but also for providing protected time of 25% of its work activities to premiere 
institutions for genuine and high research work at the global scale. 
 
7.12.6 The Committee understands that in order to address the mounting surgical 
backlogs and prolonged waiting times at AIIMS, New Delhi a dual strategy should be 
adopted. On the one hand, AIIMS should continue to expand its own capacity through 
timely completion of the Master Plan, augmentation of high-dependency units, 
strengthening of post-operative and step-down facilities and further optimization of 
operation theatre utilization. On the other hand, a decentralization strategy should be 
pursued wherein elective and non-critical procedures are systematically forwarded or 
referred to other AIIMS, Government hospitals and regional tertiary care centres, 
thereby reducing the disproportionate load on AIIMS, New Delhi. 
 
7.12.7 The Committee further recommends exploring partnerships with accredited 
private hospitals under a Public–Private Partnership (PPP) framework, where elective 
and non-critical procedures can be carried out at standardized government-notified 
rates, with provisions for reimbursement under public health insurance schemes and 
recognition of private insurance coverage. The measures so suggested would not only 
decongest AIIMS but also bring specialized surgical care closer to patients’ homes, 
reducing travel, cost and delays. In addition, AIIMS should develop a centralized digital 
referral and scheduling system linked with other AIIMS and empanelled hospitals, 
enabling patients to be allocated slots based on urgency and availability across the 
network. Such integrated & holistic approach would ensure timely access to care, 
greater efficiency in utilization of national healthcare infrastructure, and improved 
patient satisfaction.

7.14 NEONATAL INTENSIVE CARE FACILITIES 
 
7.14.1 AIIMS, New Delhi, presently operates a Level 3–4 Neonatal Intensive Care Unit 
(NICU) with a capacity of 30 beds. This unit is dedicated exclusively to inborn neonates and 

 
58 
 
caters to approximately 2,800 newborns annually. The NICU primarily serves neonates 
delivered to high-risk mothers referred from across the country, thereby functioning as a 
national referral centre for complex prenatal and neonatal cases. 
 
7.14.2 The NICU at AIIMS is equipped with world-class neonatal infrastructure, including 
hybrid incubators, advanced ventilator support systems such as high-frequency ventilators, 
point-of-care ultrasound facilities, therapeutic hypothermia devices and inhaled nitric oxide 
systems. Through multidisciplinary collaboration with other departments and specialties, the 
NICU provides comprehensive and specialized care to critically ill newborns, achieving 
commendable outcomes in neonatal survival and recovery. The NICU team comprises five 
faculty members, twelve DM residents, seven junior residents and seventy nursing officers. 
All deliveries are attended by resident doctors, ensuring round-the-clock specialized 
supervision. The Obstetric Perinatal Care services attached to the NICU unit include facilities 
for antenatal diagnosis, fetal monitoring and fetal intervention. Additionally, two dedicated 
follow-up clinics function under the unit, one for high-risk neonates and another for normal 
infants, to ensure continuous postnatal care and developmental monitoring. The 
multidisciplinary team providing continuum of care includes neonatologists, physiotherapists, 
clinical psychologists and audiologists, working in close collaboration with departments such 
as Pediatric Neurology, ENT, Orthopaedics and Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation. 
 
7.14.3 At present, the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) is exclusively dedicated to the 
care of inborn neonates. Due to the high risk of sepsis and cross-infection, the admission of 
outborn sick babies, those delivered outside the Institute, is not feasible within the existing 
NICU facility. Consequently, such neonates are currently managed in other hospital areas, 
including the general pediatric wards and the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit, depending on the 
severity of their condition. Recognizing the significant and growing need for specialized care 
for outborn neonates, AIIMS has initiated the process of establishing a Outborn NICU which 
will be implemented in two phases. Phase I, comprising four beds, is expected to be 
operational within twelve to eighteen months, while Phase II will expand the facility to its full 
capacity of thirteen beds over the next two to four years, contingent upon the recruitment of 
additional faculty members, residents, and nursing personnel. 
 
7.14.4 The Committee appreciates that Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) at AIIMS, 
possesses world class Neonatal Infrastructure and through multidisciplinary 
collaboration with other departments and specialties, the NICU provides comprehensive 
and specialized care to critically ill newborns, achieving commendable outcomes in 
neonatal survival and recovery. The Committee, however, observes that the current 
NICU infrastructure is limited to the care of inborn neonates and out-born neonates are 
presently managed in other hospital areas, including paediatric wards and the 
Paediatric Intensive Care Unit, which are not specifically designed for neonatal 
intensive care. The Committee also takes note of the initiative undertaken by AIIMS to 
establish a separate Outborn Neonatal Intensive Care Unit in two phases to address this 
gap. The Committee has been given to understand that Phase-I, comprising four beds 
would be operational within 12 to 18 month while Phase-II, expanding the facility to its 
full capacity of 13 beds over the next two to four years.  

 
59 
 
 
7.14.5 In view of the growing demand for specialized neonatal care, the Committee 
recommends that AIIMS, New Delhi, expedite the establishment of the proposed 
Outborn Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) and ensure that both phases of 
implementation are completed within the stipulated timeframe.  The Committee 
strongly recommends for enhancement in the Neo-natal facility to at least 50 more beds 
keeping in view the vast number of patients requiring Neo-natal care. 
 
7.14.6 The Committee has come across that a lot of money is shelled out by poor on 
Neonatal Care as new born, say, of 20 days old or 60 days old are admitted in a private 
hospital and the bill for the treatment ranges to the tune of Rs. 15 lakh or even Rs. 20 
lakh, therefore, Neonatal care is as important as Cardiology, Neurology and Trauma.  
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Institute needs to strengthen the 
Neonatal Care by making adequate provision for trained manpower, infrastructure and 
infection-control measures to ensure the safe and effective functioning of the Neonatal 
Care Unit at affordable cost.   
 
7.14.7  The Committee observes that newborn health interventions in the country are 
presently implemented under the broader framework of the National Health Mission 
through facilities such as Sick Newborn Care Units (SNCUs) and Newborn Stabilization 
Units (NBSUs), and that there is no standalone national programme or dedicated 
Centres of Excellence in the field of Neonatology. Considering the increasing 
importance of specialised neonatal care in reducing infant mortality and addressing 
complications related to premature births, congenital disorders and high-risk deliveries, 
the Committee is of the considered view that focused institutional strengthening in this 
domain is the need of the hour. The Committee also notes that neonatal mortality can be 
significantly reduced by strengthening the capacity of local doctors, nurses and frontline 
health workers through targeted training in essential newborn care, neonatal 
resuscitation, early identification of complications and timely referral. Continuous skill 
development of healthcare providers, particularly at peripheral health facilities, would 
ensure prompt and effective management of neonatal conditions and improve survival 
and quality of newborn care. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the AIIMS 
should examine the feasibility of developing a more structured approach for 
strengthening neonatal care services which can be a bench mark for other regional 
AIIMS alongwith other tertiary care centres to adopt. The Committee recommends for 
a collaborative approach with institutions which have a long proven legacy of providing 
neonatal care like the KEM Hospital Parel, Mumbai so as to device a affordable 
protocol for neo natal care on a population scale.

7.15.1 The Committee was apprised that AIIMS, New Delhi has instituted a robust and 
technology-driven grievance redressal mechanism to ensure accountability, transparency and 
patient satisfaction. A dedicated Grievance Cell is operational within the Institute, allowing 
for complaints to be submitted directly to the administration through multiple channels,

including email. The said multiple channels for registering and resolution of grievances has

7.15.2 In a major advancement, AIIMS has developed and introduced the Santusht Portal, an 
in-house IT initiative designed to empower patients with real-time grievance redressal with 
the objective to transform Patient Care by ensuring immediate reporting and action on issues, 
involving all levels of Hospital Staff, and significantly enhancing patient satisfaction and 
hospital stay experience. The distinct aspects of patients experience inter-alia include 
Culturally Appropriate Care, Care Coordination, Courtesy and Respect, Access to Care, 
Communication with Clinicians, Getting Information, Shared Decision Making and Self 
Management Support. The objective of the SANTUSHT Portal is to empower patient by 
offering them a voice, fosters transparency, trust & accountability and enhances overall 
service quality. Under this system, QR codes have been installed in key areas such as 
washrooms, enabling patients to instantly register complaints through text, audio, or video 
formats. Importantly, grievances registered on the portal remain open in the system until the 
complainant confirms that the issue has been satisfactorily resolved, thereby ensuring that 
patient feedback is central to the closure of complaints. 
 
7.15.3 The pilot implementation of the Santusht Portal at the Mother & Child Block has 
yielded positive outcomes, with the Institute now also using the system to capture patient 
satisfaction ratings. The SANTUSHT Pilot Project is QR code-based grievance redressal 
mechanism, Available 24X7 web-based service to inpatient of AIIMS, End-to-end closure of 
all grievances with real-time tracking, OTP-based login using mobile number, Two-way 
communication between patient and the AIIMS officials, automatic escalations to 2nd and 3rd 
levels. This includes feedback on waiting times, cleanliness, quality of food, communication 
by doctors, nursing services and the behaviour of support staff such as security personnel. 
The star-rating mechanism provides a structured way to measure and monitor patient 
experience, while reinforcing the Institute’s commitment to dignity and courtesy in care 
delivery.

7.15.6 The Committee appreciates the patient-centric initiatives undertaken by AIIMS,

nationwide. 
 
7.15.7 The Committee is also of the view that while institutional mechanisms are 
necessary, feedback collection must also be supplemented by an independent system to 
ensure credibility and transparency. The Committee, therefore, recommends AIIMS to 
explore the feasibility of engaging a reputed third-party agency to conduct regular 
patient satisfaction surveys and capture unbiased feedback on key parameters such as 
cleanliness, quality of food, waiting times, communication with doctors, nursing care 
and overall patient comfort. Such approach/initiative would ensure that patients feel 
free to share their honest experiences without fear of reprisal, thereby providing the 
administration with actionable insights for service improvement. 
 
7.15.8 The Committee observes that AIIMS, New Delhi has redefined the benchmarks 
of public healthcare delivery in India, functioning under extraordinary pressure while 
sustaining high-quality care. The unparalleled volume and complexity of work handled 
by the Institute underscores its role as the foremost national centre of excellence in 
patient care, education and research and demonstrates its indispensable place in India’s 
healthcare ecosystem. The Committee, however, observes that the current 
infrastructure and manpower is under stress due to the ever increasing volume of 
patients. The Committee, therefore, recommends that urgent steps be taken to 
strengthen infrastructure, enhance manpower and expand capacity across clinical, 
diagnostic and research domains in view of the extraordinary patient load and the 
critical role of AIIMS. The measures so undertaken would ensure that the Institute 
continues to deliver high-quality, specialized care while also advancing its mandate in 
education and medical research. 
 
8.0 HUMAN RESOURCE 
 
8.1 Human Resource Policy and Management 
8.1.1 The Recruitment and Staffing policy mandates AIIMS to follow a merit bases recruit 
based system govern by the AIIMS Act, 1956. Faculty are appointed through transparent 
selection processes, involving the Standing Selection Committee. For non-Faculty position at 
AIIMS, Delhi, the recruitment and promotion processes are governed by the rules and 
guidelines laid down by the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT), Government of 
India that inter alia include provisions related to reservation, pay scale, promotion criteria and 
service condition ensuring uniformity and transparency across Central Government 
Institutions. Under Training and Development, a regular in-service training, CME 
programmes and skilled enhancement were conducting for clinical and non- clinical staff. 

 
63 
 
AIIMS promotes academic growth through fellowships, sabbaticals (up to 2 years at a stretch 
in India or abroad), and international collaborations. For Performance Evaluation, Staff 
performance is monitored through Annual Performance and Appraisal Reports (APARs) and 
Assessment Promotion Scheme (APS). Promotions and career Progression are linked to 
academic output, clinical service, and research contributions. 
 
8.1.2 As Retention and Welfare Measures, AIIMS provides housing, healthcare, pension 
benefits, and access to institutional facilities. However, residential accommodation for faculty 
and students needs to be increased. However, attrition remains a concern, especially due to 
increased workload and attractive proposition in the private Sector. Under Digital HR system, 
implementation of Bio-metric attendance, e-office modules, SAHAS, and HR dashboard has 
improved transparency and administrative efficiency.  
 
8.1.3 The Committee takes into account Human Resource Policy and Management of 
AIIMS and opines that the AIIMS Management would undertake concerted efforts and 
measures in appointment of Faculty through a transparent Selection Process as per the 
provisions of AIIMS Act, 1956. The Committee also desires that the Recruitment and 
promotion process of non-faculty must be clearly govern by rules and Regulations as 
laid down by the DoPT keeping in view the Reservation policy, Pay Scales and service 
conditions. 
 
8.1.4 The Committee came across high rate of attrition of doctors and personnel from 
other allied services in AIIMS, New Delhi due to low salary and necessary facilities vis-
a-vis renowned hospitals thereby increasing workload on the remaining workforce. The 
Committee was impressed that the Government has imposed a cap that the salary of 
DM, Cardiologist, Nephrologist or Endocrinologist etc. would not be higher than the 
Chief Secretary, therefore, these doctors do not stay in higher institutions and leave it 
immediately after doing their super specialization to join the private sector where a new 
Cardiologist are paid to the tune of Rs. 4 to 5 lakhs whereas the Government pays 
around one lakh as per the pay structure available in the country, if so, is the fact, the 
Committee wills to point out that if the salary of the Member of Parliament is lower 
than the Chief Secretary, therefore, why not the salary of doctor can be higher than the 
Chief Secretary. The Committee is of the opinion that lot of money and time is spent to 
become a DM so for their retention in AIIMS, New Delhi it is necessary to pay them 
higher salary and better facilities available to lead a satisfied and actualised life. The 
Committee, in this regard, is of the considered view that if the Government wills to run 
super-speciality centres in AIIMS, New Delhi or all over the Country the Government 
should remove the pay barrier cap and raise the pay scale of doctors for their assured 
retention, on the one hand and to develop and standardized tertiary healthcare centres. 
The Committee strongly believes that tertiary level healthcare institutions can do more 
quality work, more research work and would be more contributory from the futuristic 
point of view once the salary of doctors in super-specialised centres is enhanced and 
made comparable to healthcare institutions in the private sector. 
 
8.1.5 The Committee is of the view that since AIIMS, Delhi envisage itself as a centre 
of excellence in Medical Education in Research and in Patient care. Its HR Policy must 

 
64 
 
be aligned with its mission and vision i.e. in consonance with meritocratic recruitment 
supported academic integrity, training programme fostering clinical and Research 
Excellence and digital HR systems aiming at enhancing the governance and 
accountability. AIIMS management should chalk out specific course of action to fill up 
gaps in such alignment viz Low Faculty to Student ratio impacts the teaching and 
research mission, Limited career progression impacts motivation and innovation, 
Overburdened staff due to high patient load affects quality of care and academic output 
and More protected time needed for research or academics.

posts, but these are still pending approval, thereby exacerbating the shortage of skilled

necessary approvals, removing administrative bottlenecks and providing adequate 

 
67 
 
budgetary backing to conduct timely recruitment. The Committee further recommends 
that a system of biannual recruitment for nursing officers and an annual recruitment 
cycle for faculty and paramedical staff be institutionalised across all AIIMS institutions 
so as to prevent the recurrence of such large-scale vacancies in the future. The 
Committee also recommends the Ministry to explore conducting NORCET more 
frequently than twice a year to increase the strength of nurse staff.   
 
8.3.12 The Committee strongly recommends that a joint monitoring mechanism 
between AIIMS Delhi and the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare be established to 
periodically review recruitment progress, ensure accountability and project manpower 
requirements in consonance with the expansion plans of the Institute. The Committee 
emphasizes that addressing these shortages on an urgent basis is imperative to 
safeguard the academic excellence and healthcare standards of AIIMS Delhi. Any 
further delay in filling up these vacancies would, in the considered view of the

positions, as the lack of opportunities has resulted in stagnation and hampered career 
progression.

noted, has resulted in widespread stagnation, outdated recruitment norms and the absence of 
clear promotion pathways, which in turn undermines staff morale, weakens retention and 
adversely affects the overall efficiency of the Institute. 
 
8.4.4 The Committee, after careful consideration of the submissions by representatives 
of various associations on pressing human resource challenges, is deeply concerned 

 
68 
 
about the prolonged neglect of cadre review, last being conducted in 1992 leading to the

8.6 ABSORPTION/REGULARISATION OF PROJECT RESEARCH STAFF 
 
8.6.1 The Project Research Staff of AIIMS, New Delhi submitted a representation before 
the Committee seeking reconsideration of the Institute’s recent order (Ref No. 14/2022-Estt 
(RCT)), which rejected their request for absorption and regularization despite over 15 years 
of continuous service in various research projects. Having dedicated some of the most crucial 
and productive years of their professional lives to AIIMS, the staff emphasized that the 
decision contradicts both the Institute’s established policy and past practices. 
 
8.6.2 The project research staff submitted that since 1992, AIIMS has had a clear policy of 
absorbing research staff with 15 years of service into regular posts, subject to their 
qualifications, experience and availability of vacancies. Historically, over 164 project staff 
has been absorbed between 1992 and 2021 under this policy, in compliance with Supreme 
Court directives, High Court judgments and decisions of the AIIMS Governing Body. 
However, despite multiple committee recommendations since 2021, the current eligible batch 
of staff continues to await absorption. 
 
8.6.3 The rejection also contradicts the recommendations of various screening and 
recruitment committees, as well as the deliberations of the Governing Body. The 160th 
Governing Body meeting held on 13th December, 2023 specifically directed the constitution 
of a committee to examine the representations for absorption of project staff completing 15 
years of service. Following this, a committee was constituted in March 2024, which after due 
examination strongly recommended absorption of eligible project research staff.  
 
8.6.4 The representation also draws attention to the legal precedents that support their case. 
In V.L. Chandra vs. AIIMS (1990), the Hon’ble Supreme Court directed the absorption of 
project employees completing 15 years of service and emphasized the creation of a core 
research cadre to strengthen the Institute’s research output. Similar directions were reiterated 
by the Supreme Court in 2003 (SLP No. 19225/02) and by the Delhi High Court in AIIMS vs. 

 
70 
 
Om Prakash (2002). These judicial pronouncements, along with AIIMS’s own precedents and 
committee recommendations, clearly establish a binding framework for absorption. 
 
8.6.5 In light of these facts, the staffs have appealed for urgent reconsideration of their 
request for absorption and regularization, arguing that their long-standing service, proven 
expertise and judicially backed rights merit regularization. They are of the contention that 
denial of absorption not only undermines institutional policy but also risks demoralizing a 
trained and experienced workforce that has significantly contributed to AIIMS’s research 
legacy over decades. 
 
8.6.6 The Committee observes with concern that the Institute’s Order (Ref. No. 14/20-
Estt.(RCT) rejecting the absorption and regularisation of the eligible research staff 
despite 15 years of continuous service in various research projects is inconsistent with 
the established policy of AIIMS, past precedents and the recommendations of multiple 
Committees, as well as the directives of the Hon’ble Supreme Court and High Court. 
The Committee takes into account that between 1992 and 2021, over 164 project staff 
were absorbed under this very framework, thereby setting a clear institutional and legal 
precedent. The Committee concurs with the representation submitted by the Project 
Research Staff and recognizes their invaluable contribution to the Institute’s research 
ecosystem. Having devoted over 15 years of continuous service in diverse projects, these 
staff members represent a highly trained and experienced human resource that has 
been instrumental in sustaining and advancing the research output of AIIMS. 
 
8.6.7 The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that AIIMS urgently reconsider 
the case of absorption and regularization of all eligible Project Research Staff who have 
completed 15 years of service. Their integration into the regular workforce is not only a 
matter of justice and policy consistency but is also essential for strengthening the 
Institute’s research capacity and output by retaining skilled manpower already trained 
and specialized in the research ecosystem of the Institute. The Committee is of the 
considered view that a core research cadre be developed, in line with judicial directives, 
to ensure long-term continuity, stability and growth of the Institute’s research 
endeavours.

8.8 WORKING HOURS OF RESIDENTS 
 
8.8.1 The Committee was informed that AIIMS, New Delhi follows the Government of 
India Residency Scheme in regulating the working hours of its resident doctors. For Junior 
Residents, the scheme stipulates that continuous active duty should not normally exceed 12 
hours a day, with a weekly holiday permitted and on-call duty limited to 12 hours at a time. In 
general, Junior Residents are expected to work around 48 hours a week, without exceeding 12 
hours at a stretch, though the Medical Superintendent may adjust working hours depending 
on workload and availability of doctors. Similarly, for Senior Residents, active duty is not to 
exceed 12 hours at a time, with one weekly holiday allowed by rotation and on-call duty 
capped at 12 hours. The overall quantum of workload, however, continues to vary from 
department to department based on specific clinical demands. 
 
8.8.2 The Resident Doctors Association submitted before the Committee their views on 
duty related matters. They submitted that they have to put in excessive duty hours, with 
residents reportedly working up to 36 hours at a stretch, well beyond the limits envisaged 
under the Residency Scheme. The working hours, while reflective of service exigencies, 
nevertheless to adversely affects the physical and mental health, diminish academic 
performance and potentially compromise the quality of patient care. Therefore, the 
Committee emphasizes the need for a balanced and humane duty structure. The Association 
proposed the formulation of an institutional policy to regulate and cap consecutive duty 
hours, along with the introduction of a mechanism for voluntary extra-duty shifts with 
appropriate compensation. It was further highlighted that during examination and thesis 
submission periods, residents face acute difficulties in reconciling clinical responsibilities 
with academic obligations. To mitigate this, the Association recommended granting six 
months of preparatory leave before final examinations and instituting temporary recruitment 
of resident doctors to manage the clinical workload during such intervals. 
 

 
72 
 
8.8.3 The Committee takes into account the submission of the Resident Doctors 
Association and expresses concern that Residents Doctors have to put in excessive duty 
hours, sometimes working upto 36 hours at a stretch well beyond the limits envisaged 
under the residency scheme. The Committee is of considered view that such extended 
working hours, while reflective of service exigencies, nevertheless to adversely affects 
the physical and mental health, diminish academic performance and potentially 
compromise the quality of patient care. Therefore, the Committee emphasizes the need 
for a balanced and humane duty structure. The Committee recommends that AIIMS 
management should strictly enforce the provisions of the Government of India 
Residency Scheme to ensure that the duty hour for Junior and Senior Residents do not 
exceed the prescribed limits. An institutional policy should be framed to regulate and 
cap consecutive duty hours, with provision for voluntary extra-duty shifts against

place to balance clinical and academic responsibilities, particularly during examination

The Committee appreciates the role played by resident doctors in providing valuable 
fillip to the infrastructure constraints of regular doctors thus forming the backbone of 
healthcare. 
 
8.8.4 The Committee, in nutshell desires the AIIMS Management and the Department

9.0 SWOT ANALYSIS AND STRATEGIC MANAGEMENT OF AIIMS NEW 
DELHI 
 
Strength 
9.1.1 AIIMS New Delhi continues to hold a distinguished position as India’s premier 
medical institution, supported by a strong global reputation and high patient trust. Its 
clinical excellence is reflected in its ability to manage more than 14,000 outpatient cases 
daily, while offering advanced super-specialty care across disciplines. The Institute 
maintains rigorous academic standards through its MBBS, MD/MS and DM/MCh 
programmes, attracting the nation’s most competitive candidates. With an annual 
research output exceeding 3,000 publications, AIIMS has established itself as a leading 
centre for clinical and biomedical research. Its autonomous governance structure, 
backed by a dedicated Act of Parliament, provides the flexibility needed to innovate in 
both academic and clinical domains. 
 
Weakness 
9.1.2 Despite these strengths, the Institute faces several internal challenges. Staff 
shortages, resulting largely from long lead times between post sanctioning and 
candidate joining; affect the balance between teaching, research and patient care. The 
absence of a structured referral system contributes to chronic overload of outpatient 
services, placing considerable strain on existing infrastructure. AIIMS also has very less 
formal collaboration with top global institutions, which limits opportunities for 
international exposure and joint research. Much of the campus infrastructure, including 
patient care and residential buildings, is over six decades old, requiring continuous 
maintenance with limited options for retrofitting. 
 
Opportunities 
9.1.3 At the same time, AIIMS is presented with significant opportunities. Digital 
transformation offers a pathway to modernize diagnostics, telemedicine and e-
governance. The Institute is well positioned to align itself with global benchmarks set by 
institutions such as Harvard, Oxford, Tokyo University Hospital and Peking Union 
Medical College, strengthening its role as a leader in medical education and research in 
the Global South. 
 
Threats 
9.1.4 Externally, the Institute faces threats such as talent attrition, with skilled 
professionals seeking better remuneration and work-life balance abroad or in the 
private sector. Technological adoption, particularly in AI, robotics and digital health, 
has progressed slowly compared to global peers. Moreover, public expectations for free, 
high-quality care continue to rise, without proportional expansion in resources or 
manpower.

weaknesses and threat part of SWOT-Analysis so that AIIMS New Delhi must adopt a

series of strategic measures to address existing institutional weaknesses and mitigate 
emerging threats. The Committee, in this regard, recommends the Institute for fast-
track faculty recruitment by introducing streamlined hiring processes and offering 
competitive compensation packages, tenure-track positions, sabbaticals and research 
grants to attract and retain high-quality talent. The Committee feels that AIIMS should 
undertake reforms and operationalize a structured national referral framework to 
reduce OPD overload and ensure that the Institute primarily receives patients requiring 
advanced tertiary-level care. 
 
9.1.6 To enhance clinical efficiency and service delivery, the Committee recommends 
that AIIMS accelerate the integration of advanced technologies, including artificial 
intelligence, machine learning, data-science, robotic surgical systems and digital 
dashboards for patient flow and resource management. In order to capitalize on its 
strengths and emerging opportunities, the Committee desires that AIIMS strengthen its 
global collaborations by establishing Memoranda of Understanding with leading 
international universities for joint research, faculty exchanges and curriculum 
development.  
 
9.1.7 The Committee is of the firm opinion that adequacy of available fund at the nick 
of the time is indispensable for completion of undertaken construction and research 
projects without time and cost overruns. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
improving financial sustainability by budgetary allocation as per projected demand. 
Moreover, AIIMS should attract CSR contributions, philanthropic funding and other 
external resources to support infrastructure development and research innovation. The 
Committee desires that AIIMS establish interdisciplinary research hubs in key areas 
such as genomics, bioengineering and public health, and promote start-up incubation 
and translational innovation through the Centre for Medical Innovation and 
Entrepreneurship (CMIE). 
 
9.2 STRATEGIC MANAGEMENT 
 
9.2.1 Responding to the Committee’s query regarding the strategic management that can be 
adopted for having Always a Better Control (ABC) with requisite coordination for having 
overall professional working equilibrium and the organizational interventions required for 
achieving such cherished objectives, the Ministry responded as under:- 
(i) Implementation of a centralized dashboard for real-time tracking of patient flow, 
inventory, HR metrics, and financials. 
(ii) Use AI-driven analytics to forecast demand, optimize scheduling, and reduce 
bottlenecks. 
(iii) Linking of departmental performance to measureable outcomes : patient 
satisfaction, academic output, and operational efficiency. 
(iv) Use of digital triage tools to redirect non-tertiary cases to appropriate centres. 
(v) Training and skill development of mid-level managers and Department Heads in 
administration, strategic planning, and change management. 

 
75 
 
(vi) Regular monthly coordination meetings across departments to resolve operational 
conflicts and align priorities.  
9.2.2 The Committee is in agreement with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare 
in regard to the requisite steps to be taken for strategic management of AIIMS, New 
Delhi in order to have Always a Better Control (ABC). The Committee is of the 
considered view that the strategic management for a better managerial control requires 
digital command and control system, performance based accountability, referral system 
strengthening, therefore, AIIMS management must strive towards this direction. The 
Committee further recommends that certain organizational interventions viz. leadership 
development programme and professionally functioning Inter-departmental 
Coordination Committees must be evolved in order to achieve efficient working 
equilibrium.

into global best practices and identifies potential areas for strategic strengthening within

10.1.2 The Committee observes that while AIIMS New Delhi is distinguished by its 
exceptionally high clinical load, strong public health role and growing research 
footprint, institutions such as Harvard Medical School, Oxford Medical School, Tokyo 
University Hospital and Peking Union Medical College represent diverse models of 
advanced biomedical research, technologically driven healthcare and structured 
academic training. Such comparative assessment highlights the unique strengths of each 
institution and provides insight into areas where AIIMS may further align with global 
best practices to enhance its academic and clinical impact. 
 
10.1.3 The Committee takes into account that AIIMS New Delhi demonstrates 
exceptional clinical service delivery and emerging research capabilities, but requires 
further strengthening in areas such as research infrastructure, faculty-to-student ratios, 
simulation-based training and adoption of advanced medical technologies. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that AIIMS New Delhi undertake targeted reforms 
to align more closely with global best practices, particularly by expanding its research 
ecosystem, enhancing interdisciplinary collaboration and increasing protected time and 
funding for investigator-led research. The Committee further recommends for 
establishment of advanced and global standard simulation and innovation centers, 
similar to those in institutions like Harvard and Oxford, to modernize clinical training 
and improve competency-based education. 
 
10.1.4 The Committee is of the considered view that AIIMS, New Delhi must explore 
international academic partnerships and faculty exchange programmes to enhance 
global exposure for students and researchers. The Committee opines that strengthening 
digital health systems, integrating AI-driven diagnostic tools and adopting structured 
referral mechanisms would go a long way in additionally improving efficiency and 
patient outcomes. 
 
10.2 Best Practices and Strategic Imperatives for Strengthening AIIMS New Delhi 
 
10.2.1 The Committee highlights that the leading global medical institutions reveals 
several best practices that AIIMS New Delhi must consider adopting to enhance its 
clinical efficiency, academic output and research excellence. One of the foremost areas is 
the development of a structured national referral system. Institutions such as the 

 
77 
 
Oxford Medical Sciences Division in the United Kingdom and Tokyo University 
Hospital in Japan function within tiered healthcare systems that regulate patient flow 
and ensure that tertiary centers receive referrals only for complex cases. For AIIMS, 
implementing a similar framework would help reduce overwhelming OPD congestion, 
streamline case load and preserve the academic and research bandwidth essential to a 
premier teaching hospital. The Committee observes that AIIMS New Delhi stands at a 
critical juncture where adopting global best practices and strengthening institutional 
mechanisms can significantly enhance its clinical efficiency, academic excellence and 
research impact. In view of the comparative assessment with leading international 
institutions, the Committee recommends that AIIMS should develop and implement a 
structured national referral framework to manage patient load effectively and preserve 
the Institute’s academic and research capacity. 
 
10.2.2 The Committee wills to pin-point another key area that relates to faculty 
development and retention. Global institutions such as Harvard Medical School and 
Peking Union Medical College offer tenure tracks, well-defined research pathways, 
competitive remuneration packages and extensive opportunities for international 
collaboration. Keeping in view, the faculty vacancies at AIIMS reportedly around 30 
percent, introducing measures such as competitive service conditions, sabbatical 
provisions and research-linked incentives would significantly strengthen faculty 
retention and professional growth. The Committee recommends that faculty 
development and retention be accorded high priority, with measures such as 
competitive compensation, sabbatical provisions, tenure-linked pathways and research 
incentives to address existing vacancies and attract high-quality talent. The Committee 
also recommends AIIMS to expand technology-driven patient care, including wider 
adoption of AI-enabled diagnostics, digital health platforms, robotics and telemedicine 
systems. 
 
10.2.3 The Committee understands that AIIMS, New Delhi would also get benefitted by 
expanding technology-driven patient care, drawing from models at Tokyo University 
Hospital and Harvard, where artificial intelligence, robotics and telemedicine are 
integral to precision healthcare. The Committee is of the considered view that scaling up 
digital health platforms such as e-Sanjeevani and integrating AI tools for diagnostics, 
triage and medical decision support would go a long way in enhancing efficiency, reduce 
waiting times and improve clinical outcomes. 
 
10.2.4 The Committee takes into account that in the domain of medical education, 
several global institutions have moved towards simulation-based learning, with Oxford 
and Harvard operating advanced simulation laboratories to train students in clinical 
skills without risk to patients. Therefore, the Committee is of the firm opinion that 
AIIMS could substantially enhance its skill-based training by investing in high-fidelity 
simulation centers and virtual reality–based learning environments. In the sphere of 
medical education, the Committee recommends that AIIMS establish advanced 
simulation and virtual reality–based training centers, similar to those in leading global 
institutions, to strengthen skill-based learning. 
 

 
78 
 
10.2.5 The Committee firmly believes that a stronger interdisciplinary research 
ecosystem is concomitant to forward looking advanced, modern and scientific pattern of 
delivering healthcare at affordable cost. Institutions like Stanford and Harvard have 
pioneered cross-disciplinary labs that integrate bioengineering, data science, and 
medicine to drive translational research. AIIMS can adopt a similar approach by 
fostering collaborations across departments and partnering with institutions such as 
IITs, IISc and other national research centers. To enable these advancements, 
administrative and financial support will be critical. The Committee advises for 
fostering interdisciplinary research ecosystems and strengthening collaborations with 
institutions such as IITs, IISc and global universities to promote innovation in-depth 
research and research collaboration. 
 
10.2.6 The Committee is of the opinion that the Governance reforms, including 
leadership development programmes for senior positions and the introduction of Key 
Performance Indicators (KPIs) for academic, clinical and research excellence, can 
promote greater accountability and strategic focus. Therefore, the Committee 
recommends that the AIIMS Management should leave no stone unturned in making 
concerted efforts in this direction in order to achieve the cherished goal.  
 
10.2.7 The Committee is of the view that the infrastructure investment is required to 
expand residential accommodations, enhance simulation and research facilities and 
upgrade digital systems for telemedicine and e-governance. Sustainable funding 
mechanisms, such as establishing endowment funds, attracting CSR or private-sector 
investments and increasing budgetary allocations for research and international 
exchange programmes, will further strengthen the Institute’s capacity. The Committee 
also recommends comprehensive administrative and financial enhancements, including 
leadership development programmes, introduction of clear Key Performance Indicators 
(KPIs), expanded infrastructure for accommodation and research, upgraded digital 
systems, establishment of endowment funds and greater engagement with CSR and 
private-sector partners.

11.2 Fellowship Programme in Super Speciality Courses 
 
11.2.1 The Committee has come across the findings of studies on the impact of 
workload on the lifespan of a modern day doctor whereby due to mental stress the 
lifespan has come down by 8 to 10 years. Unless, the strength of faculty is enhanced the 
workload will remain too much. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
Ministry may commence fellowship programme in super-speciality courses so that 
AIIMS, New Delhi can be in a position to have some additional faculty in Cardiology, 
Neurology, Nephrology, and Neo-natology, etc. The Committee believes that once the 
fellowship courses are started some candidates who are already post DM will join the 
course that would ultimately increase the faculty and thereby reduce the workload to 
some extent.  
 
11.3 Implementation of National Rare Disease Policy 
 
11.3.1 The Committee has come across that AIIMS, New Delhi has been recognized as 
the Centre of Excellence for treatment of Rare Disease and, therefore, it is but natural 

 
81 
 
that AIIMS, New Delhi should implement the National Rare Disease Policy in letter and 
spirit. However, it is quite surprising that out of total number of patients suffering from 
Lysosomal Storage Disorder only 36 patients got the treatment, 42 patients are deprived 
of Enzyme Replacement Therapy (ERT) and five patients died waiting for the 
treatment. The Committee desires to know the number of patients who got approval for 
ERT treatment and the reasons for pending approval for the rest of the patients in 
AIIMS, New Delhi. The Committee recommends that LSDs patients must get immediate 
treatment in AIIMS, New Delhi. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry 
of Health and Family Welfare must monitor that AIIMS, New Delhi implement the 
National Rare Disease Policy without fail and also display SOPs in this regard.  
 
11.4 Mental Stress Management Session for Doctors and Allied Healthcare 
Practitioners 
 
11.4.1  The Committee is well aware that due to overcrowding of patients visiting 
from across the country for completely reliable and accurate treatment of various 
diseases, the doctors, allied healthcare practitioners and other staff of AIIMS, New 
Delhi remain constantly under severe mental stress, therefore, the Committee is of the 
considered view that there should be mental stress management session for the serving 
doctors and allied practitioners so that they found themselves fit to devote their mental 
focus towards treatment and palliative care of patient. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that Music Therapy for relieving their mental stress and opportunities for 
Yoga and Mediation may be arranged for doctors and allied professionals to keep them 
physically fit to take on the medical practices as per their assignment. The Committee 
believes so as nowadays mental stress is one of the reasons for most of the diseases, 
therefore, the mental strain and status of doctors and allied practitioners need to be 
taken care of and they should be given opportunity to participate in seminars, yoga-
sessions, meditation to get stress free and afresh.   
 
11.5 Exploring possibility for OPD in night 
 
11.5.1 The Committee came across a proposal from within for AIIMS, New Delhi 
management for exploring the possibility of opening OPD in the night in order to reduce 
the workload or overcrowding. An arrangement may be made for rotation of duties for 
deploying of doctors and allied practitioners on each day and night and the rest period 
for them be arranged on Monday if their turns comes on Sunday and the vice-versa. A 
plea has been taken into consideration that if aeroplane can fly day and night and train 
can run each day and night, there is no reason that OPD cannot be conducted likewise. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends D/o Health and Family Welfare and the AIIMS, 
New Delhi management to explore the possibility of conducting OPD round the clock for 
reducing overcrowding and enabling the patient to access healthcare without much 
hassles.

AIIMS, New Delhi, however, there is urgent need to improve the quality and cleanliness 
of dress provided to patients in OT during surgery and the surgical gowns that doctors, 
nurses wear during procedure. The Committee, in this regard, recommends the 
Ministry to issue direction to the AIIMS management to ensure that surgical gowns 
must be sterilized to maintain hygiene and protection against contaminants.    
 
11.6.2 The Committee takes into account with appreciation the submission of director 
AIIMS, New Delhi that AIIMS management have been put in a lot of efforts in regard to 
cleanliness in the waiting areas and washrooms and the institute is continuing to get the 
first prize for the cleanest hospital of the country under Kayakalpa. The Committee,
